💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials.
  • In a recent development, the discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa.
  • Sources indicate that the findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.

In a recent development, the discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a upcoming approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.

Sources indicate that the findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.

Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters.

One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.

Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.

It has been revealed that scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.

The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.

"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.

"You just have to prepare it in the right way.

"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.

Sources indicate that "One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.

"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality.".

Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin.

Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.

Sources indicate that physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.

The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.

In a recent development, under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.

According to recent reports, "It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself.".

Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.

The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light.

To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.

Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.

"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he remarked. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature.".

The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.

This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.

As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.

The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.

Recent findings suggest that "This gives us a completely upcoming tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," noted Dr. Nape.

Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications.

The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several notable optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.

Recent findings suggest that one particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.

The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.

Industry observers note that communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.

Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.

"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.

"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.

"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.

"This research could lay the foundations for a newly introduced generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.

These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.

A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed.

According to recent reports, for decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.

By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.

The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.

It has been revealed that "For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.

"And astonishingly, this newly introduced behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen.".

The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.

They are a button hidden behind a keyboard, a screen that breaks on a smaller display, a permission prompt nobody tested, or an install that fails on an older version of the system. You can catch many of these problems without owning a single test phone, as long as you set up your Windows PC properly and test with a initiative.

In a recent development, this guide covers how to prepare Windows, how to choose and configure an emulator, how to install and verify APK files with Android Debug Bridge (ADB), what a good test session checks, and where virtual devices stop being trustworthy. It includes a small Python helper that explains install failures and reads launch times from ADB output, with tests. Tool versions and menu names change, so confirm details against each vendor’s current documentation.

● Emulators find the large, repeatable problems fast. Use them for functional checks, layouts and install testing, and confirm hardware behavior on real devices.

● Prepare Windows first. Enable hardware virtualization and the Windows Hypervisor Platform, and check the result with the emulator’s own acceleration check.

Sources indicate that ● Match the virtual device to real users. Test the oldest and newest Android versions you support, a small screen and a modest memory profile.

● Learn ADB. It makes installs, data resets and evidence capture scriptable and repeatable.

In a recent development, ● Do not trust emulator performance numbers. Your PC is usually faster than your owners’ phones.

Sources indicate that testing on a desktop gives you speed and control that physical phones rarely match. A fresh install takes seconds. You can wipe app data, change the screen size, switch the Android version and try again without hunting for a charger. When a tester finds a bug, they can record the screen, copy the log and attach both to a report from the same machine.

It also opens testing to people who are not developers. Product managers, support staff, designers and content reviewers can open a build, follow a script and report what they see with a full-size screen, a keyboard and a mouse. That alone shortens the feedback loop on most teams.

It has been revealed that the tradeoff is realism, which this guide returns to later. For now, the point is that an emulator is the fastest way to find the large, obvious, repeatable problems, which is exactly what you want to clear out before involving real devices.

There are two broad families of tools, and they suit different work.

In a recent development, the first is the official Android Emulator that comes with Android Studio. It simulates hardware in detail, supports a wide range of device profiles and connects directly to debugging and profiling tools. It is the right choice when you are tracing a crash, profiling memory or testing against a specific system image. It is also heavier to install and configure.

Industry observers note that the second family is general-purpose emulators built for speed and convenience. A good android emulator such as LDPlayer installs quickly, runs on ordinary hardware, can open several instances side by side, and makes it easy to drop in an APK, map keyboard controls and record the screen. Other examples include BlueStacks and Genymotion, the latter aimed at developers and test automation. Many of these tools are designed first for gaming or for general app use, so check whether they expose the Android versions, system images and debugging features your testing needs.

Many teams use both: the official tools for debugging, and a lighter emulator for broad functional testing. When you compare options, ask a few practical questions:.

Preparing Windows Before You Install Anything.

Ten minutes of preparation prevents most early frustration.

It has been revealed that turn on hardware virtualization. Emulators run dramatically faster when virtualization is enabled in your BIOS or UEFI. The setting is usually called Intel Virtualization Technology (VT-x) or SVM Mode on AMD systems. If your emulator feels slow for no clear reason, check this first.

Recent findings suggest that enable the Windows Hypervisor Platform. The Android documentation recommends the Windows Hypervisor Platform (WHPX) for Windows acceleration, and notes that you can turn it on under “Turn Windows features on or off”, then restart. Its older Android Emulator hypervisor driver is being phased out, so check the current emulator acceleration guide for your setup. Also note that a hardware-accelerated emulator cannot run inside another virtual machine.

Verify it. The emulator includes a check that reports whether acceleration is usable:.

Update your graphics drivers. Android interfaces rely on graphics acceleration. Outdated drivers cause black screens, flickering and random crashes that testers wrongly blame on the app.

Check memory and storage. As a rule of thumb, 8 GB of RAM is workable for a single virtual device and 16 GB is more comfortable for several. Leave several gigabytes of free disk space, because every virtual device stores its own system image and data.

According to recent reports, close heavy background programs. Browsers with dozens of tabs and other virtual machines compete for the same resources and make performance results misleading.

According to recent reports, the default configuration is rarely the one your audience uses. Spend a few minutes matching it to reality.

Pick a screen size and density similar to a popular mid-range phone rather than a very large display, because layout problems tend to appear on smaller screens first. Assign a sensible number of CPU cores and memory, enough to be smooth but not so much that you hide performance problems your consumers on modest phones will feel.

Choose the Android version carefully. If your app supports several versions, test at least the oldest and the newest. Behavior changes significantly between releases, especially around permissions, notifications, background activity and gesture navigation. For example, Android 13 (API level 33) introduced a runtime notification permission, so a flow that works on an older version can silently differ on a newer one.

With the Android Emulator, you can list and start saved devices from the command line, which helps when you keep several profiles:.

According to recent reports, finally, confirm the network works by loading a web page in the virtual browser. A surprising number of reported app bugs turn out to be a virtual device with no connection.

An APK is the package file Android uses to install an app. Installing one on a virtual device is easy, but doing it carefully makes your results more reliable.

Recent findings suggest that use trusted files only. Take builds from your own team, your continuous integration system or the developer’s official release page. An APK from a random download site can be modified or carry malware, and testing it proves nothing about the real product.

Sources indicate that install it. Most emulators accept a dragged APK file or have an install option. If you use the command line, Android Debug Bridge (ADB) installs a package with a single command and is the better route when you want to automate repeated installs. These are the commands you will use most:.

adb devices                          # confirm the emulator is connected.

adb install -r app-debug.apk         # install, replacing an existing copy.

adb shell pm clear com.example.app   # wipe app data for a fresh start.

adb shell am start -W -n com.example.app/.MainActivity   # launch and print timing.

adb logcat -d > session.log          # save the log for a bug report.

adb exec-out screencap -p > shot.png # take a screenshot.

Know the common install failures. If the install fails, the message usually explains why. A package built for a newer Android version than your device runs is rejected, a build compiled only for a different processor architecture may not install or may crash on launch, and an enhancement signed with a different key than the installed version is refused, in which case you uninstall the old version first. The helper below turns raw ADB output into a one-line explanation and also reads the launch time that am start -W prints:.

"""Small helpers for reading adb output during APK testing.""".

"INSTALL_FAILED_OLDER_SDK": "The app needs a newer Android version than this device runs.",.

"INSTALL_FAILED_NO_MATCHING_ABIS": "The app has no native code for this device's CPU architecture.",.

"INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE": "Signed with a different key than the installed copy. Uninstall first.",.

In a recent development, "INSTALL_FAILED_VERSION_DOWNGRADE": "The installed copy has a higher version code. Uninstall first.",.

"INSTALL_FAILED_INSUFFICIENT_STORAGE": "The virtual device is out of storage. Wipe data or enlarge the disk.",.

def explain_install_failure(output: str) -> str:.

"""Turn raw adb install output into a one-line explanation.""".

m = re.search(r"(INSTALL_[A-Z_]+)", output).

return "Unknown failure. Read the full adb message.".

return f"{code}: " + INSTALL_HINTS.get(code, "No hint recorded for this code.").

def launch_time_ms(output: str):.

"""Read TotalTime from adb shell am start -W output, or None if the launch failed.""".

m = re.search(r"TotalTime:\s*(\d+)", output).

return int(m.group(1)) if m else None.

The tests feed it realistic ADB output, including a successful install, three common failures, an unknown code, a successful launch and a failed one:.

from adbtools import explain_install_failure, launch_time_ms.

assert explain_install_failure("Performing Streamed Install\nSuccess") == "Installed.".

older = "adb: failed to install app.apk: Failure [INSTALL_FAILED_OLDER_SDK]".

assert "newer Android" in explain_install_failure(older).

abi = "Failure [INSTALL_FAILED_NO_MATCHING_ABIS: Failed to extract native libraries, res=-113]".

assert "architecture" in explain_install_failure(abi).

sig = "Failure [INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE: Package com.example signatures do not match]".

assert "Uninstall first" in explain_install_failure(sig).

assert explain_install_failure("Failure [INSTALL_FAILED_SOMETHING_NEW]").endswith("No hint recorded for this code.").

assert explain_install_failure("error: device offline").startswith("Unknown failure").

good = "Starting: Intent { cmp=com.example/.MainActivity }\nStatus: ok\nActivity: com.example/.MainActivity\nTotalTime: 523\nWaitTime: 530\nComplete".

assert launch_time_ms(good) == 523.

assert launch_time_ms("Error type 3\nError: Activity class does not exist.") is None.

Understand split packages. Many modern apps ship as bundles made of several files instead of one APK. If you are given a bundle format, you may need a tool that installs all the parts together, or a universal APK generated for testing.

Test the right build. Debug builds and release builds do not always behave the same. Release builds often apply code shrinking and optimization that can break features that worked in debug. Before sign-off, run your main flows on a release build, not only the one developers use daily.

Wandering through an app and tapping things will find some problems. A structured pass finds far more. Work through these areas on each build.

According to recent reports, capture evidence as you go. A short screen recording with the exact steps, plus the saved log, is worth far more to a developer than a paragraph of description.

A very common mistake is testing everything on one virtual device and assuming the result applies everywhere. Android is a fragmented platform, and your audience is spread across many versions, screen sizes and memory limits.

Industry observers note that create a small set of profiles and rotate through them. A low-memory profile reveals how the app behaves on budget hardware. A small screen exposes cramped layouts. An older Android version reveals compatibility gaps. A different language and region setting reveals text-length problems, date and number formatting issues and right-to-left layout errors.

Because tools such as the Android Emulator and several third-party emulators let you keep multiple saved devices, you can keep these profiles ready and compare behavior across them. This is where testing on Windows becomes efficient, turning a long list of devices you would have to buy into a handful of saved configurations.

Being honest about the limits protects you from false confidence.

In a recent development, ● Hardware features. Camera quality, fingerprint sensors, Bluetooth accessories, NFC, precise GPS behavior and motion sensors are hard to reproduce faithfully. You can simulate basic values, but real hardware behaves differently.

Sources indicate that ● Real performance. Speed on an emulator depends on your PC. A strong computer can make an app feel faster than it will on a typical phone, so never use emulator results as proof of smooth performance for consumers.

According to recent reports, ● Manufacturer customizations. Phone makers modify Android with their own battery management, notification handling and interface layers. An app can work on a clean system and fail on one brand’s modified version, particularly around background tasks and push notifications.

● Real networks. A home network is stable. Mobile networks have weak signal, handoffs between towers and restrictions that an emulator will not recreate.

● Apps that block virtual devices. Some apps, particularly in banking, security and competitive gaming, detect virtual environments and refuse to run. That is a deliberate choice by the developer, and testers should respect it instead of attempting to bypass it.

The sensible approach is to let emulators handle the broad middle of your testing, then confirm anything involving hardware, payments or notifications on a few real devices before release. The script above also only interprets a handful of ADB messages, so it is a convenience for triage, not a replacement for reading the full output.

If you want something simple to adopt, use this sequence on every build.

Start with a clean virtual device matching a common phone.

Install the latest build and run a quick smoke test, a fast pass over the main features to confirm nothing is fundamentally broken.

Test the specific areas that changed in this version in more depth.

Repeat the most vital flows on a second profile with a different Android version and screen size.

Log every problem with exact steps, the build number, the device profile and a screenshot or recording.

Before release, verify camera, location, notifications and payments on at least one physical phone.

According to recent reports, write this down as a short checklist and share it. Consistent steps make results comparable between testers and between builds, which is how you notice regressions instead of rediscovering the same bugs.

Do I need Android Studio to test an APK on Windows? Not necessarily. Many emulators accept an APK directly, and ADB can be installed on its own as part of the Android platform tools. Android Studio becomes useful when you need to debug or profile.

Recent findings suggest that why is my emulator slow? The usual causes are virtualization or the Windows Hypervisor Platform being off, outdated graphics drivers, too little memory and heavy background programs. Run the acceleration check first.

Can an emulator replace a real test phone? No. It covers the broad middle of testing, but hardware, true performance, manufacturer behavior and real networks need a few physical devices.

Is it safe to install APKs from the internet? Only from trusted sources, such as your own team, your build system or an official release page. Files from random sites can be modified or carry malware.

Recent findings suggest that testing Android apps on Windows is practical, affordable and flexible when you treat the emulator as a tool with a clear purpose. It gives you fast installs, repeatable conditions and easy access to many device profiles, which makes it well suited to functional checks, layout reviews and APK testing. It does not replace real hardware for sensors, true performance and manufacturer-specific behavior, so keep a few physical devices for the final confirmation.

Industry observers note that prepare your PC, choose a tool that fits your workflow, configure devices that resemble real owners, follow a consistent checklist and vary your environments. Do that consistently and you will catch most problems long before they reach your users.

Did anything notable happen this week? Not that I can remember. The weather was quite rainy - will that do? I'm just being silly, of course. We've had - and I suppose are still having - an historic week in video games, as Grand Theft Auto 6 arrives. It's dominated everything and I fear it's going to dominate this article too. But a reminder: next week is our "Not-GTA Week", so we'll be making a concerted effort to talk about games, probably smaller games, that aren't Godzilla blockbusters.

Industry observers note that as you know, this is our regular feature where we say a bit about the games we've been playing this week. This week, rather a lot of us have been playing GTA 6, as you can imagine, and discovering various things about it. But not all of us. Connor, ever the contrarian, has been continuing his race to level 60 in World of Warcraft: Forever, and he's agonisingly close to getting there.

Industry observers note that but enough about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Do tell all! And don't forget we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your leisurely perusal, just in case you forgot what you were playing a year or a month or a week ago.

Industry observers note that it probably comes as no surprise that I'm - much like the rest of the world - playing GTA 6 right now. While I found Chapter 1 to be quite a slow start, and where I felt somewhat restricted, I've now started Chapter 2 and found myself enjoying stealing cars, jamming along to the radio, and simply exploring Leonida - and all the strange happenings that come with it. There's so much to see and do!

I'm looking forward to deviating from the main missions for a while to do a spot of bird-watching (I like birds a lot, alright) and seeing what other side activities Leonida has to offer outside of the criminal lifestyle at the core of things. I'm also trying to be the best partner possible to both Jason and Lucia, but I'm itching to cause a bit of trouble soon... Hurting NPCs comes with so much guilt this time around though!

According to recent reports, it's slow, it's awkward, it's weird, and it's hard. It's a perfect Eurogamer game, right? Right? GTA 6's in-game lampoon of Jonathan Blow, Hideo Kojima, Dan Pinchbeck and - weirdly - Mark Z. Danielewski is a wonderful bit of top-shelf pastiche. It goes to show just how much fun Rockstar had making GTA 6, and the freedom its dev team had to install as much depth and satire in just about every nook and cranny conceivable. Don't sleep on Tenebrae Lux, it's genuinely satisfying to complete.

Sources indicate that I'm not, historically, the biggest GTA fan - although I've absolutely got a soft spot for Vice City's sublime mood - so I wasn't quite as excited to play GTA 6 as some. But it took, oh I dunno, about 30 seconds before I was sold. This thing has style. And everything else a billion dollars and some incredible development talent gets you. And it's those because-we-can details that have, in my first few hours, left the biggest impression. I spent a good five minutes just marveling at Jason dance - specifically the way his little stationary wiggle (perfectly timed to the radio beat!) shifts seamlessly into a wiggle-strut when you hit the forward button.

I love the way the setting sun seems to shine just right through the clouds when the moment calls, and those perfect needle drops. And careening through the night - amid the driving rain and smear of taillights, Kylie classic Spinning Around booming on the radio and Jason rocking a recently acquired, slightly improbable hat - this extravagant, ridiculous thing had me completely transfixed. I'm genuinely, unexpectedly excited to see where it takes me next.

Sources indicate that assuming there's lots of Grand Theft Auto 6 in this article, I'll save you from my own early impressions of this week's blockbuster release. Instead, you get more tales from an MMO. It is what it is!

It has been revealed that I'm level 58 right now, pushing my way into the endgame dungeons. I've almost maxed all my professions, and am gradually getting gear that should serve me well when the raids are added next month.

But forget all that. I got a salt shaker! As a leatherworker, you can buy a salt shaker from engineers for a little bit of gold on the auction house. These are more important than you'd assume. With them you can make one refined deeprock salt every three days - a high-end crafting material. Rather than hoard these for fancy gear, I just sold 'em back to the auction house. They're current going for 50 gold a pop on my server, which is fantastic passive income.

This is important because I'm right now saving for an epic mount: a process that hit a major roadbump after I unlocked my secondary class specialisation for 50 gold, and then blew way more than that on unlocking all the available skills (that I likely won't use) from my druid trainer (for no good reason). I'm currently sitting on 232 gold as of writing. There's a long way to go to 1000, but hey, that's the game.

I can't imagine anyone changing the radio station when Drive by The Cars begins during that first moment of proper uninterrupted freedom. The buttons to do that might as well not even be there. If you did, we're completely different people.

I'm not very far in but my major impressions of GTA 6 so far are: the performances and their presentation are wonderful, the game controls a bit sludgily and feels like it's not quite in focus on PS5, and I really like DIY.

Let's take that middle one, that criticism: I'm sure this will lift as I get used to the game and how it moves, and how the characters work. It's also just a fact of life, so to speak, that it's going to struggle a bit on PS5 rather than PS5 Pro. And I'm nitpicking; on the whole, this thing is staggeringly technically impressive.

According to recent reports, the latter point, DIY: it's absurd how much detail Rockstar has put into you doing up your shack. I especially like how it's not boring. A deeper thought related to this, and to the rest of the game, is the fantasy of self-improvement GTA 6 delivers. In GTA 6, as in all GTA games I think, you can drastically alter your life's fortunes in mere moments. I set about doing up my shack in a way I could never do in real life given a week or a month, but here, I did it in moments. That appeals to me greatly.

Recent findings suggest that honourable mention to Star Wars: Galactic Racer which I finally played this week. Love the speed, love Biddy Blas, and also really gel with the Roguelike approach, whereby you take the game in 'runs' to see how far you can progress each time. Cracking game.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(This post was authored by hlky and Sayak).

Tooling for image generation datasets is well established, with img2dataset being a fundamental tool used for large scale dataset preparation, and complemented with various community guides, scripts and UIs that cover smaller scale initiatives.

Our ambition is to make tooling for video generation datasets equally established, by creating open video dataset scripts suited for small scale, and leveraging video2dataset for large scale use cases.

“If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants”.

Industry observers note that in this post, we provide an overview of the tooling we are developing to make it easy for the community to build their own datasets for fine-tuning video generation models. If you cannot wait to get started already, we welcome you to check out the codebase here.

Typically, video generation is conditioned on natural language text prompts such as: "A cat walks on the grass, realistic style". Then in a video, there are a number of qualitative aspects for controllability and filtering, like so:.

According to recent reports, video generation models are only as good as the data they are trained on. Therefore, these aspects become crucial when curating the datasets for training/fine-tuning.

Our 3 stage pipeline draws inspiration from works like Stable Video Diffusion, LTX-Video, and their data pipelines.

Like video2dataset we opt to use yt-dlp for downloading videos.

We create a script Video to Scenes to split long videos into short clips.

Industry observers note that florence-2 microsoft/Florence-2-large to run Florence-2 tasks , , and on extracted frames. This provides different captions, object recognition and OCR that can be used for filtering in various ways.

We can bring in any other captioner in this regard. We can also caption the entire video (e.g., with a model like Qwen2.5) as opposed to captioning individual frames.

It has been revealed that in the dataset for the model finetrainers/crush-smol-v0, we opted for captions from Qwen2VL and we filtered on pwatermark < 0.1 and aesthetic > 5.5. This highly restrictive filtering resulted in 47 videos out of 1493 total.

Let's review the example frames from pwatermark -.

Two with text have scores of 0.69 and 0.61.

The "toy car with a bunch of mice in it" scores 0.60 then 0.17 as the toy car is crushed.

All example frames were filtered by pwatermark < 0.1. pwatermark is effective at detecting text/watermarks however the score gives no indication whether it is a text overlay or a toy car's license plate. Our filtering required all scores to be below the threshold, an average across frames would be a more effective strategy for pwatermark with a threshold of around 0.2 - 0.3.

Let's review the example frames from aesthetic scores -.

The pink castle initially scores 5.5 then 4.44 as it is crushed.

The action figure scores lower at 4.99 dropping to 4.84 as it is crushed.

The shard of glass scores low at 4.04.

In our filtering we required all scores to be below the threshold, in this case using the aesthetic score from the first frame only would be a more effective strategy.

In a recent development, if we review finetrainers/crush-smol we can notice that many of the objects being crushed are round or rectangular and colorful which is similar to our findings in the example frames. Aesthetic scores can be useful yet have a bias that will potentially filter out good data when used with extreme thresholds like > 5.5. It may be more effective as a filter for bad content than good with a minimum threshold of around 4.25 - 4.5.

Here we provide some visual examples for each filter as well as the captions from Florence-2.

We have created various datasets with the tooling in an attempt to generate cool video effects, similar to the Pika Effects:.

Industry observers note that we then used these datasets to fine-tune the CogVideoX-5B model using finetrainers. Below is an example output from finetrainers/crush-smol-v0:.

Recent findings suggest that we hope this tooling gives you a headstart to create small and high-quality video datasets for your own custom applications. We will continue to add more useful filters to the repository, so, please keep an eye out. Your contributions are also more than welcome 🤗.

#127648. AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious

AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious

📅 14 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a upcoming study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).
  • According to recent reports, as artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading customers, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common.
  • New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a upcoming study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).

According to recent reports, as artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading customers, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?

New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.

How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness.

Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.

"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," indicates Longin.

"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural.".

To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.

It has been revealed that another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.

A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness.

Sources indicate that the experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.

According to recent reports, however, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.

The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.

"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical.".

Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.

Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI.

The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an key insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.

It has been revealed that awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.

According to recent reports, because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.

The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.

"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, intends, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important.".

What if Vampire Survivors met Grand Theft Auto 2? Maniac is a brilliant mash-up that dares to ask that question

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that what would you get if you combined the chaotic top-down action of old-school Grand Theft Auto 2 with the chaotic top-down action of Vampire Survivors?
  • Your goal is simple: survive for as long as you can or until the 20-minute clock hits zero.
  • Maniac's debt to GTA is clear, and its chaotic action is brilliantly realised as it channels the compelling rhythms of a Survivors-style roguelite, where randomness in items and level layout makes each run fresh as you strive to unlock fresh characters, progressing a little further each time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that what would you get if you combined the chaotic top-down action of old-school Grand Theft Auto 2 with the chaotic top-down action of Vampire Survivors? That's the question Soldat and King Arthur's Gold developer Transhuman asked when it started working on 2024's roguelite shooter Maniac. The result is a delight, yet Maniac remains frustratingly underappreciated.

Your goal is simple: survive for as long as you can or until the 20-minute clock hits zero. Throughout that time, your secondary objective is to create as much mayhem as possible - painting the road with the blood of your foes, slamming cars into buildings, performing drive-bys as you rampage across the procedurally-generated city. The more carnage you cause, the higher your Wanted level, until you're fending off police and the military.

Maniac's debt to GTA is clear, and its chaotic action is brilliantly realised as it channels the compelling rhythms of a Survivors-style roguelite, where randomness in items and level layout makes each run fresh as you strive to unlock fresh characters, progressing a little further each time. It's a relatively slight experience, as its £4 price tag reflects, featuring a single compact map, just six characters, and barely any permanent progression. But Maniac makes a spirited argument for a return to a simpler time when GTA was all about shooting cops, stealing cars, and indiscriminately murdering pedestrians rather than the 'everything' game it is today.

Maniac is also a game that feels like it's trying to make good on an idea many of us had when we first played GTA 1 & 2 all those years ago: what would a better-looking, more advanced version of that look like? And for developer Michał Marcinkowski, Maniac's genesis also harkens back to an earlier time. "When I was 12, I used to come back from school and play the demo of GTA 1," he tells me over email. "It was top-down and time-limited, and all I'd do was try to cause as much chaos as possible within the 20 minutes of the demo.".

And there's perhaps a hint of a 12-year-old's exuberance to Maniac. There's the bright colour palette and gleeful chaos of its physics-driven mechanics, the adrenaline rush its aggressive enemy AI creates, and its absurd roster of playable characters, which range from Little Girl to Hotdog Guy. "Each [character] is a bit of me and a bit of you," Marcinkowski explains. "We all have a drunk Santa in us. We all have a pathetic hot-dog-suit guy inside of us. Each character failed at something and is lashing out.".

Industry observers note that as each newly introduced Grand Theft Auto game pushes further into realism, the idea of recreating the rampages seen in classic GTA feels increasingly unpalatable, but Maniac's colourful cartoon aesthetic means it can get away with more. One Achievement, with a flourish of old-school bad-taste humour, challenges players to destroy five school buses using an airstrike ability called Santa's Little Helpers. And that level of irreverent, chaotic lunacy escalates the deeper into each session you get, particularly as your Wanted level climbs: if you antagonise law enforcement enough here, they eventually break out a game-ending nuke.

Industry observers note that "This comes back to being 12," Marcinkowski says. "Nukes are just cool. I wanted the game to end with a bang, and what's more maniacal and exaggerated than a nuke? So that idea was with me for more than 20 years.".

Core to Maniac's design is the ability to change from a Survivors-like auto-shooter to a standard shooter where you're able to control your aim. The latter option is, I think, the more fitting one, particularly given how much driving you do. If you squint, it almost feels like a GTA 2 clone. And while the Vampire Survivors inspirations are plentiful - including its now-standard three-option upgrade system - the GTA elements are clearly the more prevalent.

It has been revealed that it might not play exactly like a GTA game, but it certainly captures the series' early days spirit. And Marcinkowski states he's surprised more developers haven't tried to riff on GTA: "You'd expect the most popular game in the world to have hundreds of clones, but that's not the case." There may be a reason for that.

According to recent reports, as major as modern-day GTA is, clones are apparently much less popular. "When you look at the sales data, particularly of top-down GTA clones, they don't sell well", explains Marcinkowski. "I found that out way too late, and I thought Maniac wouldn't be a hit." His publisher was initially equally buoyant too. "But then they studied the market and stopped being so hyped. That's how it felt as we got close to release. The wishlist count wasn't very high.".

According to recent reports, "I was expecting 10,000 [copies sold]," Marcinkowski tells me. "I actually started making another game two months before Maniac came out because I thought I'd go broke." But then the game released, and early worries proved unfounded. It sold more than 100K copies, comfortably blowing past its maker's modest expectations, putting it in the top one percent of games released on Steam.

Sources indicate that it's a surprise success story built on the foundations of Marcinkowski's youth, and as we chat about GTA, he reveals he's less keen on Rockstar's modern games, which lack that classic gameplay drive. "I always liked the counter-culture side of GTA, which is why I put so much of it into Maniac," he elaborates. "GTA 6 seems to have become pop culture, so it's lost its appeal for me." Marcinkowski's heart, it seems, is old-school.

A new leak suggests that Samsung is preparing to copy the iPhone’s Dynamic Island feature in the not-too-distant future, to an extent that not many other Android brands have even done thus far.

Copying the Dynamic Island was briefly like a rite of passage for some Android brands, with many wasting almost no time in delivering their own version of the feature. Samsung is now preparing its own version of the Dynamic Island, and it seems this one has a bit more meat on its bones.

It has been revealed that samMobile on Twitter/X posted a video and two still images of what appears to be a Dynamic Island clone coming to Galaxy devices. It’s mentioned as potentially coming to the Galaxy S27 series (so, One UI 9.5) and being called “Moment Effects.” A portion of the software explicitly mentions integration with Google Sports, the leak claims, while it seems Samsung is using Live Notifications here, which already support a number of third-party apps.

The current implementation of live activities showing the "chip" in the top bar is honestly far from good.

It negates one of the major pros of Android over iOS: being able to see notification icons in the top bar.

As when the "chip" of the live activity is active/shown, all notification icons will get hidden, even if there's a ton of space left between the "chip" and the constraint of the front camera area - an implementation that makes no sense whatsoever.

I honestly can't fathom how could Google come out with such poor implementation.

I don't particularly like this one from Samsung, but it surely is 1000000 times better from a UX perspective.

The kicker from a UX perspective is that Samsung’s interpretation allows you to swipe between activities, similar to Apple, but the core premise is similar with the island showing around the selfie camera cutout.

According to recent reports, when this feature might surface does remain unclear, but a One UI 9.5 debut would make plenty of sense. That enhancement is in beta now and due to launch on the Galaxy S27 series early next year.

Sources indicate that what do you think of Samsung’s alleged Dynamic Island clone? Personally, I’m on board as long as it proves useful, and it seems to be on the right track compared to most other copycats.

#127645. From Chunks to Blocks: Accelerating Uploads and Downloads on the Hub

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

From Chunks to Blocks: Accelerating Uploads and Downloads on the Hub

📅 12 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Content-defined chunking (CDC) plays a central role in enabling deduplication within a Xet-backed repository.
  • If we focused solely on maximizing deduplication, the design would call for the smallest possible chunk size.
  • It has been revealed that on Hugging Face's Xet team, we're bringing CDC from theory to production to deliver faster uploads and downloads to AI builders (by a factor of 2-3x in some cases).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Content-defined chunking (CDC) plays a central role in enabling deduplication within a Xet-backed repository. The idea is straightforward: break each file’s data into chunks, store only unique ones, reap the benefits.

In practice, it's more complex. If we focused solely on maximizing deduplication, the design would call for the smallest possible chunk size. By doing that, we’d create significant overheads for the infrastructure and the builders on the Hub.

It has been revealed that on Hugging Face's Xet team, we're bringing CDC from theory to production to deliver faster uploads and downloads to AI builders (by a factor of 2-3x in some cases). Our guiding principle is simple: enable rapid experimentation and collaboration for teams building and iterating on models and datasets. This means focusing on more than just deduplication; we’re optimizing how data moves across the network, how it’s stored, and the entire development experience.

Imagine uploading a 200GB repository to the Hub. Today, there are a number of ways to do this, but all use a file-centric approach. To bring faster file transfers to the Hub, we've open-sourced xet-core and hf_xet, an integration with huggingface_hub which uses a chunk-based approach written in Rust.

Recent findings suggest that if you consider a 200GB repository with unique chunks, that's 3 million entries (at ~64KB per chunk) in the content-addressed store (CAS) backing all repositories. If a upcoming version of a model is uploaded or a branch in the repository is created with different data, more unique chunks are added, driving up the entries in the CAS.

With nearly 45PB across 2 million model, dataset, and space repositories on the Hub, a purely chunk-based approach could incur 690 billion chunks. Managing this volume of content using only chunks is simply not viable due to:.

In short, network requests balloon, databases struggle to manage the metadata, and the cost of orchestrating each chunk skyrockets all while you wait for your files to transfer.

These challenges lead to a key realization:.

Deduplication is a performance optimization, not the final goal.

The final goal is to improve the experience of builders iterating and collaborating on models and datasets. The system components from the client to the storage layer do not need to guarantee deduplication. Instead, they leverage deduplication as one tool among many to aid in this.

By loosening the deduplication constraint, we naturally arrive at a second design principle:.

Avoid communication or storage strategies that scale 1:1 with the number of chunks.

Recent findings suggest that what does this mean? We scale with aggregation.

Aggregation takes chunks and groups them, referencing them intelligently in ways that provide clever (and practical) benefits:.

Sources indicate that together, blocks and shards unlock significant benefits. However, when someone uploads a fresh file, how do we know if a chunk has been uploaded before so we can eliminate an unnecessary request? Performing a network query for every chunk is not scalable and goes against the “no 1:1” principle we mentioned above.

According to recent reports, the solution is key chunks which are a 0.1% subset of all chunks selected with a simple modulo condition based on the chunk hash. We provide a global index over these key chunks and the shards they are found in, so that when the chunk is queried, the related shard is returned to provide local deduplication. This allows us to leverage the principles of spatial locality. If a key chunk is referenced in a shard, it’s likely that other similar chunk references are available in the same shard. This further improves deduplication and reduces network and database requests.

Recent findings suggest that the Hub at the moment stores over 3.5PB of .gguf files, most of which are quantized versions of other models on the Hub. Quantized models represent an interesting opportunity for deduplication due to the nature of quantization where values are restricted to a smaller integer range and scaled. This restricts the range of values in the weight matrices, naturally leading to more repetition. Additionally, many repositories of quantized models store multiple different variants (e.g., Q4_K, Q3_K, Q5_K) with a great deal of overlap.

Sources indicate that A good example of this in practice is bartowski/gemma-2-9b-it-GGUF which contains 29 quantizations of google/gemma-2-9b-it totalling 191GB. To upload, we use hf_xet integrated with huggingface_hub to perform chunk-level deduplication locally then aggregate and store data at the block level.

Once uploaded, we can start to see some cool patterns! We’ve included a visualization that reveals the deduplication ratio for each block. The darker the block, the more frequently parts of it are referenced across model versions. If you go to the Space hosting this visualization, hovering over any heatmap cell highlights all references to the block in orange across all models while clicking on a cell will select all other files that share blocks:.

A single block of deduplication might only represent a few MB of savings, but as you can see there are many overlapping blocks! With this many blocks that quickly adds up. Instead of uploading 191GB, the Xet-backed version of the gemma-2-9b-it-GGUF repository stores 1515 unique blocks for a total of approximately 97GB to our test CAS environment (a savings of ~94GB).

Industry observers note that while the storage improvements are significant, the real benefit is what this means for contributors to the Hub. At 50MB/s, the deduplication optimizations amount to a four hour difference in upload time; a speedup of nearly 2x:.

Similarly, local chunk caching significantly speeds up downloads. If a file is changed or a new quantization is added that has significant overlap with the local chunk cache, you won’t have to re-download any chunks that are unchanged. This contrasts to the file-based approach where the entirety of the new or updated file must be downloaded.

It has been revealed that taken together, this demonstrates how local chunk-level deduplication paired with block-level aggregation dramatically streamlines not just storage, but developing on the Hub. By providing this level of efficiency in file transfers, AI builders can move faster, iterate quickly, and worry less about hitting infrastructure bottlenecks. For anyone pushing large files to the Hub (whether you're pushing a newly introduced model quantization or an updated version of a training set) this helps you shift focus to building and sharing, rather than waiting and troubleshooting.

Sources indicate that we’re fast at work, rolling out the first Xet-backed repositories in the coming weeks and months! As we do that, we will be releasing more updates to bring these speeds to every builder on the Hub to make file transfers feel invisible.

Follow us on the Hub to learn more about our progress!

Nice to see that Xet backed repos are being rolled out on the Hub.

How can we find the chunk content using chunk hash? The CAS system only stores "block_hash -> block_content", Where does the map of chunk to block?

what does the shards store? Is it "file_name, shard_id, chunk_hash, block_hash"?

How can we find the chunk content using chunk hash?

According to recent reports, chunk hash is calculated via content-defined chunking (CDC), which means that if two chunks have the same content they will share the same hash. CDC removes the need to store the mapping between chunk hash -> chunk content because we know if two chunks share the same hash, they will have identical content.

The CAS system only stores "block_hash -> block_content", Where does the map of chunk to block?

This is explained in the "key chunks" section in the blog post above. Essentially we only store a tiny subset of chunk -> block by leveraging spatial locality in the file. Trying to store every mapping of chunk -> block can get impractical very quickly.

According to recent reports, what does the shards store? Is it "file_name, shard_id, chunk_hash, block_hash".

You can think of the shards as storing mappings between file (identified via file hash) to list of chunks that make up the file.

I hope this help explains our underlying tech better!

Recent findings suggest that if we don't store every chunk hash to block hash, how can we download a model file. For example if a model does not have a key chunk, the shard info only contains "file hash -> list of chunks", the CAS only has "block hash -> block content", how can we know which block is needed ?

For example if a model does not have a key chunk.

Two points of clarification might be in order concerning the above point:.

If we don't store every chunk hash to block hash, how can we download a model file.

When downloading a model file, a request is made to our services with the file hash. This is mapped to a list of block subranges. Logically these are chunks, but by storing the offsets we save on the metadata storage and ultimately many offsets will share boundaries inside a block (allowing us to group them together in a response) providing benefits when sending the content back to the client.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • GTA 6 players who used the Fresh Zealand trick to play early on PS5 may have inadvertently purchased a censored version of the game that’s missing a useful stamina buff.
  • With GTA 6 launching at midnight local time on November 19, impatient fans around the world used the Upcoming Zealand trick to get a head start on their adventures in Leonida.
  • While Xbox players could simply change their console’s location, PS5 owners had to create a Upcoming Zealand PlayStation account and purchase GTA 6 through the country’s digital storefront.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 players who used the Fresh Zealand trick to play early on PS5 may have inadvertently purchased a censored version of the game that’s missing a useful stamina buff.

With GTA 6 launching at midnight local time on November 19, impatient fans around the world used the Upcoming Zealand trick to get a head start on their adventures in Leonida.

While Xbox players could simply change their console’s location, PS5 owners had to create a Upcoming Zealand PlayStation account and purchase GTA 6 through the country’s digital storefront.

Unfortunately, getting into Vice City a few hours early appears to have come with an unexpected drawback.

As reported by IGN, Rockstar left out the ability to consume cocaine from your inventory in the Australian version of GTA 6, with New Zealand reportedly receiving the same version.

Recent findings suggest that in the international release, players can collect baggies of cocaine or skim some off larger bricks. Consuming cocaine through the item wheel gives players a supercharged stamina bar for roughly 30 seconds.

Australia’s video game classification rules allow depictions of illicit drug use but prohibit players from receiving gameplay benefits for taking them, even in games rated R18+.

Interestingly, Fresh Zealand doesn’t have this same restriction, but testing by GTA BOOM found that the mechanic was also absent from its New Zealand playthroughs.

Players had already suspected GTA 6 was censored in certain regions before launch when dataminers discovered a roughly 700KB discrepancy in the Australian and Upcoming Zealand game files.

Unlike Xbox users who temporarily changed their console’s location, PS5 players who bought the Upcoming Zealand edition still own that regional copy even when playing on their regular account.

Sources indicate that luckily, those affected aren’t missing out on too much. Adrenaline can still be used to boost stamina and other stats, while scripted sequences involving cocaine remain intact.

Still, it’s a rather amusing twist that some of GTA 6‘s most impatient fans ended up with less content than those who waited a few extra hours.

Tech Report: I've never known a moment like this in video games

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1366 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was hard not to spend the first hour or so of Grand Theft Auto 6's launch day in a kind of stun-lock.
  • The analogy falls apart pretty rapidly when you think about it: the heroism of writing a little article about a video game aside, the frenzy of this week has been a joy, not a horror.
  • Industry observers note that it's worth taking a moment just to actually, properly take stock of all the headlines from the past couple of days in terms of the sheer breadth and scale of its launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was hard not to spend the first hour or so of Grand Theft Auto 6's launch day in a kind of stun-lock. As far as video games editorial goes - which is not that far, in fairness; prepare for an over-flattering analogy - the effect was roughly the equivalent of Tom Hanks' experience, as his John H. Miller first set foot on Omaha beach. Tweets and reels whistled overhead, news leads stung the ears, exploding search terms blew apart some poor guides team ally on one side, while upcoming discoveries in the early game - made by the millions and millions of launch-day players all picking it apart at once - appeared by surprise like some flanking ambush on the other.

The analogy falls apart pretty rapidly when you think about it: the heroism of writing a little article about a video game aside, the frenzy of this week has been a joy, not a horror. But the point is, I've been doing this job for over a decade now, paying attention to video games for another two beyond that, and I've truly never seen anything like this before. It has been totally overwhelming. And then I thought about that for a moment before realising that - duh - nobody has ever seen anything like this before. GTA 6 is the biggest entertainment release of all time, and it's not even remotely close.

Industry observers note that it's worth taking a moment just to actually, properly take stock of all the headlines from the past couple of days in terms of the sheer breadth and scale of its launch. Parent company Take Two confirmed yesterday that GTA 6 sold 32.5m copies before it came out. By the end of its first day on sale, it had made a record-obliterating $3.79bn. By contrast, the once record-breaking GTA 5 made a once astounding $800m in the same period; the "opening" period of the largest film of all time, Avengers: Endgame, made $1.22bn, and that's totalling box office receipts across its release day until the end of the first Sunday after it.

Recent findings suggest that it has set multiple records for streaming, per StreamCharts, with 214.63m hours watched in its first two days - significantly more than the previous biggest game, Valorant, achieved with 150m hours in its entire launch week. It's garnered more watch time in those two days than Elden Ring, Hogwarts Legacy, and Cyberpunk 2077 achieved with their entire launch weeks combined. Its concurrent viewers peak so far - 6.38 million people - is nearly four times the previous record of 1.74m, again formerly held by Valorant.

According to recent reports, it crashed Reddit. More than 2 million UK and US Xbox players used the 'Newly introduced Zealand trick' to play the game early, which is more than a third of that country's entire population. Internet exchange operator DE-CIX claimed its launch led to the highest amount of concurrent internet usage in history, at 33.03 terabits per second.

Recent findings suggest that on top of all those raw numbers, it's also just felt utterly inescapable. I can't open Instagram, TikTok, BlueSky or X without being blasted with memes, viral clips of early discoveries, reactions, hot takes, feeble attempts at brand piggybacks, slightly wayward early-game tips from opportunist streamers who haven't escaped the first chapter, or makeup tutorials for looking like Lucia. I can't open my inbox without scrolling through reams of tenuous PR pitches for stories with barely the faintest connection to the game. I can't open my phone without messages from parents, friends or peers. Even the mainstream news - heaven forbid! - has gradually clocked onto this whole video games thing, this unknown artifact from the imaginary world of "online", maybe being a bit important. Dozens of my colleagues have been inundated with last-minute call-ups to provide an expert soundbite (they're so desperate they even got me on at one point).

We'll have a lot more to say about this game in the coming days and weeks (with apologies to regulars who are already sick of it - counterprogramming starts this Monday!). It's the richest of texts, a near endless comedy clip generator, a total technical marvel and all the rest - you already know. But it felt worth it to just sit still for a moment, and take stock of what's happening here.

Sources indicate that this is the single biggest moment any piece of entertainment media has ever had. But more than that it's felt like a kind of party. The vibes in some corners are orgiastic, as streamers uncover spooky twists, outlandish reactivity, and easter eggs I'd never got close to in a hundred-odd hours with the thing - all of this pure dynamite for the audience. Given the budgets involved and the particularly unique blend of circumstances around it - the changing shape of video game funding; of how attention is monopolised; of how development may happen in the future and the sheer amount of time and subsequent anticipation built up since the previous entry - we will likely be waiting decades for another moment like it. If there's ever a moment like it again. Part of the sense of ecstasy going around comes, perhaps subconsciously, from the acknowledgment that in pure hype and attention terms, this might be as good as it ever gets.

For the briefest time, the world belongs to video games. Rockstar and Take-Two's executives and shareholders will no doubt reap the greatest rewards from all this - all part of the great irony that makes this game's central premise all the more interesting. But I sincerely hope its developers - especially the 34 fired by the company last year, now awaiting the outcome of their tribunal over alleged union-busting, and those who hope to form a union from the currently open vote - are able to feel a particular sense of pride.

Just as this launch has been unprecedented in its success, the last two or three years have been unprecedented in their grimness for video game workers across most of the world, certainly the once-dominat western part. If we're very lucky - and frankly, I have my doubts - this burst of attention and visible profitability might go some way to helping the industry claw its way back, perhaps via attracting, as a knock-on from all the new-found attention, some kind of more sustainable investment. If we're not, and this is really the last behemoth, the last video game monument of its kind, the last rave before the police come raiding at dawn, at least we've gone out with one hell of a bang.

Industry observers note that GTA 6 - again, it's been mentioned before now - is such a curious thing. A game of goofiness, self-awareness, prestige, pretentiousness, childish humour, astute commentary, ironic cultural criticism, surprising player expression and - above all of that - the most mind-boggling, brain-scrambling level of profoundly human craft. There's something kind of perfect about this.

Industry observers note that it's a good thing, actually, that video games' greatest export is also its most contradictory. Video games are contradictory things in themselves. If the non-specialist media might still occasionally slip into treating video games like some kind of object from outer space, then we might as well put forward the best possible candidate for a capsule. It's the same way you'd think about it if you had to stick one thing in a vacuum-sealed box, to send out into the universe in an attempt to symbolise humanity: something that summarises close to all of it; that we're proud of; and crucially, that captures the spirit of it too.

Industry observers note that there are many more that might've put a more respectable foot forward - certainly that have a less chequered history, or maybe a more sophisticated, nuanced, or inventive use of the form. But there's really no better video game for exemplifying the full, chaotic range of the medium. It seems right, when you think about it, for GTA to be the one out there sitting under the spotlight, in the biggest moment this silly, serious artform might ever have.
