People are taking an unapproved weight-loss drug. AI found something surprising

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1448 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that an experimental weight-loss drug that has not yet received regulatory approval is already attracting consumers willing to obtain unapproved versions online.
  • Sources indicate that the drug, retatrutide, belongs to a latest generation of GLP-1 medications designed to help regulate appetite and body weight.
  • Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania analyzed nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments from approximately 40,000 users to investigate these accounts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that an experimental weight-loss drug that has not yet received regulatory approval is already attracting consumers willing to obtain unapproved versions online. Now, scientists are using artificial intelligence to investigate their experiences, uncovering unexpected symptom reports that differ from those documented in clinical trials.

Sources indicate that the drug, retatrutide, belongs to a latest generation of GLP-1 medications designed to help regulate appetite and body weight. Although it remains under investigation and is not approved for use, people are purchasing unapproved formulations that are not intended for human consumption and discussing their experiences on internet forums.

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania analyzed nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments from approximately 40,000 users to investigate these accounts. Their study, published in JAMA Network Open, provides the first systematic examination of potential side effects reported by people claiming to use unapproved retatrutide.

According to recent reports, one finding stood out. Among users whose reported symptoms could be classified, increased appetite was the most common complaint. That was particularly unexpected because retatrutide is designed to suppress hunger, and its Phase 2 clinical trials primarily identified digestive problems as the most frequent side effects.

AI Uncovers Unexpected Weight-Loss Drug Reports.

According to recent reports, "Our goal is to identify hypotheses in online conversations that we could test. AI helps us find recurring patterns in people's self-reports, including experiences that may be missed by conventional drug-safety monitoring," says Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Research Associate Professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS), Director of Penn's Computational Social Listening Lab and senior author of the study.

However, the researchers emphasize that the findings should not be interpreted as proof of previously unknown side effects. Reddit owners represent a very different population from clinical trial participants, and their accounts cannot establish whether the drug caused the symptoms they described.

According to recent reports, there is also considerable uncertainty about what these individuals are actually taking. Products sold outside regulated medical channels may differ from the genuine experimental medication in their ingredients, purity, and dosage.

"We can't say that retatrutide is causing these symptoms, or even that Reddit customers are actually taking genuine retatrutide, since the drug is not legally available, and gray market formulations vary," says Lyle Ungar, Professor in CIS and a co-author of the study.

Rather than confirming fresh risks, the research offers scientists an opportunity to identify questions that warrant more rigorous investigation.

"This is the first glimpse into the experiences of a population that is otherwise outside conventional drug safety monitoring because they are taking unapproved versions of a drug that has yet to finish clinical trials," says Neil Sehgal, the study's first author and a doctoral student in CIS.

How Researchers Analyzed 150,000 Reddit Posts.

The project builds on previous research by the University of Pennsylvania team. In that earlier investigation, scientists used large language models (LLMs), the type of artificial intelligence that powers many modern chatbots, to examine more than 400,000 Reddit posts discussing semaglutide and tirzepatide.

That analysis revealed reports of possible side effects, including menstrual irregularities, that may not have been fully documented in clinical trials or official drug safety records.

"We wanted to apply the same methodology to gray-market retatrutide," says Sehgal.

Retatrutide is particularly interesting because it works differently from existing GLP-1 medications. Semaglutide acts on one hormone receptor involved in blood sugar control and appetite regulation, while tirzepatide targets two. Retatrutide activates three receptors, potentially producing a different combination of effects throughout the body.

To investigate what people were experiencing, the researchers used AI to examine nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments. They identified approximately 14,000 customers who claimed to have personally taken an unapproved version of retatrutide.

In a recent development, the AI systems then extracted descriptions of symptoms that owners associated with the medication and translated those descriptions into standardized medical terminology. This allowed researchers to compare reports even when different people used different words to describe similar experiences.

After excluding expected effects such as weight loss and reduced appetite, the team identified 7,823 owners who reported at least one symptom that could be medically classified.

"A researcher might be able to examine a few thousand Reddit posts by hand, but looking at nearly 150,000 would be an enormous undertaking," states Sehgal. "AI makes it possible to analyze these conversations at scale, identifying patterns in what people are sharing that would otherwise be difficult to recognize.".

A Surprising Appetite Paradox Emerges.

The most striking difference involved hunger.

It has been revealed that in retatrutide's Phase 2 clinical trials (the drug is currently in Phase 3 trials, the final step before FDA approval), participants most commonly experienced gastrointestinal complaints, including nausea. These effects are familiar concerns with medications that influence appetite and digestion.

Industry observers note that but among Reddit consumers who reported taking unapproved retatrutide, the pattern looked different. Increased appetite emerged as the most frequently described classifiable symptom, despite the substantial weight-loss effects demonstrated in clinical testing.

The researchers also compared the latest findings with their earlier analysis of semaglutide and tirzepatide.

In a recent development, compared with those earlier Reddit reports, discussions involving unapproved retatrutide contained proportionally more mentions of appetite-related changes, sleep disturbances, increased heart rate, and muscle-related symptoms. Reports of nausea and other digestive complaints were proportionally less common.

These differences could reflect how retatrutide interacts with the body. However, they could also result from differences between the groups of people discussing the medications, their other drug use, or the contents of the unapproved products.

"Retatrutide works differently from existing GLP-1 drugs, so it's possible that its effects on the body are different, too," states Jena Shaw Tronieri, Senior Research Investigator at Penn's Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a co-author of the study.

"But the people discussing it on Reddit also may be different," she notes. "Owners willing to obtain an unapproved medication on the gray market likely differ from other clinical populations. Some may be taking multiple experimental peptides, and we can't verify exactly what they're taking. We need more research to understand what, if anything, these differences in self-reported symptoms mean.".

Can AI Detect Drug Safety Concerns Earlier?

Beyond the findings about retatrutide, the study demonstrates how AI could potentially improve the early detection of drug safety concerns.

Recent findings suggest that traditional monitoring systems depend heavily on clinical trials, reports submitted to regulators, and information collected by healthcare professionals. People obtaining experimental medications through unapproved channels may not be represented in those systems.

Sources indicate that social media offers another source of information, allowing researchers to identify recurring experiences that might otherwise escape attention. However, these reports must be independently investigated before they can be considered reliable evidence of a drug-related problem.

The Penn team has already seen an example of how this approach can help guide further research.

It has been revealed that in their previous investigation of semaglutide and tirzepatide, researchers identified online reports of menstrual irregularities. Those findings subsequently encouraged another scientific team to examine similar symptoms using the FDA's database of reported adverse drug events.

The follow-up study, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology, also detected disproportionate reports of certain menstrual changes. Although those findings did not establish causation, they provided additional reasons to investigate the potential connection.

The researchers hope their retatrutide findings will lead to similar independent studies, particularly as the drug advances through clinical development.

"That's what we hope will happen with this study," indicates Sehgal. "Other researchers can take what we find on Reddit and look for the same patterns in other datasets, using entirely different methods. Whether those signals hold up or not, the goal is to build a better understanding of what people are actually experiencing.".

According to recent reports, the research was conducted through the University of Pennsylvania's School of Engineering and Applied Science and Perelman School of Medicine. Benjamin Rader of Boston Children's Hospital also contributed as a co-author. Funding was provided in part by the University of Pennsylvania's Penn Medical Communication Research Institute. Tronieri disclosed receiving an investigator-initiated grant from Novo Nordisk on behalf of the University of Pennsylvania, along with consulting fees from Currax Pharmaceuticals, LLC. No conflicts of interest were reported by the other authors.

"It stayed alive for so long" - Behind the wheel with the Last Riders saying goodbye to GTA Online, amidst GTA 6's world-changing launch

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in the decade or so since Grand Theft Auto Online's arrival, its roads have become a kind of home; well-loved by its racers, its gear heads, and speed freaks.
  • So when the GTA Online community decided to host Last Ride events this week - a sort of mass in-game road trip and a communal farewell before attention inevitably turned to GTA 6 - I was keen to join in.
  • In a recent development, kirsty is one of the many long-time players who chose to embark on their own last drive as part of the event.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in the decade or so since Grand Theft Auto Online's arrival, its roads have become a kind of home; well-loved by its racers, its gear heads, and speed freaks. It's a game that allows players to lose themselves in the roleplay, the heists, and the crime sprees. But for me, an occasional dipper into its major updates, the car folk have always been the engine driving its appeal.

So when the GTA Online community decided to host Last Ride events this week - a sort of mass in-game road trip and a communal farewell before attention inevitably turned to GTA 6 - I was keen to join in. The Last Drive was scheduled to begin an hour before GTA 6's launch, and would see numerous groups embarking on their own journey across GTA Online's servers, all taking the same route: starting at Los Santos' Del Perro Pier and following the highway around Los Santos' entire perimeter before finally rolling up to its airport. Players would then fly off into the sunset, close the game, and move on. Some just for a while, others perhaps forever.

In a recent development, kirsty is one of the many long-time players who chose to embark on their own last drive as part of the event. She runs the Fast Crew racing community in GTA Online and has been playing since the beginning in 2013, even meeting her fiance through the game. Unlike some, however, she prepares to stick around in GTA Online after GTA 6's release, at least until the new game's equivalent comes along.

Sources indicate that it's the social dynamic of GTA Online that makes it special, Kirsty tells me when we speak online, and she calls it a community of players "that thrives from supporting each other, racing together and just having fun". She points to GTA Online's 30-player sessions as one reason for its enduring appeal "That's key for people in communities like ours," she explains. "Gaming is an escape to many people, a distraction or a coping method. GTA is special because it stayed alive for so long, giving people that escape.".

Then there's Brittany, who leads the GTA Online Ascent racing community. Brittany has a real-life kart racing background, and built race tracks across various Xbox 360 games before arriving in GTA Online. As with many of the players I spoke with, the in-game connections Brittany made have blossomed into real-life friendships, all built around racing.

"GTA Online introduced me to many lifelong friends," they explain. "Hell, I even met my girlfriend Ari through the GTA Racing community. Every year, five-to-six of us go to the Indy 500 and all of us met through my [GTA Online] PC racing community BRITCAR." Brittany was also planning their own Last Drive, using old cars from the game's earlier years.

It's clear GTA Online has become more than just a game to many people, and I was eager to see how players might choose to say goodbye. So as GTA 6 loomed, I booted up GTA Online and prepared for my own Last Drive, waiting near the pier in a random online lobby. Slowly, other people started to arrive - all seemingly strangers - and at the allotted time, we slowly began making our way around the map as one.

Sources indicate that what I saw was brilliant. A snaking line of customised cars, custom paint jobs, and underlighting, slowly navigating the island; a peaceful, reverential convoy of players who weren't blasting away at each other with weapons for once. The chaos of the typical GTA Online lobby never broke out. Instead, there was a sort of unspoken armistice between those eager to enjoy one last moment in a game they'd spent so much time in. Gradually, more people joined our conga line.

Besides being a lovely way to close a chapter for many, it allowed for a cheeky bit of peacocking too. Many players pulled up in truly exceptional rides: there were supercars, bulky muscle cars, and street-racer lightshows, all as much an expression of their owners' personalities and tastes as any human avatar.

Recent findings suggest that at one point, the leader of this snaking pack made a wrong turn, taking us into a dockyard and an unfortunate dead-end. We then all had to slowly reverse out - a time-consuming, if amusing, process which allowed one opportunistic spectator to pull up and take a few of us out with a well-placed RPG. But after we'd all reconvened nearby, the respectful atmosphere resumed. No flying Oppressor Mk II rained missiles on us, and there weren't any kamikaze crashes interrupting our final drive.

It has been revealed that when we did finally reach the airport, people left their vehicles and things took a more knockabout turn. Together we huddled for a few moments, letting off gunfire and fireworks into the night. Then the cops came, and the group rushed to steal planes and helicopters before things got wilder still.

In a recent development, slowly, eventually our group began to disperse. Players either went on to cause some final havoc before GTA 6's arrival, or they did as I did, flying over the ocean into the sunset before leaving the server once and for all. It sounds sappy but it was moving. Here, a game perhaps best known for its player-versus-player hijinks had - thanks to a close-knit community consisting of people like Kirsty, Brittany, and all their friends - became a wholesome drive along. A send off to the game as it was, before ushering in a latest dawn.

According to recent reports, it speaks to what is special about GTA Online, really. A playground people have spent years in, clearly still important to them, and a chance to say a farewell of sorts from the place they feel most comfortable: behind the wheel.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Nest app is officially dead, but it’s worth taking a step back and remembering that, while there are some rough edges, the Google Home app is a better smart home experience than Nest alone ever could have been.
  • Industry observers note that the Nest app has been on life support for years now.
  • Realistically, even long-time Nest owners have had no reason to continue using the app over Google Home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Nest app is officially dead, but it’s worth taking a step back and remembering that, while there are some rough edges, the Google Home app is a better smart home experience than Nest alone ever could have been.

Industry observers note that the Nest app has been on life support for years now. Google has been migrating legacy products into the Home app for a while and the last few puzzle pieces came in Nest Protect support, the death of the earliest Nest Thermostats, and other assorted adjustments.

Realistically, even long-time Nest owners have had no reason to continue using the app over Google Home.

It has been revealed that having been personally, deeply invested in Google’s vision for the smart home over the past decade, I’ll say that the Google Home app we have today is better than the Nest app ever was or ever could be. A huge part of that comes from Google Home’s ability to pull together devices from third-party ecosystems. Being able to control your entire smart home from a single app is how the smart home always should have been, and between Google’s work and the Matter standard, we’re finally able to enjoy that pretty seamlessly for the most part. Automations, Google’s actually-useful AI features, and more only sweeten the deal. I’m also a big fan of what the Home app has become from a UX perspective. While there are always rough edges and bugs to clean up, the customizable homepage and well-organized sections make for a good – not perfect, but good – experience for the end user.

That mentioned, there is one thing that the Nest app’s limited scope benefitted from, and that’s a focus on making your own product great.

Google’s move to the Home app for Nest devices has been a 5-year run of trying to clean things up, improve on the app, and basically bring back the way things were in the Nest app as far as the first-party cameras and thermostats are concerned. It’s taken ages, but we’re finally up to speed, mostly. I still hate that you have to reset Nest Cams to change Wi-Fi when the Nest app just let you change it, and the Nest app’s settings were much less overwhelming, but I’d say the pros far outweigh the cons at this point.

It has been revealed that the Nest app was good at its job, but the Google Home app is a worthy successor, finally, and now the Nest app can finally rest. I mostly think the same applies to Gemini vs Google Assistant, with the newer assistant a better overall experience, but it’s easier to poke holes in that argument.

Sources indicate that disagree? What do you think of the Google Home app, and were you still using the Nest app?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’ve optimized your model. Your pipeline is running smoothly. But now, your cloud bill has skyrocketed. Running 1B+ classifications or embeddings per day isn’t just a technical challenge—it’s a financial one. How do you process at this scale without blowing your budget? Whether you're running large-scale document classification or bulk embedding pipelines for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), you need cost-efficient, high-throughput inference to make it feasible, and you get that from having a well optimized configuration.

Sources indicate that these tasks often use encoder models, which are much smaller than modern LLMs, but at the 1B+ inference request scale it's still quite a non-trivial task. Just to be clear, that's English Wikipedia 144x over. I haven’t seen much information on how to approach this with cost in mind and I want to tackle that. This blog breaks down HOW to calculate cost and latency for large scale classification and embedding. We’ll analyze different model architectures, benchmark costs across hardware choices, and give you a clear framework for optimizing your own setup. Additionally we should be able to build some intuition if you don't feel like going through the process yourself.

You might have a couple questions:.

Here is the code to make it happen: https://github.com/datavistics/encoder-analysis.

tl;I'm not gonna reproduce this, tell me what you found;dr.

With this pricing I was able to get this cost:.

To evaluate cost and latency we need 4 key components:.

Industry observers note that I’ll be leveraging Inference Endpoints for my Hardware Options, as it allows me to choose from a wide range of hardware choices. Do note you can replace that with your GPUs of choice/consideration. For the Deployment Facilitator I'll be using the ever so useful Hugging Face Hub Library which allows me to programmatically deploy models easily.

For the Inference Server I’ll also be using Infinity which is an amazing library for serving encoder based models (and more now!). I’ve already written about TEI, which is another amazing library. You should definitely consider TEI when approaching your use-case, though this blog focuses on methodology rather than framework comparisons. Infinity has a number of key strengths, like serving multimodal embeddings, targeting different hardware (AMD, Nvidia, CPU and Inferentia) and running any newly introduced models that contain remote code that have not been integrated into huggingface’s transformer library. The most crucial of these to me is that most models are compatible by default.

Industry observers note that for Load Testing I'll be using k6 from Grafana which is an open-source load testing tool written in go with a javascript interface. It’s easily configurable, has high performance, and has low overhead. It has a lot of built-in executors that are super useful. It also pre-allocates Virtual Customers (VUs), which can be much more realistic than throwing some testing together yourself.

I'll go through 3 use-cases that should cover a variety of interesting points:.

According to recent reports, optimization is a tricky matter, as there is a lot to consider. At a high level, I want to sweep across important load testing parameters and find what works best for a single GPU, as most encoder models will fit in a single GPU. Once we have a baseline of cost for a single GPU, the number of GPUs and throughput can be scaled horizontally by increasing the number of replica GPUs.

For each use-case this is the high-level flow I’ll use:.

Since you have the code, feel free to adjust any part of this to your:.

In a recent development, VUs and Batch Size are notable because these influence how well we take advantage of all the compute available in the GPU. A large enough Batch Size makes sure we are fully utilizing the Streaming Multiprocessors and VRAM. There are scenarios where we have VRAM left over but there is a bandwidth cost that prevents throughput from increasing. So experimentation can help us. VUs allow us to make sure we are fully utilizing the batch size we have available.These are the main parameters I'll be testing:.

Depending on your model you might want to consider:.

According to recent reports, K6 is great because it allows you to pre-allocate VUs and prevent some insidious bugs. It's quite flexible in how you are sending requests. I decided to use it in a specific way.

Industry observers note that when I'm calling a k6 experiment, I mainly want to know what the throughput and average latency is for the requests, and have a few sanity checks for the load testing parameters I have chosen. I also want to do a sweep which means many experiments.

I use the shared-iterations executor (docs) which means K6 shares iterations between the number of VUs. The test ends once k6 executes all iterations. This allows me to have a reasonable time-out, but also put through enough requests to have a decent confidence that I can discriminate between load testing parameters choices in my sweep. In contrast to other executors, this allows me to be confident that I'm simulating the client working as hard as possible per VU which should show me what the cheapest option is.

I use 10_000 requests† and have a max experiment time of 1 min. So if 10_000 requests aren’t finished by 1 minute, then that experiment is over.

† I use less max requests for the Vision Embeddings given that the throughput is much lower and images are heavy.†† P95 means that 95% of requests complete within this time. It represents the worst-case latency for most users.

You can find the 3 notebooks that put the optimization workflow together here:.

The main purpose was to get my experiments defined, launch the correct Inference Endpoint with the right parameters, and launch k6 with the right parameters to test the endpoint.

I made a couple design choices which you may want to think through to see if they work for you:.

According to recent reports, text Classification can have a variety of use-cases at scale, like Email Filtering, Toxicity Detection in pre-training datasets, etc. The OG classic architecture was BERT, and swiftly many other architectures came about. Do note that in contrast to popular decoder models, these need to be fine-tuned on your task before using them. Today I think the following architectures† are the most notable:.

† Do note that for these models, you typically need to fine-tune this on your data to perform well†† I'm using “Engineering performance” to denote anticipated latency/throughput.

Recent findings suggest that I chose DistilBERT to focus on as it’s a great lightweight choice for many applications. I compared 2 GPUs, nvidia-t4 and nvidia-l4 as well as 2 Infinity Docker Images.

Industry observers note that text Embeddings are a loose way of describing the task of taking a text input and projecting it into a semantic space where close points are similar in meaning and distant ones are dissimilar (example below). This is used heavily in RAG and is an important part of AI search (which some are fans of).

There are a large number of architectures which are compatible, and you can see the most performant ones in the MTEB Leaderboard.

ModernBERT is the most exciting encoder release since DeBERTa back in 2020. It has all the ahem modern tricks built into an old and familiar architecture. It makes for an attractive model to experiment with as it's much less explored than other architectures and has a lot more potential. There are a number of improvements in speed and performance, but the most notable for a user is likely the 8k context window. Do check out this blog for a more thorough understanding.

Sources indicate that it's crucial to note that Flash Attention 2 will only work with more modern GPUs due to the compute capability requirement, so I opted to skip the T4 in favor of the L4. An H100 would also work really well here for the heavy hitters category.

It has been revealed that colQwen2 is a Visual Retriever which is based on the Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct and uses ColBERT style multi-vector representations of both text and images. We can see that it has a complex architecture compared to the encoders we explored above.

There are a number of use-cases which might benefit from this at large scale like, e-commerce search, multi-modal recommendations, enterprise multi-modal RAG, etc.

ColBERT style is different than our previous embedding use-case since it breaks the input into multiple tokens and returns a vector for each instead of 1 vector for the input. You can find an excellent tutorial from Jina AI here.This can lead to superior semantic encoding and better retrieval, but is also slower, and more expensive.

I'm excited for this experiment as it explores 2 lesser known concepts, vision embeddings and ColBERT style embeddings†. There are a few things to note about ColQwen2/VLMs:.

Industry observers note that scaling to 1B+ classifications or embeddings per day is a non-trivial challenge, but with the right optimizations, it can be made cost-effective. From my experiments, a few key patterns emerged:.

In a recent development, your data, hardware, models, etc might differ, but I hope you find some use in the approach and code provided. The best way to get an estimate is to run this on your own task with your own configurations. Let's get exploring!

Sources indicate that it's vital to scale sanity checks as your complexity scales. Since we are using subprocess and jinja to then call k6 I felt far from the actual testing so I put a few checks in place.

Industry observers note that the goal of task performance is that for a specific configuration we are performing similarly to what we expect. Task Performance will have different meanings across tasks. For classification I chose accuracy, and for embeddings I skipped it. We could look at average similarity and other similar metrics. It gets a bit more complex with ColBERT style since we are getting many vectors per request.

Even though 58% isn't bad for some 3 class classification tasks, it's irrelevant. The goal is to make sure that we are getting the expected task performance. If we see a significant change (increase or decrease) we should be suspicious and try to understand why.

Below is a great example from the classification use-case since we can see an extremely tight distribution and one outlier. Upon further investigation the outlier is due to a low amount of requests sent.

Industry observers note that we should expect to see no failed requests as Inference Endpoints has a queue to handle extra requests. This is relevant for all 3 use-cases: Classification, Embedding, and Vision Embedding.

sum(df.total_requests - df.successful_requests) allows us to see if we had any failed requests.

In a recent development, as described above we are using a nice strategy of using exponential increases and then a binary search to find the best number of VUs. But how do we know that we tried enough VUs? What if we tried a higher amount of VUs and throughput kept increasing? This is a key chart as for many use-cases there is a maximum latency that a user can experience. Usually if we allow the latency to increase we can increase throughput creating a trade-off scenario. That's true in all the use-cases I've looked at here. Having a pareto curve is great to help visualize where that tradeoff is.

According to recent reports, lastly it's key to build intuition on what is happening when we try these different settings. Do we get beautiful idealized charts? Do we see unexpected gradients? Do we need more exploration in a region? Could we have problems in our setup like not having an isolated environment? All of these are good questions and some can be tricky to answer.

#127638. MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells

📅 23 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1463 w)

MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A swimming robot does not necessarily need a bulky motor or powerful mechanical parts to move through water.
  • The engineers developed an extremely thin swimming robot that uses living muscle tissue to move its fins.
  • By directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A swimming robot does not necessarily need a bulky motor or powerful mechanical parts to move through water. MIT researchers have demonstrated that a single, carefully engineered layer of living muscle cells can generate enough force to propel a tiny robot forward.

The engineers developed an extremely thin swimming robot that uses living muscle tissue to move its fins. Described in a new study published in Advanced Functional Materials, the device has a flexible gel framework roughly the length and width of a stick of gum. The gel forms two fins, each coated with a layer of muscle cells far thinner than a human hair. These cells have been genetically modified to contract when exposed to light.

By directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water. Adjusting which fin receives light and how frequently it is illuminated allows the team to control both its speed and direction.

In experiments, the remarkably thin robot successfully swam and turned through a simple underwater maze. At maximum speed, it covered approximately four times its body length per minute. Although that is much slower than an Olympic swimmer, who can travel up to 65 body lengths per minute, it is comparable to the swimming pace of a cow shark moving leisurely through the ocean.

"It takes a lot of force to move through water versus air," indicates study author Ritu Raman, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT. "The robot's quite strong, given its size. ".

A New Generation of Robots Powered by Living Muscle.

The device represents the first demonstration of a very thin, two-dimensional robot that can move from place to place using living muscle tissue.

Sources indicate that most existing biohybrid robots rely on relatively large, three-dimensional structures made from laboratory-grown skeletal muscle. Producing these structures typically requires millions of cells. Raman explains that thinner designs could reduce manufacturing costs while potentially improving movement efficiency.

Sources indicate that "Presently, biohybrid robots from our group and others' are built from bulky, 3D chunks of lab-grown skeletal muscle that require millions of cells to fabricate," states Raman, who notes that thinner, less bulky designs such as the team's new bot could be cheaper to build and could move more efficiently. "We believe that biohybrid robots powered by living muscle could one day perform delicate jobs like exploring environments too fragile or unpredictable for conventional hardware, because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself.".

The MIT research team also included first author Maheera Bawa, along with Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, and Seanbiron Johnson.

From Artificial Muscle to a Swimming Robot.

According to recent reports, the new swimming robot builds on an earlier achievement by Raman's laboratory. Last year, the researchers created an artificial muscle disk inspired by the human iris, demonstrating how a thin layer of living cells could produce precisely controlled movements.

For that project, the engineers patterned a gel disk with grooves extending outward from its center and forming concentric circles. They then placed living muscle cells on the surface, where the cells grew into a thin layer following the patterned channels.

When illuminated, the muscle tissue contracted in different directions, causing the disk to stretch and compress. Its movements resembled the way the iris of the human eye changes shape as the pupil expands or narrows.

The experiment established that researchers could grow extremely thin muscle layers in intricate arrangements and use light to control their movements along multiple directions.

Industry observers note that "People hadn't seen this muscle architecture engineered from scratch before," Raman indicates. "And the cells were moving in multiple directions. But they only moved about 100 microns. From a robotics perspective, their movements were tiny.".

For the latest project, the researchers wanted to dramatically increase the amount of movement and force generated by the muscle cells. Their goal was to produce contractions powerful enough to propel a robot through water.

They determined that achieving this would require a better foundation for the living muscle tissue.

It has been revealed that the earlier artificial iris had used fibrin, an exceptionally soft gel, as its underlying structure. However, the team found that fibrin could rapidly shrink under the forces exerted by contracting muscle cells, limiting the effectiveness of the resulting movement.

To overcome this problem, the engineers investigated three characteristics of the gel foundation: its chemical composition, its stiffness, and the dimensions and geometry of the grooves used to organize muscle growth.

"For engineering any type of tissue, it's known that these are knobs you can tune," Raman states. "And we wanted to optimize all these parameters to support live muscle cells.".

Engineering a Stronger Muscle-Powered Robot.

Finding the right supporting material required testing gels with different formulations, stiffness levels, and surface patterns.

Sources indicate that the researchers compared several groove shapes, including narrow channels with square profiles and longer channels with curved bottoms. They discovered that muscle cells aligned more effectively inside square-shaped grooves.

Recent findings suggest that this alignment was notable because muscle cells that grow in the same direction are more likely to merge into fibers. Those fibers can then form stronger muscle tissue that contracts in a coordinated way. The square grooves therefore provided a more effective structure for producing force.

The team also replaced fibrin with gelatin methacrylate (GelMA), a material commonly used to grow and engineer biological tissue.

By adjusting the formulation of GelMA, the researchers produced supporting gels with varying degrees of stiffness. They then examined how muscle cells developed on each surface and measured their ability to generate force.

Stiffer gels produced the best results. On these firmer surfaces, muscle cells grew in better alignment and generated stronger contractions.

The engineers next investigated how thick the gel should be. They determined that a film measuring approximately half a millimeter offered an effective balance. It was sturdy enough to support a single layer of muscle cells while remaining sufficiently lightweight to prevent the contracting cells from detaching from the surface.

The team further improved muscle performance through a form of exercise. Repeated pulses of light stimulated the cells to contract, strengthening the muscle tissue before it was incorporated into the swimming robot.

How Light Makes the Living Robot Swim.

With the gel structure optimized and the muscle cells strengthened, the researchers assembled their swimming device.

Recent findings suggest that the finished robot consisted of a thin gel framework divided into two fins. Both sides of the gel were patterned with square-bottomed grooves and covered with living muscle cells. As the cells developed, they fused into organized muscle fibers capable of contracting together.

Each fin could be activated independently using light, giving the researchers a simple way to control the robot's movements.

Sources indicate that "You can think of the robot as having two independent muscles," Raman indicates. "If we shine a light on just one, only that muscle moves. If shining on both, they both flap.".

In a recent development, to test the device, the researchers placed it inside a large petri dish filled with water. They then moved a light source by hand, illuminating the fins to guide the robot through a maze positioned inside the dish.

Recent findings suggest that as the muscles contracted, the fins flapped and propelled the robot through the water. By changing the light stimulation, the engineers successfully controlled its movement and helped it navigate the obstacles.

In a recent development, although the robot demonstrated the ability to swim and steer, its current shape remains relatively simple. The primary objective of the experiment was to establish that an exceptionally thin layer of engineered muscle tissue could generate enough force for swimming.

The researchers now blueprint to refine the robot's body to improve its speed. Beyond demonstrating a latest approach to biohybrid robotics, the technology could eventually be useful for monitoring aquatic environments or operating in locations where conventional rigid machines might cause damage.

It has been revealed that "Our next goal is to optimize the body design to enable faster swimming," Raman says. "But even at slow swim speeds, one could imagine a muscle-powered swimmer being used for purposes like environmental monitoring in aquatic environments.".

The Office of Naval Research provided partial funding for this research.

#127637. Industry News: Queen's Domain review

Industry News: Queen's Domain review

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2352 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that where to start with Queen's Domain?
  • In a recent development, all this begins with an island.
  • Sources indicate that there is so much to say about Neasied.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that where to start with Queen's Domain? It's tempting to begin with King's Field; after all, FromSoftware's seminal first-person action-RPG is an explicit inspiration for developer Freshly Baked Games. But 40 hours later, it feels like so much more. It's equally tempting to invoke another FromSoftware game: Dark Souls. Queen's Domain owes an obvious debt to that game's celebrated level design: the dazzling interconnectedness of its vertiginous world. But that's not quite right either. The deeper you delve, the more there's something of the spirit of The Legend of Zelda, a touch of Metroidvania too. Until finally you concede that Queen's Domain, with its remarkable world of densely packed secrets, is very much its own.

In a recent development, all this begins with an island. You, Prince Beruim, are a castaway, washed ashore on Neasied. Your father, the king, has disappeared, and your search has brought you, somewhat circuitously, here. As you clamber to your feet and survey the island, it makes an immediately striking impression: all strange peaks and crooked spires; a cramped, chaotic mass of landmarks lost amid the dense undergrowth. Pyramids perch atop steep plateaus; a vast, moss-tinged mausoleum sprawls across the land to one side while the other is dominated by an imposing tower. It's a world made all the stranger by Queen's Domain's retro aesthetic. Here, shimmering low-res textures and low-poly shapes converge to create elaborate spaces and structures that feel slightly at odds with the lo-fi vibe. It's not quite old, not quite upcoming; instead, something of a world lost outside of time. It makes for an enigmatic, disorientating landscape. And when paired with a soundtrack that delights in discordance, as it swings from gentle ambience to pulsing synths, it's a mood that refuses to resolve.

Sources indicate that there is so much to say about Neasied. And so much I absolutely will not spoil. But very early impressions don't do it justice at all. As you take your first tentative steps onto the island, presented with a forking path that eventually winds back in on itself, it's easy to mistake Queen's Domain for a first-person Dark Souls - especially if, like me, you're only passingly familiar with King's Field. As in most Soulslikes, early progress is defined by a punishing inch-by-inch crawl from one brutal encounter to the next; where death - via chicken-cricket hybrids, ladybird-rats, and other wonderfully odd things - comes fast and frequently, respawning you back at the last Crystal Monument you visited. And because its wilfully old-school design eschews modern-day niceties such as a combat lock-on or dedicated roll button, there's a looseness to fighting that takes a while to click. But it does, slowly, click.

This is a game that demands you lean into its limitations, encourages you to find ways to make them work. At first, those Souls-honed instincts are likely to be your undoing as you naturally scramble for a dodge button that isn't there. But soon a different sort of pattern emerges: you realise that to avoid a ladybird attack, you simply need to step back - but not so far you don't have time to nip in and strike while your opponent takes a pause. A charging enemy might require a different approach - a well-timed backstep and swivelling sideways strafe to put you in the right place for a counter. And in this way, combat becomes a compelling sort of puzzle as you learn each of the 100+ enemies' little ticks - including rock, paper, scissors-style weaknesses to different weapon types - and figure out how to respond.

Industry observers note that there's more to consider. Your melee damage output, for instance, is directly tied to your stamina bar: the more stamina you have, the harder you'll hit; too low and it's a waste of a swing. That forces you to choose your moments carefully, moving out to safety while your bar refills. And there's a charge attack, also linked to your stamina, that does more damage still. Already combat has a distinctively deliberate rhythm, but then come your first throwing knives. These are most immediately useful against enemies ordinarily out of reach - like the laser-spewing foliage dogging your journey early on - but they're equally valuable for luring individual enemies away from the throng. Throwing weapons take a while to return to your pouch, meaning they too need to be deployed with purpose. And while knives are just the start - you'll acquire an increasingly exotic selection of throwables including poison-tipped darts and homing blades - they all fundamentally work the same way.

And the interplay of these various warm-ups and cooldowns creates an increasingly engaging rhythm as you learn to juggle between your variously equipped weapons to maximise their damage potential. You might, for instance, fire off a one-two-three volley of homing darts, then use a magic lantern to toss out a massive fireball that bounces destructively around the room. And it's there, in the ensuing chaos, you'll charge up your blade, letting rip then returning to your darts again. Combat might encourage a methodical pace, but that doesn't mean you can't fight fast, and there are some fascinating synergies among the various weapons, many having their own wonderfully distinct mechanisms. There's a brawling gauntlet that lifts you clean off the ground and a vampiric blade capable of stealing an enemy's life force. There are hammers, creatures, and an unexpected mid-game weapon class, utilising a third rechargeable power source, that I am definitely not spoiling. Queen's Domain's 100 or so weapons create ample space for experimentation and customisation, and the further from its cautious beginnings you stray, the brisker, the more exhilarating its combat becomes. In my current, late-game form, I'm a whirl of blades and blasts and up-close attacks that feels anything but Soulslike.

Queen's Domain isn't just a nippier sort of game, though. It promptly reveals itself to be friendlier, more accommodating. Levelling, for instance, happens passively as you play, meaning every swing feels like it's contributing to your progress. Weapons level independently too, encouraging specialisation. There are no flasks, no accumulated currency you'll need to worry about dropping on death, no subsequent corpse runs. And progress can be saved at any time using the nearest Crystal Monument, meaning that when you respawn, you won't have to grind through the same opponents again. Enemies do eventually reappear of their own accord, so you can't exploit the save system indefinitely. But unlike Souls-style bonfires, Crystal Monuments only repopulate the world when you explicitly tell them to - when you Rest to clear status effects and restore health - giving you considerably more agency. You can decide when to push forward, when to retreat and lock in your progress, and when to reap the benefits of a rest and reset. Together, it makes for a breezier, less punishing, more consistently rewarding riff on the traditional Souslike, while never losing that I-can-do-this just-one-more-turn allure.

But as immensely enjoyable as Queen's Domain's combat is, the real draw here, unquestionably, is the world. Neasied is extraordinary. Right from the start, as you pick yourself off the sand and survey the landscape, its enigmatic huddle of peculiar landmarks isn't just intriguing, it's inviting. These odd pyramids, these curious plateaus practically demand to be explored. But how? The answer comes perhaps an hour in when, fancily clad skeleton boss successfully slain, you get your hands on the Holy Sword Endu. It's an immediate boon, far more lethal than the rubbish rusty blade you've been wielding so far. And its secondary attack - a long-range jab that propels you forward - is handy too. It's also your key to unlocking Neasied.

Endu's violent forward momentum can, you see, fling you across previously uncrossable gaps, gradually carrying you further and further as more upgrades reveal themselves. Suddenly, Queen's Domain takes flight, quite literally, becoming something closer to an exploratory sandbox as it adopts the spirited acrobatics of a platform game. And as you experiment with your newfound freedom, the more paths you explore, the island begins to take on a dizzying new form. Neasied, when viewed from up high, reveals itself to be a vastly intricate traversal puzzle. That peculiar structure in the distance? If you can find an appropriate ledge to fling yourself from, it's now yours for the investigating - and from there, one, two, three more tantalising branches are revealed. Neasied is an astonishing piece of design: a ludicrous, elaborate tangle of hidden pathways and secrets, forever folding in and around itself, that's crafted to invite curiosity and then constantly reward.

It has been revealed that freshly Baked Games always feels one step ahead. I can't recall a single moment where my exploratory What-ifs - What if I throw myself this way? What if I do a falling mid-air turn? What if I toss myself down this hole? - didn't bear fruit. Sometimes your prize is a steaming platter of boon-granting food, sometimes it's another bit of increasingly exotic weaponry. Perhaps you'll find a strange NPC with a favour to ask; fish eggs and mysterious skulls; a shopkeeper with a thing for ducks (who, in a typically lovely touch, festoons his store with the goods you're willing to sell), and so many mysterious upcoming puzzle threads to pull. As you fling and probe and push on forward, that thing you've been carrying around for hours - or, conversely, that thing you saw hours ago - suddenly finds new purpose. There's a definite touch of Metroidvania as old areas reveal new truths the further you go. And because there's so little handholding, so little explicit direction, every discovery feels like your own.

It has been revealed that but just as you think you're starting to get a handle on Queen's Domain's shape, along comes another surprise: dungeons as vastly intricate as the world outside. You'll navigate labyrinthine waterlogged caverns of angry fish where progress involves puzzling past ancient mechanisms. Later, an arcane tower where gargoyles prowl. Here, the convoluted upward route takes circuitous laps among the endless bookshelves, spilling out the windows onto teetering precipices with alarming sea views. Then down, however briefly, to eerie chambers below. Suddenly, the mood is less Soulslike, more Zelda, and your expectations shift again. And still new discoveries lead to new paths and fresh mysteries.

Recent findings suggest that and it keeps on going. As Freshly Baked Games gradually peels back Neasied's layers, it constantly finds latest ways to awe: yet more surprises, yet more secrets, your exploratory digressions earning still more intriguing rewards. There comes a point where you think surely you must have seen everything, explored its deepest caverns and most mysterious tombs, but down you go again. And somewhere around the midpoint, Queen's Domain takes a truly audacious turn. There is a - let's call it a tonal lurch for fear of spoilers - that signals another shift. Suddenly, there are new toys to play with, an autumnal landscape so complex in its demands, it genuinely made my brain pulse. And then it's over. Until it's not.

There are, it turns out, secrets beneath the secrets; a still more intricate web of interconnected threads spun throughout this already fascinating, impossibly complex world. The Neasied that welcomes you really is just the tip of it all. Exactly when you'll come to this realisation depends how thorough you are in the earlier hours - how willing you are to explore its darker corners and brave its more punishing realms - but for me the before-and-after managed to divide my 40-ish hour playthrough neatly in two. You reawaken with a sense of a quest unfulfilled, a hint that more is required. And so, in lieu of more explicit direction, you set out again, probe deeper, explore further, and slowly the vaguest shape of a latest objective - a succession of tiny threads seemingly all leading in the same direction - begins to emerge. Tucked along uncharted paths, perhaps, or in suspicious corners, or in item descriptions that suddenly feels like clues.

It's here in this second half - something of a dark mirror to the first, in classic Zelda style - that Queen's Domain takes on a more esoteric air; its web of distantly scattered enigmas requiring real dedication to unfurl. Why this pot on a stick? Why this book? How do these unlit lanterns relate to this thing, and that thing, and this other thing on the other side of the world?

It's clever stuff, even if navigating its late-game threads can occasionally feel just a little too much, a little too abstruse, and you'll potentially face a lot of needle-in-a-haystack backtracking if you haven't been taking judicious notes as you go. Do I have any other quibbles? There are perhaps too few boss encounters that feel like genuine events. And while combat generally feels fair and balanced, serving as a propulsive drumbeat to the broader exploratory rhythms, there are a few late-game all-the-enemies-at-once-style difficulty spikes that go just a bit too far. But then another 'What if?' and the world responds, and those frustrations melt away.

I remember a time in my youth - back before dataminers and FAQs - when video games felt unknowable. Endless enigmas built from creativity and code. It felt like anything could be hiding in there if only you knew where to look, and it was easy to let your imagination run wild. Queen's Domain is so full of secrets, so full of mystery and wonder, it feels like the sort of game my enthusiastic child-brain might have dreamed up all those years ago. 40 hours in, I've seen an ending, but it feels like I'm still far from through. So many mysteries still linger, so many things remain on my checklist of speculative to-dos. Out in the real-world, I've got a Zelda and a GTA awaiting. But it states everything about Queen's Domain - this brilliant, vast, deep enigma; this absurdly audacious thing - that I'm still not yet ready to let go.

A copy of Queen's Domain was provided for this review by Future Friends Games.

Industry observers note that the Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is worth spending more on if you want longer battery life, a brighter outdoor display, and specialized features for trail running and diving. The Galaxy Watch 9 is the better fit if you want Samsung’s latest everyday health tools in a smaller, lighter watch.

Both, however, are fantastic smartwatches with limitless potential. They share a Snapdragon Wear Elite processor and many of Samsung’s newest wellness features, so deciding between them is really about figuring out your priorities when it comes to buying a wearable this holiday season. We’re here to help you figure that out.

This post is sponsored by Samsung.

Industry observers note that as we covered in our Galaxy Watch 9 and Watch Ultra 2 comparison, both watches move to Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite platform. Both also ship with Wear OS 7 and One UI 8 Watch.

According to recent reports, that shared foundation includes useful health insights. Vitals brings overnight measurements together to establish your personal baseline, while Daily Cardio Load helps you understand training demands and recovery. Hearing monitoring can flag potentially unsafe noise levels, whether you’re at a concert or somewhere unexpectedly loud.

Both also get five years of Wear OS updates and security patches, making either a useful long-term partner for your Samsung device, like the Galaxy S26 Ultra or Galaxy Z Fold8.

Recent findings suggest that the clearest differences are size, battery capacity, display brightness, and outdoor capabilities. Here’s how the lineup breaks down:.

As you can tell, the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is considerably bigger and heavier, but you get a lot more capability for that additional size.

The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 makes its strongest case when your plans regularly take you beyond a desk, a gym, or a charger.

Samsung rates the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for up to 60 hours with the always-on display enabled, compared with up to 30 hours for the Watch 9, and that extra headroom is appealing when your day starts with a workout and finishes well into the evening.

Industry observers note that then there’s the screen. In our hands-on with both watches, the Ultra 2’s brightness stood out immediately, with a higher peak that gives it an advantage when checking workout information outdoors, even in the bright sun. And its titanium frame provides added durability.

Industry observers note that the Ultra 2 also adds Trail Run tracking for elevation and terrain impact, route guidance using compatible GPX files, and Nutrition Alert hydration guidance. These are tangible reasons to upgrade if your usual run involves trails instead of pavement.

According to recent reports, diving is another differentiator. Samsung specifies recreational diving support to depths of up to 40 meters, with automatic tracking of depth, dive time and water temperature — a remarkable feat for a piece of technology that lives on your wrist.

The best choice becomes clearer when you picture your own routine:.

Choose the Galaxy Watch 9 for everyday wellness, a lighter fit, and strong value. Choose the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for longer adventures, more demanding outdoor activities, and greater freedom between charges.

Sources indicate that if you’re replacing an older Galaxy Watch, both offer a compelling newly introduced generation of health insights and long-term support. Both last a long time and look absolutely awesome with running shorts or a business suit. But the Watch Ultra 2 can take you that extra mile, literally and figuratively, and may be worth spending more on during Best Buy’s Holiday Deals event.

#127635. Tired of GTA 6? Here's 23 lesser-known gems that might beat it at its own game

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2720 w)

Tired of GTA 6? Here's 23 lesser-known gems that might beat it at its own game

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2720 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that you can do a lot of things in GTA 6: fishing, golfing, running, jumping, dancing, racing, roaming, shopping.
  • Industry observers note that so what if you were in the mood for some of this stuff but away from Leonida?
  • Available on: Android, iOS, PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch, Switch 2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that you can do a lot of things in GTA 6: fishing, golfing, running, jumping, dancing, racing, roaming, shopping. It goes on! There's romancing, birdwatching, DIY, and even more besides. It really is an everything game. But GTA 6 isn't for everyone.

Industry observers note that so what if you were in the mood for some of this stuff but away from Leonida? Where else might you go? Consider this the slightly tenuous set-up, as we continue a week of Not-GTA, for us to highlight some of our favourite smaller games; brilliant lesser-known titles from the last 12 months or so that, in their own special way, beat GTA 6 at its own game.

Available on: Android, iOS, PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch, Switch 2.

Recent findings suggest that it's very sweet that the central, driving force of GTA 6 is the strained romance between Jason and Lucia. You are, essentially, playing a virtual matchmaker, helping these star-crossed lovers reconnect and rediscover each other after fate conspires to drive a wedge between them. But you know what's better than that? Being an actual matchmaker, matching icons on a grid and enjoying the microdose dopamine rush when you clear a line on a board.

So here's Titanium Court, which goes even further: with every line cleared, you come closer to escaping a weird, 80s-core fairy castle in a game that's partly telling a story about introspective self-doubt, and partly about warring fairies. If you're getting tired of texting your virtual lover every 10 minutes, perhaps try lighting a virtual cigarette in Titanium Court, instead - I've heard it does wonders for your health.

Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch 2.

Sources indicate that how do you find out if you can really depend upon someone? That's a question at the heart of GTA 6. And the answer is: play Major Walk. There's nothing like gesturing through the window of a sound-proofed room hoping your friend or loved one will understand what two arms waggling around means. It means 'the high-pitched warbling sound plaque', obviously. Big Walk's wonderfully stripped-back world is also an antidote to GTA 6's maximal world. The silence and space in the game is absolutely the point. What will you fill it with?

It's not all roof repairs and late night paintjobs. Sometimes home improvement requires more drastic measures. And in Virtue and a Sledgehammer, that's taken to violent extremes. This is a game, in developers Selkie Harbour and Deconstructeam's words, about family, tradition, and being a misfit. Where an entire town - the protagonist's childhood home - faces a total spiritual teardown. Here, a brutal sledgehammer-swinging reckoning awaits as you unearth memories - some happy, some decidedly not - through violent destruction, cutting through mechanical human facsimiles with the faces of the ones you love. It's haunting, devastating stuff; a very different kind of do-it-yourself.

Available on: Android, iOS, PC (Steam).

You work, you sleep, and then you die. That's how it's got to be. So if you're going to toil mercilessly for the man, you can at least hope for an interesting employee. And what's more interesting than the weirdo threesome at the centre of Servant of the Lake?

Developer Rusty Lake's eponymous series returned this year with another macabre blend of point-and-click puzzling and room-escape-style adventure. And it's a corker. Perhaps not as dazzlingly experimental as some other recent entries, but it's still a delightfully grim time as you work through your three days of servitude, butlering for the oddball Vanderboom family. Beware the blood moon.

Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch 2, Xbox Series X/S.

In a recent development, you work, you sleep, and then you die. But! What if you dream of breaking free? Escaping the chains of drudgery? That's the starting point of Denshattack!, a Jet Set Radio-inspired adventure all about sticking it to the man. Or, more specifically, a shady megacorp trying to suppress human ingenuity, creativity, and spirit. It is, as Dom put it in their five-star Denshattack! review, a game of "anti-capitalist, pop-punk optimism", which sees you careening across a colourful Japan - as a speeding, trick-flipping train, of all things - to bring the Miraidō corporation to its knees. Stylish and satisfying.

Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch 2, Xbox Series X/S.

Sources indicate that umph-umph-umph-umph umph-umph-umph-umph. Oh yeah, that's the good stuff. If you want to shoot things and see them explode, and do that with immense satisfaction and a hypnotic, pulsating electronic soundtrack, this is the one. Sektori takes the feedback of a satisfying trigger pull and boils that down to its purest essence, often in spiralling, kaleidoscopic form. Hitting a full set of letters - M-I-R-A-G-E, S-E-K-T-O-R-I, etc. - summons a rainbow of action that feels like genuine ecstasy. Pure blasting and survival.

Available on: Android, iOS, PC (Steam), Switch, Switch 2, Xbox Series X/S.

Umph-umph-umph-umph umph-umph-umph-umph. But this time imagine it's a disco beat. Let's breathe in the night, bask in those pulsing lights, and pretend we'll live this moment forever. Or, you know, we'll just shuffle our way through the throng of the dancefloor like a massive game of sokoban. That latter's the premise of developer Miracle Tea's Club Soko; a game about traversing an underground nightclub - one shunt at a time - to discover the secrets it holds. And it's good 'un, bringing a thinkier rhythm to its pounding beat.

Most people think of fishing as a calm escape from the hustle and bustle of daily life - that's certainly the case of GTA 6. But relaxation, I say, is for posers, which brings us to How to Fish. In developer Dazed Games' silly, chaotic physics-based fishing sim, you're given an arsenal of guns to unload upon fish and foe alike. Beware the seagulls, who have learned to love the taste of human flesh over the bounty of humble chip shops. It's great fun, especially co-operatively, so grab some pals and have a blast.

Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch 2, Xbox Series X/S.

Industry observers note that neasied, the island where Queen's Domain unfolds, might not be as dizzyingly expansive as some open-worlds, but the stuff it manages to pack into a relatively compact space is astonishing. This is a game crammed with secrets, rich with mystery; a world so dense with enigmas it's a joy to explore. There's more than a touch of FromSoftware to its broader retro-inspired combat rhythms, but there are hints of Zelda and Metroidvania too. It's one of the best games this year - full of surprise and wonder as its absurdly elaborate puzzle threads unfurl - and an extraordinary adventure.

Money too tight to mention? How about ditching the life of crime for a spot of restaurant entrepreneurialism? That's the idea behind Nivalis Night - and, actually, the life of crime is still an option. First seen in 2020 courier adventure Cloudpunk, Nivalis is a striking, sprawling cyberpunk dystopia of flying cars, neon lights, and suffocating smog that sets itself apart with its lo-fi style. And in this year's follow-up, you can finally get out of your car and live in the world. But it's not just a nifty first-person tycoon sim, it's a game of stories, and developer Ion Lands imbues its city with real warmth and humanity; a perfect accompaniment, it turns out, to all the Vangelis-like synths and sushi.

Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S.

It has been revealed that there's street racing and then there's developer Milestone's Screamer. It's a narrative-focused racing game which leans into a far arcadier sort of drive compared to the more realistic Grand Theft Auto. It's also got a great anime aesthetic, so you can live out any MF Ghost fantasies you have tucked away. Or maybe Initial D for the drifting aficionados among you.

According to recent reports, okay, fine, so it's more of a slap than a punch, but developer Double Fine's Thank You Bus Driver still packs in more violence than you'd expect from a driving sim. This game jam experiment turned full release feels a bit like a first-person Crazy Taxi as you try and get passengers to their destination before time runs out. Happy passengers means more 'thank yous', which means more time for more pick-ups, and it's a brilliantly chaotic loop.

Sources indicate that it's got bags of personality - its scrappy black-and-white doodle town and oddball passengers are a treat - and a bunch of neat hooks. Most notably, HQ intermittently imposes fresh rules - no talking! No toenail clipping! - which is where slaps come in. Rulebreakers need discipline if you don't want to lose your 'thank yous', so you spin around and wallop them about the chops. Just try not to drive off the road.

Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5.

Sure, Leonida's landscape holds its own kind of sunkissed beauty, but The Game Bakers has created something really special with Cairn. It might be a game focused on mountain climbing, but it's hard not to stop and admire the view whenever you reach the next plateau. As you make your way up Mount Kami, you're greeted with almost constant lovely views, some of the most gorgeous vistas released this year. Cairn is the sort of game that warrants putting the controller down and just taking the sights in for a moment or two.

Recent findings suggest that as a doctor of dubious repute once noted, where we're going, we don't need roads! So wave goodbye to metropolitan squalor, farewell to suburban suffocation, and hello the great outdoors. Over the Hill, the follow-up to Funselektor's brilliant Art of Rally, is all about off-road roaming through the vast, untamed wilderness. It's a game of purposeful meandering and patient delights and you explore the secrets of, among other places, its starlit deserts and rolling forest hills. You'll bounce your 4x4 over rocks, crawl sluggishly up hills, and winch through squelching mud, and it's all so slow. That's deliberate though. And as the result, amid the gentle strum of soothing guitar, is a wonderfully meditative game.

Available on: PC (Steam, Epic, GOG).

Industry observers note that there are few other games released this year that nail the ruthlessness of vehicle-to-vehicle combat like Airframe Ultra. An absolutely gorgeous battle-racer in which you take control of a bulky airframe. You can smack the daylights out of other riders with chains, bats, and other makeshift melee weapons. Failing that, ramming into people at full speed works wonders too. A gritty game that pleases the eye and nourishes the violent soul.

In a recent development, life, eh? One minute it's all Leonida sunshine and motorboating, the next you're on the run. But it's how you deal with each roll of the dice that matters. And that's very much the premise of Cosmo D's wonderfully weird Moves of the Diamond Hand. It's back to the jazz-drenched, oddball world of Off-Peak City we go, this time as election day looms. The legendary Circus X has returned to town and you want a place in its show. What follows is a first-person narrative adventure that takes the tabletop RPG-inspired dice-throwing of Cosmo D's acclaimed 2022 game Betrayal at Club Low and turns it into something richer, deeper, wilder, and weirder. And yes, it's got a killer soundtrack.

Available on: PC (Steam, Epic), PlayStation 5, Switch 2, Xbox Series X/S.

I see you smirking, pal - cut it out. Early on in GTA 6 you're tasked with hosing off a boat in the marina. And if that scratches an unknown itch within you, PowerWash Simulator 2 has all the nozzle blasting you could hope for. Yes, it's a slightly older one, but all 2026's DLC means it still feels upcoming. Even more grimy buildings and filthy objects are waiting for a hero with a soap dispenser, just begging for a deep clean. Is that you? Then live your dream!

In a recent development, browsing the tourist traps and fashion emporiums for the next substantial look is all well and good, but have you ever considered taking matters into your own hands? Dressmaking might not seem like the most appealing way to spend your time if you're not particularly into wearing dresses or seamstressing. (It's me, I'm that person.) However, Dressmaker and the sheer amount of clothing combinations it makes possible are a very pleasant surprise.

Industry observers note that weaved throughout it all is a story that sees you designing dresses for different characters and the events they're attending, then stitching your ideas to life piece by piece with tactile minigames, And you can design your own dresses too! I can only imagine GTA 6's Jason might even enjoy designing a dress or two for Lucia if he had Dressmaker on his JoyStation...

Creator, writer, director, composer, and 'perceptual architect' Johannes Zuch's Tenebrae Lux might be wowing the critics in GTA 6, but for my money this year's best game-within-a-game is Forbidden Solitaire. It's 2019 and you've stumbled upon an old copy of notorious CD-ROM adventure Forbidden Solitaire. It was pulled from the shelves amid some mysterious deaths, but that won't stop you from playing. What follows is a wonderfully creepy haunted media yarn - told across police records, press clippings, 90s local news reports, grisly photos, even a recreation of a cheesy true-crime-style mystery show - which brilliantly evokes the 90s multimedia boom with its lurid, awkward pre-rendered game-in-a-game visuals. It also, in case you're wondering, plays a damn good game of solitaire.

Industry observers note that I like birds. I like them so much that it's at the top of my bucket list to find a Wonga Pigeon one day. So, you can imagine how I felt finding out that GTA 6 has over 60 birds to spot, alongside binoculars and a phone camera to fulfil my bird-watching dreams.

In a recent development, before GTA 6 however, there came a lovely little multiplayer game called Flock Around developed by Friend Shaped Games that lets you explore multiple biomes while trying to snap photographs of birds from around the world and fill out your guide book. I was enamoured by its simple loop of wandering around and waiting for birds to strike a perfect pose, take selfies with them, and maybe even watching them empty their insides all over your friends. I don't think it's possible to be pooped on by a bird in GTA 6, so by default, Flock Around takes the crown as one of the best games for snapping pics of birds this year.

GTA 6 might use the gorgeous relationship between Lucia and Jason to demonstrate what basic human empathy looks like in a culture that promotes instant gratification and selfishness, but Penguin Colony uses a, erm, penguin colony to highlight the existential dangers of fascism and the pervasive threat of racism and colonialism. I know which piece of social commentary I prefer.

Available on: PC (Steam, itch.io).

Sources indicate that it's not hard to have a better cleaning regimen than GTA 6's Jason: the man apparently isn't aware his nethers need a wash too. But designer Robert Yang's Rinse and Repeat's has a solution for those struggling at showertime: get someone else to help you. Rinse and Repeat is a "steamy first-person showering game ... about consent and safety" and got a remaster earlier this year as part of Yang's Radiator Forever compilation. Yang's award-winning work frequently explores queer subculture, and the NSFW compilation also contains three other games - Hurt Me Plenty, Succulent, and Stick Shift - with more to follow. Better yet, it's completely free.

Forget cracking safes in GTA 6, what about cracking the codes in a machine that seems to be, well, more than it seems? This is the hook in Inkle's TR-49, a game about a machine that once lurked in the depths of Bletchley Park's legendary codebreaking vaults, alongside the Enigma Machine. This machine works differently. It's effectively an archive you search around using codes in the format of letter-letter, number-number, hence TR-49. But the codes you use and what you find, and how you find them: that's up to you. And sure, there's probably not gold bullion on the other side of this code, but perhaps there's something even more rewarding.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google this weekend rolled out the latest update to Pixel Weather with a newly introduced reporting feature and small interface tweaks.

According to recent reports, on the homepage, cities that have active weather warnings no longer have bright red card backgrounds. The pill-shaped container retains its Dynamic Color theming with just the text of the warning in red. This change also extends to the card on the city page. Finally, the source, like “Google Weather,” at the very bottom is now themed.

The main change today is a “Report current weather” feature to “Share the current weather condition to improve local forecasts.” The card appears at the very bottom of your current location and can be moved up the feed.

Google says to “Submit a report if the weather conditions don’t look right.” Tapping “Submit a report” brings up a “Report weather in [city]” sheet. You can submit two pieces of information:.

Industry observers note that on the privacy front: “Your feedback, device location and some diagnostic information will be collected to help improve forecasts. This information will not be associated with your Google account.”.

This is rolling out with version 1.1.20261012.x of Pixel Weather that widely rolled out this weekend.
