Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (967 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them?
  • The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results.
  • Recent findings suggest that quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising newly introduced method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.

The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.

Recent findings suggest that quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.

A Latest Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy.

The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.

Quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can rapidly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.

But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," claims Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties.".

According to recent reports, rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the latest approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify important interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.

"From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy.".

Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator.

To evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.

After this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, highlighted that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.

This represents an important step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.

Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems.

The next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.

Recent findings suggest that "This is particularly important because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important.".

The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.

Looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.

"After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," states Peter Zoller.

According to recent reports, this shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how quickly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.

It has been revealed that the findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

Materials provided by University of Innsbruck. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Indian Institute of Science IISc and ARTPARK partner with Hugging Face to enable developers across the globe to access Vaani, India's most diverse open-source, multi-modal, multi-lingual dataset. Both organisations share a commitment to building inclusive, accessible, and state-of-the-art AI technologies that honor linguistic and cultural diversity.

The partnership between Hugging Face and IISc/ARTPARK aims to increase the accessibility and improve usability of the Vaani dataset, encouraging the development of AI systems that better understand India's diverse languages and cater to the digital needs of its people.

Released in 2022 by IISc/ARTPARK and Google, Project Vaani is a pioneering initiative aimed at creating an open-source multi-modal dataset that truly represents India's linguistic diversity. This dataset is unique in its geo-centric approach, allowing for the collection of dialects and languages spoken in remote regions rather than focusing solely on mainstream languages.

Vaani targets the collection of over 150,000 hours of speech and 15,000 hours of transcribed text data from 1 million people across all 773 districts, ensuring diversity in language, dialects, and demographics.

Sources indicate that the dataset is being built in phases, with Phase 1 covering 80 districts, which has already been open-sourced. Phase 2 is currently underway, expanding the dataset to 100 more districts, further strengthening Vaani's reach and impact across India's diverse linguistic landscape.

This information is valuable for researchers, AI developers, and language technology innovators looking to build speech models tailored to specific regions and dialects. To explore the detailed district-wise language distribution, visit: Vaani Dataset on HuggingFace.

According to recent reports, if you need to access only transcribed data and you would like to skip untranscribed audio-only data, a subset of the larger dataset has been open sourced here. This dataset has 790 Hrs of transcribed audio, from ~7L speakers covering 70K images. This resource includes smaller, segmented audio units matched with precise transcriptions, allowing for different tasks including:.

This additional dataset complements the main Vaani dataset, making it possible to develop end-to-end speech recognition systems and more targeted AI solutions.

The Vaani dataset offers several key advantages, including extensive language coverage (54 languages), representation across diverse geographical regions, diverse educational and socio economic background, very large speaker coverage, spontaneous speech data, and real-life data collection environments. These features can enable inclusive AI models for:.

It has been revealed that these AI models can power a wide range of Conversational AI applications. From educational tools to telemedicine platforms, healthcare solutions, voter helplines, media localization, and multilingual smart devices, the Vaani dataset can be a game-changer in real-world scenarios.

According to recent reports, IISc/ARTPARK and Google have extended the partnership to Phase 2 (additional 100 districts). With this, Vaani covers all states in India! We are excited to bring this dataset to all of you.

Disney is making a $20 million bet on Character.ai. Here’s what it’s really buying

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that never pay peak hype prices for unproven technology.
  • Never pay peak hype prices for unproven technology.
  • The tech giant was once valued in the billions as a darling of the Silicon Valley consumer AI boom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that never pay peak hype prices for unproven technology. Chatbot startup Character.ai filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in Delaware after facing severe legal, regulatory, and operational pressures. The company was once valued in the billions as a darling of the Silicon Valley consumer AI boom. Now it is putting its assets up for a court-supervised sale that will wrap up by early December. If a buyer does not step up to purchase and run the whole platform, the service will shut down completely. Standing at the front of the line in bankruptcy court is the Walt Disney Co. Through its affiliate Disney Worldwide Services, the entertainment giant stepped in as the opening bidder with a $20 million offer for a nonexclusive, perpetual license to key Character.ai intellectual property. If you run a growing company, look closely at the sequence of events that led to this moment. Disney did not get swept up in fear of missing out during the height of the chatbot frenzy. Instead, the company executed a ruthless, patient acquisition strategy that every business leader should study. Enforce your boundaries before you negotiate  When a fast-moving startup uses your assets without permission, you do not have to rush into a reactive partnership. Before Disney ever put a bid on the table, it threatened Character.ai with legal action over copyright infringement and unauthorized chatbots using its characters. Other media executives panicked about falling behind in artificial intelligence. Disney simply held the line on its intellectual property. It watched the startup burn through cash trying to figure out an expensive consumer business model. At the same time, Character.ai faced mounting scrutiny over child safety and teen mental health lawsuits. You lose all negotiating power the moment you act desperate for a new trend. Protect your core assets first. Let unproven competitors absorb the early regulatory blows and compute costs on their own dime. Hire the brain trust directly  A technology company is only as valuable as the leaders and engineers sitting in the building. In 2024, Google proved this by rehiring Character.ai cofounders Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas. Google also paid for a nonexclusive licensing deal while leaving the stand-alone startup behind. Last month, Disney made its own surgical strike. Rather than buying the struggling company outright, Disney hired Character.ai CEO Karandeep Anand to serve as its chief technology officer. Several technical employees came over with him. Now, as part of the $20 million bankruptcy bid, Disney will use those former Character.ai employees to provide transition services during the court sale. Before you write a massive check to acquire a struggling competitor, ask yourself what you are actually buying. Often, you do not need the messy cap table or the legacy corporate entity. You just need the top three leaders who know how to build the product. Hire them directly. Isolate the technology from the liability  The smartest part of Disney’s $20 million offer is not what the company is buying. It is what the company is leaving behind. Character.ai is weighed down by devastating product liability claims. Families have alleged in lawsuits that its chatbots contributed to teenage self-harm and mental health crises. Earlier this year, Character.ai and Google agreed in principle to settle several of those cases, including a Texas lawsuit involving a teenager and limits on his screen time. The startup also carries the massive server costs of hosting millions of free users. Wait for the hype cycle to break Right now, dozens of AI startups are burning through venture capital without a clear path to profitability. Many of them have built impressive tools inside broken business models. Stop letting industry hype pressure you into rushing a deal. Whether you are looking to acquire a smaller competitor, buy software assets, or bring new technology into your business, patience is your greatest weapon. Wait for operational reality to set in, recruit the best builders when they are ready to jump ship, and buy the technology for pennies on the dollar when the bill finally comes due. —By Ash Kumra This article originally appeared on Fast Company’s sister website, Inc.com. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, AMD has set a new GPU overclocking world record by pushing the Radeon RX 9060 XT to 4,837 MHz.
  • According to recent reports, if you were expecting to see this record from AMD's high-end RX 9070 XT, you're not crazy.
  • According to recent reports, A UPCOMING @microcenter in Austin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, AMD has set a new GPU overclocking world record by pushing the Radeon RX 9060 XT to 4,837 MHz. Veteran overclocker Bill Alverson and AMD VP Jack Huynh found the limits of this particular chip as part of a celebration of the opening of a new Micro Center location in Austin, Texas. According to the OC World Record Museum database maintained by SkatterBencher, Huynh and Alverson set the new record on November 15.

According to recent reports, if you were expecting to see this record from AMD's high-end RX 9070 XT, you're not crazy. The record was indeed achieved using the midrange RDNA 4 part rather than AMD’s flagship GPU. The RX 9060 XT uses a smaller Navi 44 GPU featuring 2,048 shading units (32 compute units), a 160W TDP, 16GB of GDDR6 memory on a 128-bit bus, and a stock boost clock speed of up to 3,130 MHz.

According to recent reports, A UPCOMING @microcenter in Austin. An INCREDIBLE community. And a GPU WORLD RECORD. I had an absolute blast celebrating with Austin's gamers, PC builders, and creators. From meeting fans and snapping photos to building PCs and sharing our passion for all things tech. And then came an even BIGGER moment... I joined forces with Bill Alverson and our @AMD overclocking team. Armed with liquid nitrogen and pushing frequencies to the absolute limit, we set our sights on something MAJOR: breaking the GPU FREQUENCY WORLD RECORD! And we did it! 4.837 GHz! And we captured the whole thing on camera, including the moment we broke the record! Epic energy. Epic builds. WORLD RECORDS!November 24, 2026.

The upcoming frequency record was achieved using liquid nitrogen cooling. At 4,837 MHz, the GPU was running approximately 54.5% faster than its advertised boost frequency. A GPU-Z screenshot confirms the record breaking frequency with the GPU temperature at -49°C, 62W power draw, and voltage at 1.434V.

According to recent reports, of course, nobody should expect these numbers to bear any relationship to the clock speeds that can be achieved from any stock, air-cooled RX 9060 XT. Liquid nitrogen and liquid helium are commonly used in extreme overclocking, as they bring component temperatures well below what air and liquid cooling at ambient temperatures can achieve, essentially removing thermal limits from an overclocking attempt and enabling large amounts of power to be pushed into a chip for the highest clocks.

But these coolants require careful preparation of hardware, constant monitoring, and custom heatsinks to contain them while an extreme overclocking run is in progress, and they're only useful for short durations due to evaporation.

Such record-breaking frequencies are primarily intended to demonstrate the absolute limits of the hardware itself, rather than serve as an example of sustained performance for everyday use cases.

This isn’t the first time enthusiasts have pushed AMD’s RDNA 4 GPU to extreme frequencies. The RX 9060 XT previously reached 4,769 MHz in February 2026, followed by another attempt in June which reportedly reached 4,789 MHz. The latest attempt is 48 MHz higher compared to the previous record, bringing AMD’s latest GPU IP closer than ever to the elusive 5 GHz milestone.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

For the average gamer, the biggest obstacle to getting the most out of an RX 9060 XT isn't its overclocking headroom, but its high price in late 2026. The RX 9060 XT 16GB had an MSRP of just $349, but these cards are right now selling for over $700, making this formerly budget-friendly enthusiast card a poor value today. Achieving a world-record GPU frequency on one of these chips is an impressive achievement in extreme overclocking, but it's unlikely to translate into more Radeon gamers any time soon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the heart of a forest near the Newberry Volcano in central Oregon, a Texas company has struck a different kind of liquid gold than the other wildcatters searching for oil and gas.
  • In the heart of a forest near the Newberry Volcano in central Oregon, a Texas manufacturer has struck a different kind of liquid gold than the other wildcatters searching for oil and gas.
  • It has been revealed that mazama Energy has already drilled past 10,000 feet and is pushing toward a goal of over 15,000 to tap into the vast reserves of underground heat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the heart of a forest near the Newberry Volcano in central Oregon, a Texas company has struck a different kind of liquid gold than the other wildcatters searching for oil and gas. Mazama Energy has already drilled past 10,000 feet and is pushing toward a goal of over 15,000 to tap into the vast reserves of underground heat. The operation is part of a pilot program by the geothermal energy startup to prove it can dig deeper and create clean energy more cheaply than its competitors. Company CEO and president Sriram Vasantharajan calls the Oregon project a “proving ground,” a chance for the Frisco, Texas-based company to show that its approach can work even in states without a history of drilling. Mazama plans to plug into the grid to deliver power by 2029. “When you create that blueprint or template, you can then rinse and repeat,” Vasantharajan remarked. “That, to me, is when superhot rock has gone from just viable to creating a repeatable and bankable path to unleashing this incredible potential at scale.” Like many startups in Texas’s burgeoning geothermal sector, Mazama has deep roots in the oil and gas industry. (Shell and ConocoPhillips supported its last funding round, helping bring the company’s total funding to $171 million since its founding in 2023.) Vasantharajan worked in engineering and executive roles for both Mobil Oil and Blade Energy Partners—a fitting background, as much of the experience and technology needed to drill deep underground comes from long-term investments made by companies seeking to extract fossil fuels. How to Build Conference Talk Slides With AI Without Looking Generic

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1562 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Industry observers note that conference talks fail on slides more often than on content.
  • This article explains how conference slides differ from other decks, why AI-generated decks look generic and what specifically causes it, a workflow that uses an AI presentation maker for speed while keeping the talk distinctive, how to handle the slide types that matter most in a talk (the opening, the demonstration, the data, the close), and a checklist to run before the talk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Industry observers note that conference talks fail on slides more often than on content. The speaker knows the material and has something worth saying, but the deck is a wall of bullets, or a template everyone in the room has seen before, or forty slides for a twenty-minute slot. AI presentation makers can now produce a complete deck from an outline in minutes, which solves the time problem and creates a newly introduced one: the output tends toward exactly the uniform, stock-image, bullet-heavy style that audiences have learned to tune out.

This article explains how conference slides differ from other decks, why AI-generated decks look generic and what specifically causes it, a workflow that uses an AI presentation maker for speed while keeping the talk distinctive, how to handle the slide types that matter most in a talk (the opening, the demonstration, the data, the close), and a checklist to run before the talk.

A conference talk is spoken, timed and performed to a room. That changes the rules compared with a reading deck or a business presentation.

The causes are specific and therefore fixable.

Template uniformity. Every slide uses the same layout family, so the deck has no visual rhythm. Audiences read the sameness as mass-produced.

In a recent development, bullet default. Given a paragraph, the tool produces three to five bullets. Given twenty paragraphs, twenty bullet slides.

According to recent reports, stock imagery. Icons and photos chosen by keyword match the topic superficially and add no meaning. A talk about database indexing gets a picture of a filing cabinet.

Label titles. “Introduction”, “Background”, “Key Challenges”, “Conclusion”. Titles that name the category rather than make the point.

In a recent development, flattened emphasis. The tool does not know which of your ideas is the one the audience should leave with, so every slide gets equal weight.

In a recent development, no pacing. Every slide carries the same amount of content, so there is no build, no pause, no payoff.

Each of these is a default that can be overridden, either in how the input is prepared or in a short editing pass afterwards.

It has been revealed that step 1: Write the talk before the slides. Not a script necessarily, but the argument: what the audience knows at the start, what they know at the end, and the four to six moves that get them there. Write the one sentence you want them to repeat to a colleague afterwards. If this is not clear, no deck will fix it.

Step 2: Write the slide titles as the things you will say. Each title is a sentence, in your voice, that states the point of that moment in the talk. “Indexes make reads fast by making writes slower” is a title. “Index trade-offs” is not. Read the titles in order; they should be the talk in miniature.

Step 3: Mark the pacing. Next to each title, note whether the slide is a hold (a key point, stays up while you talk for a minute or more), a beat (a quick slide in a sequence), or a reveal (something shown, a demo, a result). This tells you where to put effort.

Step 4: Generate. Paste the titles with one or two sentences of content under each into an ai presentation maker. Ask for a slide count close to your title count. Pick the plainest theme available; distinctiveness will come from your content, not the template.

Step 5: Strip the bullets. On every hold slide, delete the bullets and leave the title, or the title plus one image or one number. On beat slides, keep at most one short line. The content that was in the bullets goes into speaker notes, which is where it belonged.

Step 6: Replace every stock image. Delete icons. Replace keyword-matched photos with your own material: a screenshot, a diagram you drew, a chart from your data, a photograph you took, a single large word. If a slide has no genuine visual, a title alone on a plain background is better than a filler image.

Step 7: Build the reveals by hand. Demos, before-and-after comparisons, the key chart. These are the slides the audience will remember, and they need more care than a generator can give. See the section below.

Step 8: Break the layout rhythm deliberately. Make the two or three most important slides look different: full-bleed image, a single enormous number, a black slide with one line of white text. Contrast is what makes a moment land.

It has been revealed that step 9: Rehearse with a timer. The slide count will be wrong in the first rehearsal. Cut, merge or split until the pacing matches the time.

The opening. Not a title slide with your name and a logo while you say hello. Open on something that earns attention: a surprising number, a question, a screenshot of the problem, a single provocative sentence. Your name and affiliation can come on slide two, or be said rather than shown.

It has been revealed that the problem statement. One slide, one sentence, stays up while you explain why the audience should care. No bullets.

According to recent reports, the demonstration. If the talk has a demo, record it. Live demos fail in rooms with unreliable connections and unfamiliar projectors. A recorded demo with the audio off, narrated live, gives the same effect with none of the risk. If you must go live, have the recording ready as a fallback.

In a recent development, the data. One chart per slide, one message per chart, the message in the title. Strip gridlines, legends and secondary series. Highlight the one line or bar that matters in colour and grey out the rest. Label directly. Type large enough to read from the back.

The “so what.” After the evidence, a slide that states what it means in one sentence. This is a hold slide; give it time.

The close. The one sentence you want them to repeat, alone on the final slide. Not “Thank you” or “Questions?”; those can be remarked. The last thing on screen while you take questions should be your point.

Because the slides are now sparse, two things need handling.

Sources indicate that first, the speaker notes must carry what you intend to say, in cue form: the key phrases, the number you must not forget, the transition to the next slide. The generator will have put the stripped bullet content there; edit it into cues rather than prose.

Sources indicate that second, the shared deck. Attendees who download a sparse deck afterwards get little from it. Options: export with notes visible; publish a companion blog post or document; or build a second “reading” version with more text on each slide. Many speakers do the first and link to a post.

Recent findings suggest that for a twenty-minute talk, fifteen to twenty-five slides is typical once hold and beat slides are counted. For a forty-five-minute talk, thirty to fifty. Build-up sequences of several quick beats inflate the count without inflating the time, which is fine. What is not fine is a deck of forty dense slides for twenty minutes; that is a talk that will run over and leave the audience behind.

Rehearse at least twice with a timer, once alone and once with a listener. Cut the content you rush. Nobody has ever complained that a talk finished two minutes early.

Lightning talks (five to ten minutes). Five to eight slides, almost all holds. One idea, one piece of evidence, one takeaway. Cut everything else.

Workshops and tutorials. More slides, more text, because attendees will refer back and follow along. The reading-deck rules apply more here; still, keep each step to one slide.

According to recent reports, panel contributions. Often no slides at all, or two or three for a specific point. Resist bringing a full deck.

Keynotes. Fewer slides, longer holds, more full-bleed images and single sentences. The speaker carries almost everything; the slides punctuate.

Remote talks. The screen is small and the audience is distracted. Larger type still, more frequent slide changes to hold attention, and a recorded demo is essential because screen-sharing a live one adds another failure point.

How much of the deck should the AI tool produce? The structural first draft: layouts, consistency, speaker notes populated. Expect to edit every slide and rebuild the key ones.

Is it acceptable to have slides with only a title? Yes, and it is often the strongest format for a spoken talk. The audience listens instead of reading.

Industry observers note that what about code on slides? Short excerpts only, in a large monospace type, with the relevant lines highlighted and the rest dimmed. Anything longer belongs in the companion post.

It has been revealed that should I use animations? Simple builds (revealing elements in sequence) help pacing. Transitions and effects distract. Keep to the former.

Recent findings suggest that how do I make the deck distinctive if I cannot design? Your material is what makes it distinctive: your screenshots, your data, your diagrams, your sentences. Design restraint plus real content beats decorated templates every time.

Coca-Cola ditched AI for its new holiday ad

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, after two years of AI-generated holiday ads that spawned plenty of real-world backlash, Coca-Cola went live-action for its latest holiday campaign.
  • After two years of AI-generated holiday ads that spawned plenty of real-world backlash, Coca-Cola went live-action for its latest holiday campaign.
  • Coca-Cola’s new spot “Enjoy Joy” shows real human actors as friends and family engaged in fall and winter activities, like playing football and having a turkey dinner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, after two years of AI-generated holiday ads that spawned plenty of real-world backlash, Coca-Cola went live-action for its latest holiday campaign. Coca-Cola’s latest spot “Enjoy Joy” shows real human actors as friends and family engaged in fall and winter activities, like playing football and having a turkey dinner. It ends with the word Enjoy written in its new tall, serifed typeface. Directed by Paul Dektor and produced by Mayan Productions, the commercial builds on last year’s “Refresh Your Holidays” campaign meant to position the soft drink brand as a point of connection between people during the holiday season. Unlike last year’s advertising, however, it’s human-made. A spokesperson for Coca-Cola tells Fast Company the spot was created without the use of generative AI. This year, brands have gone to great lengths to prove their ads aren’t AI as public opinion turns against the technology. Apple, Levi’s, Prada, and others took an analog, handcrafted approach to their recent advertising, and Coca-Cola is another data point in a trend. Still, the company states viewers shouldn’t read into the choice too much. “This does not signal a broader shift, as Coca-Cola continues to explore different creative approaches and emerging technologies to bring its storytelling to life,” says Madison Chandler, a spokesperson for the company. “Human storytellers remain at the center of the creative process, with AI serving as a tool to support and enhance creative expression where appropriate.” Coca-Cola was an early adopter to AI marketing, offering an online, AI-generated holiday card maker in 2023. It followed that up with its AI-generated remakes of “Holidays Are Coming” in 2024. Despite online criticism, it released yet another AI-generated ad last year that indicated AI-generated snowscapes, winter creatures, and localized elements for geo-specific media buys, like a “Welcome to Boston” billboard in Boston. While Coca-Cola’s AI-generated ads were picked apart on social media, the company mentioned those spots actually passed its own Christmas ad benchmarks. Pratik Thakar, Coca‑Cola’s global head of generative AI, has said the ads were a proof point for the possibilities of creating personalized, programmatic content at scale. Good numbers or not, it’s hard to deny that there’s been a vibe shift in the perception of AI advertising. An August Gallup poll found 62% of U.S. adults believe it’s “very” or “somewhat unacceptable” for businesses to use AI to create people or voices in ads, and 46% said the same thing about using AI to create the final text, image, or video. In 2024, market research firm NielsenIQ found that AI-generated advertising may have a negative brand halo, and that it elicits weaker memory activation. This year, Coca-Cola decided to embrace the trend and go human-made. But 2027? It’s a whole new year, and a whole new ad landscape.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A team at Google's DeepMind AI labs has performed a complete formal proof of the code that implements the encryption mechanism for the Signal private chat application. The scientists call their procedure AlphaProof Code and claim it can be applied to other situations requiring complete end-to-end verification of computer code, meaning Signal is safe, and you can find the full paper and the code repository detailing the proof.

More explicitly, the team reviewed an Arm-compiled version of libsignal, the library that the Signal application itself incorporates and uses, with some minimal scaffolding around it. Note that the verification wasn't done against the source code: it was purposely executed against an AArch64 binary, meaning the method can be reused for future verifications of other software.

In a similar vein to the AI labs' work on mathematics, the bulk of the work was done in Lean, a purpose-built language for formal proofs. There's a key difference for this effort, though. Lean is primarily used to prove the underlying math in algorithms, which in this case would be the specifications for Signal's encryption.

However, what the scientists actually did was create millions of lines of Lean proofs that were run against the actual implementation, in this case checking that the final binary executable corresponds to the initial specification.

It has been revealed that everyone knows about code tests in software development, but a mathematical proof of code is a different beast altogether, and one particularly elusive over the history of computing. It's akin to being able to check that an entire factory campus produces the actual parts it was designed to make, with the same exact inputs, with zero variation, no matter what else is happening.

Recent findings suggest that the DeepMind scientists mention previous year-long efforts in this vein to create formal proofs for relatively small pieces of software. The seL4 microkernel purportedly took twenty years to prove, while CompCert's C compiler took six. This may sound like going way overboard on software engineering, until you consider that remarked programs are now, in practical terms, bulletproof and cannot fail due to a code flaw, at least for the inputs they control.

While it'd be a questionable use of resources to formally prove all software on Earth, AlphaProof Code providing the ability to do so for mission-critical code like the Signal comms protocol is quite a boon.

Sources indicate that as an oversimplification, the actual AlphaProof Code workflow comprised various stages of back-and-forth between humans and Gemini 4 Carbon agents. The first steps were laying out the groundwork and infrastructure. The team defined the base scope of work, and then created textual bot skills to prepare agents for their future tasks, among them specification writers, proof workers, and orchestration.

Then, it was time to have agents create the first set of Lean definitions for AArch64 instructions, how registers, memory, and system calls work, and how Linux processes operate. At this point, however, nothing is proven about Signal or any other application. That came next, as the team and its army of agents drafted fully revised specifications for libsignal's cryptography implementation. This then generated just over 1.2 million lines of Lean, for checking the mathematical reasoning behind the protocol.

The bulk of the agentic work was generating 5.3 million lines of Lean to verify that each binary instruction matched the previously defined AArch64, CPU, and process formal behaviors. During this stage, the agent flagged one percent of the codebase for humans to review and verify. When it was all complete, the team had fully verified that the cryptographic engine in the binary did indeed match all the generated proofs, down to the last processed bit.

As the researchers point out: "the most important lesson from our experience is that, once proofs become cheap, the hard question is what to prove," adding that "the majority of our effort went not into proofs but into specifications," and underscoring that this is particularly important for software topics like cryptography.

Interestingly, they mention that "writing specifications against real code also turned out to be a stress test for the literature," an insightful note on verifying that one did write the software's specifications properly to begin with.

Recent findings suggest that with the disclaimer that this is a note about security in general and we think Signal is indeed top-notch as a private messaging application: Google's team "only" proved that libsignal works exactly as advertised. If a malicious actor were to booby-trap the Signal app — or any other one — with additional code to copy your messages, this sort of proof likely wouldn't catch it. Likewise, the fact that a third-party app implements the Signal protocol for encryption doesn't automatically mean it offers full privacy.

According to recent reports, bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music indicates and festivals.

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, somewhere inside a hollowed-out volcano, a bald man stroking a white cat is playing a Barry White LP and dimming down his lair’s halogens with the F4 lighting console.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Somewhere inside a hollowed-out volcano, a bald man stroking a white cat is playing a Barry White LP and dimming down his lair’s halogens with the F4 lighting console. Or perhaps operating an orbital weapon. I want one. The control panel. The orbital weapon, too. Maybe a synthetic polar bear rug while we’re at it. Designed and made by Sacrebleu, a one-person workshop in Washington state run by Alex Dufetel, the F4 is a home automation console that resembles a tiny audio mixing board. The 13 x 7.5 x 3.5-inch device has four motorized faders, a fat aluminum knob, four metal keys, and a small screen, all wrapped in walnut. [Photo: Sacrebleu] It costs $1,700. It does absolutely nothing my phone can’t already do, but who cares. I just can’t resist the ’70s vibes. And physical controls are just better. While manufacturers avoid them to save on costs, many people want them back. As Dufetel tells me, “Our hands want physical feedback: something to push against, and a response they can feel.” Dufetel used to run a Meta team working on how people interact with virtual and augmented reality (remember Zuck’s metaverse?). The F4 is 2,000% a much better use of his talent and time. Just look at the faders. They work like the motorized sliders on a significant recording studio desk. They move by themselves. If you dim your original 1962 Flos Arco lamp—because, if you have $1,700 to sink into a lighting console, you have an original Arco lamp—in your living room using your phone’s home automation app, the matching fader glides down following your finger. The big knob allows you to dim a whole room in one go or, with a press, connect to another room in your house. When you do that, the four faders slide into place to mirror that room’s lights. If you move a fader, your phone will reflect the change. And, if you put a thumb on a fader midslide, the motor simply gives up. “Your hand wins,” as the organization puts it. Overengineered for Warp 9 nerd joy Each of the faders can run a single lamp or a group of lamps. You can also set them to change color temperature or even color instead of brightness, if your light can produce different hues. The four metal keys are for saved scenes, four per room. Oh, and if a light doesn’t dim, the fader goes into what Dufetel calls “snap mode”: it fights your thumb for a moment, then slams to the end of its travel, imitating the way a toggle does it. There’s no spring or detent inside. “The motor does all of it,” Dufetel tells me. As you push, the motor pushes back harder and harder, “then past a certain point it lets go and drives the fader the rest of the way, so it snaps over like a wall switch.” He tuned that feel by hand at his bench. [Photo: Sacrebleu] It doesn’t stop at lighting. You can use the knob as a volume dial for Sonos or any other speaker hooked up to Home Assistant. The 2.4-inch AMOLED screen reveals the track information, because of course it does. It’s small and mostly monochrome on purpose, though. “The screen isn’t meant to be the hero of the product,” Dufetel states. The F4 talks to the hub you probably already own, whether it’s Philips Hue, Lutron Caséta, or Home Assistant, the open-source platform that can run lights from Ikea, Lifx, Nanoleaf, and others. [Photo: Sacrebleu] Dufetel writes that the console grew out of “a nostalgia for old hi-fi gear: solid materials, and controls you could feel.” He tells me that, if he had to name one influence from the stereos he grew up with, he says, “it would be the old Marantz receivers, with their wood cases and aluminum controls.” The four faders come from Alps, a Japanese component maker, he says in his FAQ. The keys are NKK switches. According to the designer, the knob, key caps, and front panel are anodized aluminum cut from solid stock. The oiled walnut case comes out of his workshop near Seattle, its four sides mitered from a single plank “so the grain wraps around the corners,” he tells me. He designed it to stay on the table for decades. Sacrebleu is taking $50 refundable deposits on 100 units, with shipping beginning sometime after March 2027 to the U.S. and Canada for now (you can add your name to an international waiting list). It comes with a two-year warranty and a 30-day return window. My favorite thing about Dufetel’s physical gadget pitch is the last item in his FAQ: “Couldn’t I just use my phone to control my lights?” The answer is three words long: “Yes, you could.” Would Blofeld use a phone app to control his laser to kill Bond? Yeah. Exactly.

A Deepdive into Aya Vision: Advancing the Frontier of Multilingual Multimodality

📅 04 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1624 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With the release of the Aya Vision family, our new 8B and 32B parameter vision-language models (VLMs), we are addressing one of the biggest challenges in AI: bringing multilingual performance to multimodal models.
  • Recent findings suggest that aya Vision is Cohere For AI's latest open-weight multilingual and multimodal model family, designed to be a strong foundation for language and vision understanding across 23 languages.
  • As a result, our models perform well in a variety of tasks, including image captioning, visual question answering, text generation, and translating both text and images into clear, natural-language text.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the release of the Aya Vision family, our new 8B and 32B parameter vision-language models (VLMs), we are addressing one of the biggest challenges in AI: bringing multilingual performance to multimodal models.

Recent findings suggest that aya Vision is Cohere For AI's latest open-weight multilingual and multimodal model family, designed to be a strong foundation for language and vision understanding across 23 languages. It builds on the success of Aya Expanse, state-of-the-art multilingual language models, and extends it using a combination of advanced techniques. These include synthetic annotations, scaling up multilingual data through translation and rephrasing, and multimodal model merging – key methods that improve both language and vision understanding in a multilingual setting.

As a result, our models perform well in a variety of tasks, including image captioning, visual question answering, text generation, and translating both text and images into clear, natural-language text. We evaluated Aya Vision models on a set of datasets, including our upcoming open-ended vision-language benchmark AyaVisionBench and a multilingual version of Wild Vision Bench (mWildVision) that is translated into 23 languages, which we release both of them for research.

In pair-wise comparison, Aya Vision 32B outperforms models more than 2x of its size, such as Llama-3.2 90B Vision, Molmo 72B, and Qwen2.5-VL 72B by win rates ranging from 50% to 64% on AyaVisionBench and 52% to 72% on mWildVision average across 23 languages.

Our compact and more efficient model Aya Vision 8B achieves the best performance in multilingual multimodal in its parameter class, outperforming leading models such as Qwen2.5-VL 7B, Pixtral 12B, Gemini Flash 1.5 8B, Llama-3.2 11B Vision, Molmo-D 7B, and Pangea 7B by up to 79% win-rates on AyaVisionBench and 81% on mWildBench.

In a recent development, we release both 8B and 32B models as open weights for the research community to further accelerate multilingual multimodal progress. In this blog post, we share the key technical details behind Aya Vision models.

Industry observers note that for a high-performance vision-language model, it is notable to process images with arbitrary resolutions, especially high-resolution images. To enable this capability in Aya Vision, we dynamically resize and split any higher-resolution images into multiple tiles to generate rich image features from the image encoder. In Aya Vision models, we use the recently released SigLIP2-patch14-384 model as the initialization for the vision encoder.

While dynamic resizing enables processing high-resolution images, it also leads to a larger number of image tokens passing through the vision-language connector and LLM decoder. To improve latency and throughput, we use a downsampling method called Pixel Shuffle, to compress the number of image tokens by 4x. After downsampling, image tokens are aligned to the language model input embeddings through a vision-language connector and passed to an LLM decoder.

Recent findings suggest that for the text decoder, we use our multilingual language models. For Aya Vision 8B, we use an LLM that is initialized from Cohere Command R7B for improved instruction following and world knowledge and further post-trained using the Aya Expanse recipe consisting of diverse multilingual data, model merging, and preference training. For Aya Vision 32B, we initialize the language model from Aya Expanse 32B based on its state-of-the-art multilingual performance.

Recent findings suggest that we trained Aya Vision models in 2 stages – vision-language alignment and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). In the vision-language alignment stage, only the vision-language connector is trained, while the vision encoder and the language model weights are kept frozen. This enables rudimentary vision-language understanding by mapping the image encoder features to the language model embedding space. In the SFT stage, we train both the connector and the language model on a diverse set of multimodal tasks in 23 languages.

According to recent reports, one of the biggest challenges in developing a multilingual vision-language model is ensuring strong performance across underrepresented languages. To address this, we first gather synthetic annotations using a diverse pool of high-quality datasets in English, which lay the basis for our multilingual multimodal annotation. Following the synthetic annotations of English datasets, we translated a large volume of the data into 23 languages. To avoid translation artefacts and maintain fluent textual characteristics with high precision in answers, we then rephrased translated prompt/generation pairs by matching them with the original high-quality synthetic samples, expanding language coverage where real-world datasets are scarce. This improves both linguistic fluency and alignment between vision and text, allowing Aya Vision to exhibit superior image understanding in multiple languages.

Our 8B model, when only supervised fine-tuned with original academic datasets, reaches a 40.9% win rate across 23 languages in AyaVisionBench against Pangea 7B, which is a multilingual VLM, whereas synthetic annotations and scaling up the multilingual data lead to a 58.1% win rate with a gain of 17.2%. This significant improvement showcases the impact of significant investment in multilingual data coverage.

Recent findings suggest that A state-of-the-art vision-language model should excel not only in image understanding but also in conversational context, where the model is expected to generate a high-quality response to both image and text inputs. To address this, inspired by our previous research on model merging, a technique that combines multiple trained models, we merge the base language model with the fine-tuned vision-language model.

Model merging enhances the generative capabilities of our final model that leads to a 70% win rates across 23 languages on AyaVisionBench against Pangea 7B, improving the multimodal win rate by 11.9% compared to the model before merging.

Multimodal model merging also enables our Aya Vision models to excel in text-only tasks as measured in mArenaHard datasets compared with the other leading vision-language models.

Finally, we scale our recipe from 8B to 32B, resulting in the state-of-the-art open-weight multilingual vision-language model – Aya Vision 32B which reveals significant improvements in win rates due to the stronger initialization of the text-backbone, and outperforms models more than 2x of its size, such as Llama-3.2 90B Vision, Molmo 72B, and Qwen2.5-VL 72B by win rates ranging from 49% to 63% on AyaVisionBench and 52% to 72% on mWildVision average across 23 languages.

Together with Aya Vision models, we also release a high-quality multilingual vision-language benchmark called AyaVisionBench, constructed based on real-world applications, covering 23 languages and 9 distinct task categories, with 135 image-question pairs per language.

Sources indicate that we make this evaluation set available to the research community to push forward multilingual multimodal evaluations. This dataset is designed to assess a model’s ability to perform a diverse range of vision-language tasks, including captioning, chart and figure understanding, identifying differences between two images, general visual question answering, OCR, document understanding, text transcription, reasoning involving logic and math, and converting screenshots to code. By incorporating multiple languages and task types, the dataset provides a broad and challenging evaluation framework for assessing cross-lingual and multimodal understanding.

To create this dataset, we first selected images from the Cauldron held-out test set, a large collection derived from 50 high-quality datasets, ensuring they had not been seen during training. For each image, we then generated a corresponding question that explicitly required visual context for an answer. These questions were synthetically generated and subsequently refined through a two-stage verification process. First, human annotators reviewed and validated each question to ensure it was clear, relevant, and truly dependent on the image. This rigorous selection and validation process ensures that the dataset serves as a robust benchmark for evaluating vision-language models in multilingual and real-world settings.

In a recent development, communication happens in many forms and in many languages. With our leading research and development, we’ve released a model that facilitates connection, whether in text or visual, in 23 different languages today.

It has been revealed that aya Vision has a wide range of practical applications, where one notable example is its availability on WhatsApp, one of the most broadly used communications platforms in the world. This allows a massive audience of global citizens who speak a multitude of languages to utilize the capabilities of Aya Vision on a platform they use to communicate every single day.

Black Friday is bad for the planet. These brands are opting out

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Black Friday is an environmental disaster.
  • In a recent development, researchers from the University of Leeds in the U.K.
  • The term “Black Friday” goes back to the 1950s, when the police in Philadelphia used the term for the chaos after Thanksgiving when suburban shoppers flooded the city.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Friday is an environmental disaster. Researchers from the University of Leeds in the U.K. found that up to 80% of items bought on that day, along with the plastic packaging they come in, end up in a landfill, incineration, or at best, low-quality recycling. All this after a very short time of use, sometimes as little as a few weeks. Shipping contributes to the damage; emissions from trucking spike 94% during the week including Black Friday. The term “Black Friday” goes back to the 1950s, when the police in Philadelphia used the term for the chaos after Thanksgiving when suburban shoppers flooded the city. In 1961, the city’s merchants tried and failed to rename it “Big Friday.” In the 1980s, the retail industry tried to reconceptualize it as the day that they go from being in the red to being in the black. Today, however, Black Friday is no longer a day. It’s an entire season stretching from late October to early December. And as a marketing ploy, it works well: Americans spent a record $11.8 billion online on Black Friday last year. The urgency of shopping these deals often leads to regret: 42% of shoppers in one survey conducted by Self Financial, a credit building tech giant, noted they wished they hadn’t made at least one Black Friday purchase. According to the National Retail Federation, retailers expect 17% of holiday sales to be returned, and roughly 9.5 billion pounds of returned merchandise goes into U.S. landfills every year. Opting out is bad for business. Black Friday weekend is one of the most lucrative stretches in the retail year, as consumers are primed to open their wallets. But a handful of brands is choosing to take a stand and abstain from sales. Here are brands that are confirmed to opt out on November 27. REI The outdoor co-op first chose to skip Black Friday in 2015 with its “Opt Outside” launch, starting a national conversation about Black Friday’s impact. And while the brand lost sales that Friday, it led to a major brand boost in the form of social impressions. In 2022, REI decided to make its store closure on the day permanent. All REI stores, distribution centers, call centers, and headquarters will be closed. Customers can still order online, and fulfillment resumes the next day. On its website, REI offers ideas for opting outside. Instead of shopping, it encourages customers to go on a hike, a neighborhood walk, or a picnic in the park. That sure sounds more pleasant than endlessly refreshing social media for newly introduced deals. Patagonia Patagonia declared war on Black Friday in 2011 when it took out a full-page New York Times ad telling people “Don’t buy this jacket.” This year, it has no Black Friday sale. It has a Black Friday microsite that pokes fun at the false sense of urgency the day often entails. It states that its emphasis on creating high quality gear “is an unlimited time deal that has nothing to do with Black Friday or Cyber Monday. Honestly, the best jacket is the one you already own.” Its website remains open on Black Friday, but there is no sale. Instead, the brand encourages you to shop its secondhand “Worn Wear” collection. In a radical move Patagonia recently put its secondhand products alongside its new products on its website. And if you do choose to buy something new, it encourages you to buy products that will last a lifetime, and offers care and repair guides. More importantly, it lays out ways to give back, including its network of grassroots environmental nonprofits. The Ordinary (Deciem) When Deciem first went dark on Black Friday in 2019, it called the closure “a moment of nothingness” and encouraged customers to “buy less, but better.” On November 27, the websites for all of Deciem’s brands—The Ordinary, Niod, Loopha and The Chemistry Brand—will be closed, as will its standalone stores. Instead, it will transform stores, including those in New York and Toronto, into sites for a blood drive. In its London and Copenhagen stores, it will invite customers to identify their blood type, so they can be equipped to participate in other blood drives. Lush Lush doesn’t run Black Friday sales. The company says its prices reflect the true cost of its ingredients, such as the organic Peruvian jojoba oil in its Gorgeous moisturizer. Instead, it has long used the day for activism. In 2016, it “switched off” its websites around the world on Black Friday, drawing people’s attention to the nonprofit Access Now. In 2021, it chose Black Friday to announce that it was quitting a number of social media channels; Mark Constantine, the CEO, said he was “happy to lose” $13 million. In the U.K., Lush stores will be using the Black Friday and Cyber Monday period to raise money through Charity Pot, a lotion that funds grassroots groups. Freitag The Zurich bag maker, which launched in 1993 creating bags from old truck tarps, has been saying no to Black Friday since 2019, encouraging customers: “Don’t shop, just swap.” Since then, its online store has been closed every Black Friday, and visitors are redirected to S.W.A.P. (Shopping Without Any Payment), its bag exchange platform. Over the years, Freitag has offered fun swap events at its stores. The company hasn’t revealed its 2026 aims yet, but it’s a good bet that it won’t be running a Black Friday sale. Veja The French sneaker brand hasn’t held a Black Friday sale since 2017 and apart from its outlets, it doesn’t offer any discounts. Instead, it has turned the day into “Repair Friday.” In 2024, it invited people to its Paris headquarters to have things repaired by experts for free, from shoes and clothing to furniture, computers, and phones. In 2025, every Veja cobbler offered two hours of free repairs, and anyone could drop off one pair of sneakers from any brand. (Veja provides shoe repair in nine stores in Europe, North and South America.) Veja hasn’t announced its 2026 plans yet.

Industry News: US blacklists Megaspeed, but leaves potential loophole for lower-performance chips

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (764 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Department of Commerce has added Megaspeed and six affiliated entities to its Entity List due to concerns about diversion of advanced AI accelerators to China.
  • Chris McGuire, a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and a former Biden administration official who dealt with export controls at the National Security Council, noted that neither Megaspeed nor any of the six associated entities received a so-called Footnote 4 designation on the Entity List.
  • McGuire claims that without the application of the Entity List-specific FDPR, the new restrictions will have essentially no effect on Megaspeed's ability to procure Nvidia's AI processors since, while they are developed in the U.S., the vast majority of them are produced by TSMC in Taiwan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Department of Commerce has added Megaspeed and six affiliated entities to its Entity List due to concerns about diversion of advanced AI accelerators to China. However, unlike previous additions of companies suspected of similar activities, the department did not apply a special foreign direct product rule (FDPR) designation to Megaspeed, which raised questions about the effectiveness of the restrictions. While the omission potentially limits the scope of the sanctions, existing U.S. export controls should still restrict Megaspeed's access to advanced processors from AMD and Nvidia. Former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset, is the woman at the heart of the Jensen Huang scandal, which saw Nvidia's CEO resign and then be reinstated as head of the organization in recent days.

Chris McGuire, a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and a former Biden administration official who dealt with export controls at the National Security Council, noted that neither Megaspeed nor any of the six associated entities received a so-called Footnote 4 designation on the Entity List. According to McGuire, the Department of Commerce had previously applied the designation to Chinese companies blacklisted over concerns about their access to advanced AI processors.

McGuire claims that without the application of the Entity List-specific FDPR, the new restrictions will have essentially no effect on Megaspeed's ability to procure Nvidia's AI processors since, while they are developed in the U.S., the vast majority of them are produced by TSMC in Taiwan.

Industry observers note that while McGuire acknowledged that upcoming U.S. export controls that took effect on November 19 already require licenses for shipments of high-end AI accelerators to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil, with exemptions for U.S.-based companies and their subsidiaries (i.e., Google or Microsoft can get Rubin-based machines for their data centers in the noted countries, but Megaspeed or other local players cannot), he questioned the rationale behind Megaspeed's addition to the Entity List without Footnote 4.

It is necessary to note that the new country-wide controls impose a license requirement, not an outright ban, whereas the addition of Megaspeed to the Entity List subjects license applications to a presumption of denial, which is a reason why the designation has practical effect even without Footnote 4. Meanwhile, McGuire suggested that the omission could be either a regulatory oversight or a deliberate decision to reduce the scope of restrictions.

Companies on the Entity List typically cannot procure products subject to the U.S. Export Administration Regulations (EAR) without a license from the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS). Such license applications are reviewed with a presumption of denial, and this certainly concerns Megaspeed and entities linked to it. Footnote 4 substantially expands the scope of products subject to the EAR to include foreign-made goods that use American technology or are made using American technologies.

In a recent development, meanwhile, advanced AI accelerators from AMD and Nvidia are already subject to a separate Advanced Computing FDPR (§734.9(h) of the EAR), which has worldwide geographical coverage irrespective of where the chips are made. In fact, BIS explicitly retained the worldwide scope of this provision in its November 19 amendments to the EAR. Therefore, Megaspeed's addition to the Entity List should effectively cut the firm off from qualifying advanced AI accelerators even in the absence of Footnote 4.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

It has been revealed that what the absence of Footnote 4 could mean, though, is that Megaspeed may retain access to certain foreign-made lower-performance AI GPUs, networking chips, and other data center hardware that falls outside the scope of the EAR. At this point, it remains unclear whether the Department of Commerce deliberately opted for a narrower set of restrictions.

Meanwhile, Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry revealed on Tuesday that it would advise all data center operators in the country against the provision of infrastructure, space, or services to the seven blacklisted entities, a move that could affect Megaspeed's ability to operate its existing AI infrastructure in Malaysia, regardless of the scope of U.S. export restrictions.

#127578. Breaking: This Thanksgiving, let’s just not talk about AI

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1419 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: This Thanksgiving, let’s just not talk about AI

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1419 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that maybe we just don’t talk about AI this Thanksgiving.
  • Maybe we just don’t talk about AI this Thanksgiving.
  • Of course, we need some common conversation topics to throw around the dining room with friends and relatives we haven’t seen in a while.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that maybe we just don’t talk about AI this Thanksgiving. Of course, we need some common conversation topics to throw around the dining room with friends and relatives we haven’t seen in a while. And though AI seems to be showing up everywhere now, we still have a lot of other stuff to talk about—sports, food, movies, and the like. Or there’s always that thing where you go around the table and everybody notes something they’re thankful for. Unless somebody actually says “Claude” (which is fine). Mostly there are good reasons to avoid the subject of AI at your gathering this year. Too political. Talking politics in mixed firm at the Thanksgiving table can have unpredictable, sometimes explosive results. AI has become very political, mainly because of AI data centers. A surprising number of midterm voters cited an aversion to new AI data centers as the main rationale for their swing toward Democrats. Studies have shown that data centers do indeed contribute to rising energy costs, not to mention the noise pollution they produce. In fact, data centers are already so prevalent that there’s a decent chance one of your Thanksgiving guests lives near one. (You may recognize them by the way they keep saying, “Huh? What? Huh?”) Sore subject. Too technical. The last major tech wave, mobile computing, was pretty easy to conceptualize. They turned cellphones into internet devices with big screens and made computer programs called apps to run on them. AI is different. Very few laypeople can explain how a neural network is trained and how it operates. Even PhDs don’t know exactly how AI models develop new skills, some of which have come as a complete surprise. That creates a problem for Thanksgiving conversation. Somebody at the table who listens to a lot of podcasts may seize the moment to nerd-splain AI to everybody. Or worse, they may go on and on about how LLMs are just stochastic parrots—word-guessing machines that will never be capable of anything more. Pedantry, jargon, and boredom will waft through the air around the table. With luck, the speaker will take the blank stares looking back at him as a signal to put a turkey leg in his mouth. Too painful. Somebody at the table might own a bunch of Nvidia or SpaceX stock and get depressed. Or somebody might remind everybody that their retirement accounts are already bound up in risky AI-dependent stocks like SpaceX. Someone may gaze up from their stuffing with a faraway look and recall those simpler times when Jensen Huang was a one-woman man and everybody believed that all the AI companies buying up Nvidia GPUs would actually be able to pay for them, with nary a revenue stream to match. Heady days! They are over. Nvidia has lost 20% of its value this year because maybe bankrolling your profit-free customers the cash to buy your product isn’t the most sustainable business initiative. So just don’t bring it up; heavy drinking may ensue. Too personal. Don’t ask people what they use AI for. It can lead to some bad places. Just last year, a 22-year-old sitting across the table from me began talking about all the personal stuff she discussed with ChatGPT. I rapidly tuned her out, of course, but there was something in there about an antifungal cream, a GLP-1 “crisis,” and a neurodivergent ex-boyfriend. Too anxiety-inducing. Somebody in the house Thursday may have that soon-to-be-unemployed vibe about them, and it’s quite possible that an AI has already learned to do their job. Challenger, Gray & Christmas found that AI was the top-stated reason for U.S. job cuts through October. Soon that person will be spending their days in the uncanny valley, doing video interviews with wooden-faced AI avatars, only to be passed over (and over) by a candidate-screening algorithm that was offended by their Zoom background. On a more serious, and more anxious, note, whether people realize it or not, our relationship with AI is pretty different from what it was at this time last year. The models aren’t perfect, or even trustworthy in some applications, but they’ve clearly become more intelligent. We hear about teams of AI agents working tirelessly on big problems, coding agents building entire apps, and models solving some of the world’s hardest math problems. We may be headed for a world where we coexist with coequal, nonbiological intelligences that are generally as smart as humans. Discussing where this is all headed can make for an uncomfortable conversation, and not one suitable for a holiday gathering. I’d leave it be this Thanksgiving. Turkey legs and existential angst just aren’t a good mix. The trouble is, AI has seeped into everything, raising the constant question: How is AI affecting this? So you must listen closely for signs of conversational drift toward the AI thing and have some safe, go-to topics ready to throw in. Like these: Remember the World Cup this summer? Wasn’t that nice? For the first time in a while, I felt a tinge of real national pride as I watched the crowds of foreign football fans having a ball alongside Americans in our cities and stadiums. Americans got rave reviews for their hospitality—everybody from Uber drivers to hotel staff to strangers who helped our international guests get around. My favorites were those videos of Europeans discovering the simple joy of chicken tenders, pizza, and french fries slathered in ranch dressing. Returning to the moon. In April, NASA’s Artemis II mission sent a crew of astronauts on a loop around the moon, taking them 252,756 miles from Earth—farther than any humans had ever traveled. They spotted a crater on the lunar surface and named it after the crew commander’s late wife, Carroll. The return of the jaguar. A jaguar nicknamed “Cinco” is roaming southern Arizona’s mountains, only the fifth jaguar seen there since monitoring began 15 years ago. Researchers say it’s the latest sign that the endangered species may be gaining a foothold in the region. They also say that Cinco has a distinctive mark on its face that resembles Groucho Marx’s mustache. Beating cancer. For the first time, 70% of Americans diagnosed with cancer survive at least five years, the American Cancer Society says. In the mid-1970s, only half did. Fewer overdose deaths. U.S. overdose deaths fell about 14% in 2025, the third straight annual drop and the longest decline in decades, according to provisional data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. And finally, Costco’s hot dog and soda combo still costs $1.50, the same as it did in 1985. You can thank me later. Happy Thanksgiving.

Maybe we just don’t talk about AI this Thanksgiving.

Of course, we need some common conversation topics to throw around the dining room with friends and relatives we haven’t seen in a while. And though AI seems to be showing up everywhere now, we still have a lot of other stuff to talk about—sports, food, movies, and the like. Or there’s always that thing where you go around the table and everybody states something they’re thankful for. Unless somebody actually says “Claude” (which is fine).

Mostly there are good reasons to avoid the subject of AI at your gathering this year.

On a more serious, and more anxious, note, whether people realize it or not, our relationship with AI is pretty different from what it was at this time last year. The models aren’t perfect, or even trustworthy in some applications, but they’ve clearly become more intelligent.

It has been revealed that we hear about teams of AI agents working tirelessly on big problems, coding agents building entire apps, and models solving some of the world’s hardest math problems. We may be headed for a world where we coexist with coequal, nonbiological intelligences that are generally as smart as humans. Discussing where this is all headed can make for an uncomfortable conversation, and not one suitable for a holiday gathering. I’d leave it be this Thanksgiving. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are pleased to announce our partnership with JFrog, creators of the JFrog Software Supply Chain Platform, as part of our long-standing commitment to provide a safe and reliable platform for the ML community.
  • Sources indicate that we have decided to add JFrog's scanner to our platform to continue improving security on the Hugging Face Hub.
  • Interested in joining our security partnership / providing scanning information on the Hub?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are pleased to announce our partnership with JFrog, creators of the JFrog Software Supply Chain Platform, as part of our long-standing commitment to provide a safe and reliable platform for the ML community.

Sources indicate that we have decided to add JFrog's scanner to our platform to continue improving security on the Hugging Face Hub. JFrog's scanner brings new functionality to scanning, aimed at reducing false positives on the Hub. Indeed, what we currently observe is that model weights can contain code that is executed upon deserialization and sometimes at inference time, depending on the format. This code is oftentimes a non harmful practicality for the developer. As our picklescan scanner only performs pattern matching on module names, we cannot always confirm that usage of a given function or module is malicious. JFrog goes a step deeper and will parse and analyze code it finds in models weights to check for potential malicious usage.

Interested in joining our security partnership / providing scanning information on the Hub? Please get in touch with us over at security@huggingface.co.

Sources indicate that to share models, we serialize weights, configs and other data structures we use to interact with the models, in order to facilitate storage and transport. Some serialization formats are vulnerable to nasty exploits, such as arbitrary code execution (looking at you pickle), making shared models that use those formats potentially dangerous.

As Hugging Face has become a popular platform for model sharing, we’d like to help protect the community from this, hence why we have developed tools like picklescan and why we are integrating JFrog in our scanner suite.

Pickle is not the only exploitable format out there, see for reference how one can exploit Keras Lambda layers to achieve arbitrary code execution. The good news is that JFrog catches both of these exploits and more in additional file formats – see their Model Threats page for up to date scanner information.

Read all our documentation on security here: https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/security 🔥.

There's nothing you have to do to benefit from this! All public model repositories will be scanned by JFrog automatically as soon as you push your files to the Hub. Here is an example repository you can check out to see the feature in action: mcpotato/42-eicar-street.

Note that you might not see a scan for your model as of today, as we have millions of model repos. It may take us some time to catch up 😅.

In total, we have already scanned hundreds of millions of files, because we believe that empowering the community to share models in a safe and frictionless manner will lead to growth for the whole field.
