#127576. Industry News: The surprising — and fun — way brands are AI-proofing themselves

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1664 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The surprising — and fun — way brands are AI-proofing themselves

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1664 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Play is becoming the route to making truly creative, human work.
  • Industry observers note that play is becoming the route to making truly creative, human work.
  • Industry observers note that externally, that impulse is showing up everywhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Play is becoming the route to making truly creative, human work. As AI makes polished output cheap, abundant, and instantaneous, brands are increasingly looking to offer expressions of character, and ways to stand apart from the inevitable homogenization of content and communications. Externally, that impulse is showing up everywhere. Brands are lifting the lid on the creative process through behind-the-scenes content, embracing deliberately handmade visual expression and even using “No AI” disclaimers, like recent campaigns from Apple or Aerie.Each is an attempt to signal the presence of human thought and distinguish meaningful creative work from the flood of so-called slop. Internally too, creativity is the priority. A Marketing Week study in 2025 found that almost two-thirds of brand marketers had increased their focus on creative quality, while 63.9% rated it among the more influential factors in marketing effectiveness. Yet striving for more creativity is not the same as knowing how to enable it. Brand managers are often asked to protect consistency, reduce risk, and deliver at speed. Briefs are often loaded with history, data, and preconceptions; teams are rewarded for control; often, ideas are filtered out before they have room to develop. And the idea of true creativity can be abstract, intimidating, and unattainable. Play might sound unserious in that environment. But in fact, it can be a working method, helpful and inspiring; permission to experiment and make unexpected connections, combined with the expertise to select and execute the right idea. Unlocking its commercial advantage requires leaders to rethink how they brief teams, frame creativity, and manage brands. Here’s how to get started. Make room to play Original thinking needs guardrails, but also room to grow. A strong brief should get teams to the point where they can begin exploring, not overwhelm them with years of history and layers of data. The best chief marketing officers or brand managers get it. They do the research in advance, then set out the ambition for the brand with a suggested set of parameters and say “go and play’”(as Chris Willingham, CMO at Brompton Bicycle, did in our recent work together), offering clarity and trust to create the conditions for better work. This also makes the notion of creativity less obscure or intimidating. “Get creative” can feel like a loose and impossibly lofty instruction. “Go and play” is an invitation to explore. It shifts the focus from finding the right answer immediately to following ideas and seeing where they lead. The wrong idea can still reveal the right solution; rejected routes also clarify what a brand is not. Play demystifies creativity without lowering the standard. One time, a workwear manufacturer client challenged us to create something that looked deliberately “not right.” It was the perfect invitation to play, and resulted in a design that felt structured and familiar but punctuated by unusual interactions. Play to consumer intelligence Alongside a change in language needs to come an appreciation of a changing consumer and their needs. Brand consistency once offered reassurance. But today, the consumer expects their brands to be more animated, dynamic, nimble and responsive to the times we’re living in. Like people, brands can—and should—have different facets. Reliable in one moment, spontaneous or surprising in another. Wise, the money transfer platform, is a great example of a brand getting that balance right; the experience feels trustworthy, but also conversational, quirky, and human. Interactions with Wise are like talking to my intelligent, funny friend. It is an experience miles ahead of what banks like Barclays offer. It also highlights how important the notion of play is in the expressions of a brand—visual, verbal, behavioral. A brand doesn’t need to be irreverent or rebellious to embrace play. You can be one of the most serious companies but still allow playful elements of your brand to convey trust, accessibility or a more human approach. The connectivity provider rSIM, for example, offers a serious B2B product to healthcare, banking, and other utilities. But its brand and articulation are full of vim and vigor. It turns up with a unique character in a very technical field. Embrace the unexpected A more playful mindset also allows you to make unexpected connections, to produce the leap that makes an idea distinctive. Take the International Olympic Committee’s multiyear licensing agreement with Sonic the Hedgehog. Is it consistent with the famously strict Olympic brand guidelines? Debatable. But would Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Olympic Games, approve? Absolutely. It’s a contemporary articulation of the Olympic ideal, which is to bring the youth of the world together in peaceful competition—and Sonic is a way to connect with young people around the world. Strategic play can uncover those connections, giving established purpose a fresh and culturally relevant expression. But it will always go hand in hand with judgment. The point is not about endless play or ideation. The commercial advantage comes from combining freedom with craft, self-editing, and the confidence to stop when the right idea appears.

GrapheneOS shows off how it prepares RCS support without Google Messages

💡 Key Takeaways
  • RCS is coming to GrapheneOS without Google Messages, as a proof-of-concept app indicates how the privacy-focused version Android can implement the messaging standard.
  • It has been revealed that as virtually all Android phones and now iPhone support RCS messaging, the standard is key to communication in 2026.
  • It’s a problem that Graphene’s developers have been trying to work out for a while now, and it seems progress is being made.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

RCS is coming to GrapheneOS without Google Messages, as a proof-of-concept app indicates how the privacy-focused version Android can implement the messaging standard.

It has been revealed that as virtually all Android phones and now iPhone support RCS messaging, the standard is key to communication in 2026. But GrapheneOS consumers, by default, are still stuck with SMS/MMS as RCS is typically locked behind Google Messages on Android.

It’s a problem that Graphene’s developers have been trying to work out for a while now, and it seems progress is being made. A proof-of-concept messaging app with RCS was shared on Twitter/X, showing Graphene’s RCS implementation working with both Google Messages and iOS with end-to-end encryption and full features including typing indicators and reactions.

While this app skips the need to use Google Messages directly, the app does still use Google’s services as most carriers rely on Google for RCS. GrapheneOS still needs a sandboxed version of Google Play, for now, for this to work, but the developers say that a standalone version for carriers that support Google-less RCS will be coming.

We made a proof of concept RCS messaging app. It already has end-to-end encryption with MLS compatible with Google Messages and iOS, typing indicators, delivery/read receipts, reactions and media/file sharing. We'll use what was learned to integrate RCS into our Messaging app. pic.twitter.com/jzCTCCKrIQ.

There’s still no firm timeline for this new RCS support on GrapheneOS, but Google Messages can still be used in the meantime.

TouchTunes just added a social feed to your local jukebox

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2710 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the streaming jukebox giant TouchTunes wants to be the online social hub for your local bar.
  • The streaming jukebox giant TouchTunes wants to be the online social hub for your local bar.
  • The Latest York-based company boasts jukeboxes in more than 60,000 locations that consumers can control through touch screens or apps on their own smartphones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the streaming jukebox giant TouchTunes wants to be the online social hub for your local bar. The Newly introduced York-based company boasts jukeboxes in more than 60,000 locations that owners can control through touch screens or apps on their own smartphones. Now, it has added a “social feed” that lets users of its apps communicate with each other and see who’s connected to the jukebox in a particular establishment, even when they’re not physically there. App users can add comments and emoji-style reactions to recently played songs or share their own text posts, photos, and GIFs to a shared feed for a particular bar, restaurant, or other site with a TouchTunes jukebox. “We’re trying to transform from just the jukebox company to being the center of in-person social entertainment, and this is the natural next step of that,” says Scott Levine, the TouchTunes CEO. The company envisions that in addition to complimenting—or teasing—whoever’s playing the current song on the jukebox, users could visit a location’s feed for other discussions relevant to that spot, like planning to watch a game, recruiting players for a darts league, or sharing photos of a memorable night out. While Levine acknowledges TouchTunes is unlikely to replace existing group chats, and it’s not intended to compete with general-purpose social media apps, he anticipates the feed helping break the ice between fans of a particular venue and serving as a hub for good-natured discussions of what goes on there. “Maybe you have a smaller list or group of people—you’re going to communicate using message, or WhatsApp, or whatever,” he says. “But then when you’re there, you’re going to post a photo and your buddy that’s not there [will say] ‘oh man, I wish I was there.’”  Already, the company sees reactions being posted roughly every 15 seconds, and Wednesday, when young people traditionally return to their hometown bars the night before Thanksgiving, will likely make for a test of the new features. TouchTunes celebrates Thanksgiving Eve as National Jukebox Day, and Levine says it’s among the company’s biggest sales days, at least on par with St. Patrick’s Day. When jukebox fans first use the TouchTunes app to connect to a jukebox after the social feed is enabled, a pop-up message discloses the new feature and invites users to visit the app’s settings menu, where privacy options include opting out of having their usernames visible in the list of people at a venue and the list of songs being played. That’s intended to make sure that users feel in control of their privacy options, even if that leads to making themselves less visible, Levine says. “We bring you right to the screen to toggle it off,” he says. [Image: TouchTunes] But privacy experts question whether users will make informed decisions about what they’re sharing, particularly if they simply tap through the pop-up to access the normal jukebox menu, potentially while distracted—or intoxicated—in a busy bar. “I think a lot of times people are going to be at a bar, and they want a song being played,” says Sara Geoghegan, director of the consumer privacy program and senior counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center. “That is not the scenario that is best suited or most apt to understand your data and how it’s being used.”  Privacy concerns may naturally be greater for certain groups, like domestic violence survivors or immigrants, she says. They may also arise if someone encounters a creepy person at a bar who can use TouchTunes to figure out when they return or where they head next. In general, she says, tech companies rolling out new features can help mitigate concerns by ensuring that settings default to those maximizing privacy. “If they had the default [as] that privacy-protective option, we would have all of the benefits of the social media feed, and bringing people together, and having people enjoy music together in a shared space without the privacy concerns,” says Geoghegan. Still, Levine emphasizes that users can adjust their privacy settings—and block particular TouchTunes users from seeing information about them—whenever they choose. They can also report inappropriate posts that appear on particular venues’ feeds, similar to the options from other social media companies, and change their displayed usernames at any time. “We’re giving privacy controls on every single thing, and we’re trying to remind users, ‘Hey, you have control,’” he says. “And if you don’t like what somebody’s talking about, you can block them.”  Some TouchTunes users appear to use usernames derived from their real names or screen names they also use on other services. But others use what appear to be anonymous strings of words or characters that would make it difficult for strangers to identify them and link them to their lives outside the jukebox. “The first line of defense is to choose something like, I don’t know, HappySquirrel23,” says Jelena Mirkovic, a principal scientist at the University of Southern California Information Sciences Institute and research associate professor at USC’s Department of Computer Science who has studied privacy concerns in social and payment apps. “And so now no one knows it’s me, but I can still use the app and have full functionality.”  In general, she says, app developers can help by considering privacy trade-offs, like whether information about someone’s location should be visible publicly or only to friends, and prompting users to reevaluate their privacy settings over time once they’ve become familiar with an app’s features. “Then you know people have a way to act on that, and that would be informed consenting at that time,” she says. Since the TouchTunes social feature is still new, it’s likely too early to say how jukebox fans and the bars and restaurants that serve them will use it in practice, versus sticking to existing social and location-sharing platforms. Levine envisions the company releasing additional tools to make it easy for venues to communicate with customers, such as publicizing specials or events, and leaderboards that could reward users who play crowd-pleasing songs as determined by reactions and likes. TouchTunes is also testing a feature that would let users dedicate a song to another user, or to a location at large, he says. Already, the TouchTunes app allows users to customize their profiles; they can add a brief bio and profile photo, select their favorite music genres, and even specify what they’re looking for, from “new tunes” and “pool players” to a “drinking buddy” or a “relationship.” Future versions of the app may include the ability to add other users as friends and potentially receive relevant notifications, says Levine. “If my buddies are all going out to the pizza restaurant down the street, and I want to go play a song for them because I know they’re there, I’ll be able to do that and join in,” he says. While cynics might argue TouchTunes is building digital infrastructure for conversations bar-goers used to have in person—such as when gathered around old school, physical jukeboxes with coins or dollar bills in hand—Levine argues the app can indeed help bring people together within venues, to applaud each other’s selections or offer to buy a round for someone playing fun songs. “They’re using their phones to do it, but it’s not about living in the phone,” says Levine. The app can also potentially let people participate in the community at a particular spot even if they’re not present, spotting photos of their friends at a particular bar, figuring out where to grab a meal or drink, or even playing a song from afar. Even before the social feed rolled out, Levine says he heard from a business associate who used the app to pick bars to visit, looking for venues where jukeboxes had a long queue of songs, since they were likely to be lively. The feed will only make it easier for music fans to find venues that match their wants and needs and play the jukebox once they get there, he says. “Users win, a location wins, TouchTunes wins,” he says. “It’s this nice, simple, synergistic triangle.”.

The streaming jukebox giant TouchTunes wants to be the online social hub for your local bar.

The Latest York-based company boasts jukeboxes in more than 60,000 locations that consumers can control through touch screens or apps on their own smartphones. Now, it has added a “social feed” that lets users of its apps communicate with each other and see who’s connected to the jukebox in a particular establishment, even when they’re not physically there. App users can add comments and emoji-style reactions to recently played songs or share their own text posts, photos, and GIFs to a shared feed for a particular bar, restaurant, or other site with a TouchTunes jukebox.

“We’re trying to transform from just the jukebox firm to being the center of in-person social entertainment, and this is the natural next step of that,” indicates Scott Levine, the TouchTunes CEO.

The tech giant envisions that in addition to complimenting—or teasing—whoever’s playing the current song on the jukebox, users could visit a location’s feed for other discussions relevant to that spot, like planning to watch a game, recruiting players for a darts league, or sharing photos of a memorable night out. While Levine acknowledges TouchTunes is unlikely to replace existing group chats, and it’s not intended to compete with general-purpose social media apps, he anticipates the feed helping break the ice between fans of a particular venue and serving as a hub for good-natured discussions of what goes on there.

According to recent reports, “Maybe you have a smaller list or group of people—you’re going to communicate using message, or WhatsApp, or whatever,” he notes. “But then when you’re there, you’re going to post a photo and your buddy that’s not there [will say] ‘oh man, I wish I was there.’”.

Sources indicate that already, the company sees reactions being posted roughly every 15 seconds, and Wednesday, when young people traditionally return to their hometown bars the night before Thanksgiving, will likely make for a test of the fresh features. TouchTunes celebrates Thanksgiving Eve as National Jukebox Day, and Levine claims it’s among the company’s biggest sales days, at least on par with St. Patrick’s Day.

When jukebox fans first use the TouchTunes app to connect to a jukebox after the social feed is enabled, a pop-up message discloses the new feature and invites users to visit the app’s settings menu, where privacy options include opting out of having their usernames visible in the list of people at a venue and the list of songs being played. That’s intended to make sure that users feel in control of their privacy options, even if that leads to making themselves less visible, Levine claims.

“We bring you right to the screen to toggle it off,” he says.

But privacy experts question whether consumers will make informed decisions about what they’re sharing, particularly if they simply tap through the pop-up to access the normal jukebox menu, potentially while distracted—or intoxicated—in a busy bar.

“I think a lot of times people are going to be at a bar, and they want a song being played,” states Sara Geoghegan, director of the consumer privacy program and senior counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center. “That is not the scenario that is best suited or most apt to understand your data and how it’s being used.”.

According to recent reports, privacy concerns may naturally be greater for certain groups, like domestic violence survivors or immigrants, she says. They may also arise if someone encounters a creepy person at a bar who can use TouchTunes to figure out when they return or where they head next. In general, she says, tech companies rolling out new features can help mitigate concerns by ensuring that settings default to those maximizing privacy.

“If they had the default [as] that privacy-protective option, we would have all of the benefits of the social media feed, and bringing people together, and having people enjoy music together in a shared space without the privacy concerns,” claims Geoghegan.

According to recent reports, still, Levine emphasizes that owners can adjust their privacy settings—and block particular TouchTunes users from seeing information about them—whenever they choose. They can also report inappropriate posts that appear on particular venues’ feeds, similar to the options from other social media companies, and change their displayed usernames at any time.

“We’re giving privacy controls on every single thing, and we’re trying to remind users, ‘Hey, you have control,’” he claims. “And if you don’t like what somebody’s talking about, you can block them.”.

It has been revealed that some TouchTunes users appear to use usernames derived from their real names or screen names they also use on other services. But others use what appear to be anonymous strings of words or characters that would make it difficult for strangers to identify them and link them to their lives outside the jukebox.

“The first line of defense is to choose something like, I don’t know, HappySquirrel23,” says Jelena Mirkovic, a principal scientist at the University of Southern California Information Sciences Institute and research associate professor at USC’s Department of Computer Science who has studied privacy challenges in social and payment apps. “And so now no one knows it’s me, but I can still use the app and have full functionality.”.

In a recent development, in general, she notes, app developers can help by considering privacy trade-offs, like whether information about someone’s location should be visible publicly or only to friends, and prompting users to reevaluate their privacy settings over time once they’ve become familiar with an app’s features. “Then you know people have a way to act on that, and that would be informed consenting at that time,” she says.

Since the TouchTunes social feature is still fresh, it’s likely too early to say how jukebox fans and the bars and restaurants that serve them will use it in practice, versus sticking to existing social and location-sharing platforms. Levine envisions the company releasing additional tools to make it easy for venues to communicate with customers, such as publicizing specials or events, and leaderboards that could reward users who play crowd-pleasing songs as determined by reactions and likes. TouchTunes is also testing a feature that would let users dedicate a song to another user, or to a location at large, he says.

Already, the TouchTunes app allows users to customize their profiles; they can add a brief bio and profile photo, select their favorite music genres, and even specify what they’re looking for, from “new tunes” and “pool players” to a “drinking buddy” or a “relationship.” Future versions of the app may include the ability to add other users as friends and potentially receive relevant notifications, says Levine.

“If my buddies are all going out to the pizza restaurant down the street, and I want to go play a song for them because I know they’re there, I’ll be able to do that and join in,” he indicates.

While cynics might argue TouchTunes is building digital infrastructure for conversations bar-goers used to have in person—such as when gathered around old school, physical jukeboxes with coins or dollar bills in hand—Levine argues the app can indeed help bring people together within venues, to applaud each other’s selections or offer to buy a round for someone playing fun songs. “They’re using their phones to do it, but it’s not about living in the phone,” says Levine.

The app can also potentially let people participate in the community at a particular spot even if they’re not present, spotting photos of their friends at a particular bar, figuring out where to grab a meal or drink, or even playing a song from afar. Even before the social feed debuted, Levine claims he heard from a business associate who used the app to pick bars to visit, looking for venues where jukeboxes had a long queue of songs, since they were likely to be lively. The feed will only make it easier for music fans to find venues that match their wants and needs and play the jukebox once they get there, he says.

“Users win, a location wins, TouchTunes wins,” he says. “It’s this nice, simple, synergistic triangle.”.

So if you can fit a small model comfortably on your device try to use a bigger quantized model instead, it might have a better performance.

Let's start by defining the model formats our app is going to support and their repositories. Of course llama.rn is a binding for llama.cpp so we need to load GGUF files. To find GGUF repositories for the models we want to support, we can use the search bar on Hugging Face and search for GGUF files for a specific model, or use the script quantize_gguf.py provided here to quantize the model ourselves and upload the files to our hub repository.

Sources indicate that the HF_TO_GGUF object maps user-friendly model names to their corresponding Hugging Face repository paths. For example:.

The modelFormats array contains the list of model options that will be displayed to users in the selection screen, we chose Llama 3.2 1B Instruct, DeepSeek R1 Distill Qwen 1.5B, Qwen 2 0.5B Instruct and SmolLM2 1.7B Instruct as they are the most popular small models.

Next, let's create a way to fetch and display available GGUF model files from the hub for our selected model format.

When a user selects a model format, we make an API call to Hugging Face using the repository path we mapped in our HF_TO_GGUF object. We're specifically looking for files that end with '.gguf' extension, which are our quantized model files.

Once we receive the response, we extract just the filenames of these GGUF files and store them in our availableGGUFs state using setAvailableGGUFs. This allows us to show owners a list of available GGUF model variants they can download.

According to recent reports, now let's implement the model download functionality in the handleDownloadModel function which should be called when the user clicks on the download button. This will download the selected GGUF file from Hugging Face and store it in the app's Documents directory:.

In a recent development, we could have implemented the api requests inside the handleDownloadModel function, but we will keep it in a separate file to keep the code clean and readable. handleDownloadModel calls the downloadModel function, located in src/api, which accepts three parameters: modelName, downloadUrl, and a progress callback function. This callback is triggered during the download process to revision the progress. Before downloading we need to have the selectedModelFormat state set to the model format we want to download.

Inside the downloadModel function we use the RNFS module, part of the react-native-fs library, to access the device's file system. It allows developers to read, write, and manage files on the device's storage. In this case, the model is stored in the app's Documents folder using RNFS.DocumentDirectoryPath, ensuring that the downloaded file is accessible to the app. The progress bar is updated accordingly to reflect the current download status and the progress bar component is defined in the components folder.

Let's create src/api/model.ts and copy the code from the src/api/model.ts file in the repo. The logic should be simple to understand. The same goes for the progress bar component in the src/components folder, it's a simple colored View where the width is the progress of the download.

In a recent development, congratulations you've just built the core functionality of your first AI chatbot, the code is available here ! You can now start adding more features to the app to make it more user friendly and efficient.

The app is now fully functional, you can download a model, select a GGUF file, and chat with the model, but the user experience is not the best. In the EdgeLLMPlus repo, I've added some other features, like on the fly generation, automatic scrolling, the inference speed tracking, the thought process of the model like deepseek-qwen-1.5B,... we will not go into details here as it will make the blog too long, we will go through some of the ideas and how to implement them but the whole code is available in the repo.

According to recent reports, the app generates responses incrementally, producing one token at a time rather than delivering the entire response in a single batch. This approach enhances the user experience, allowing users to begin reading the response as it is being formed. We achieve this by utilizing a callback function within context.completion, which is triggered after each token is generated, enabling us to upgrade the conversation state accordingly.

Recent findings suggest that auto Scrolling ensures that the latest messages or tokens are always visible to the user by automatically scrolling the chat view to the bottom as new content is added. To implement that we need we use a reference to the ScrollView to allow programatic control over the scroll position, and we use the scrollToEnd method to scroll to the bottom of the ScrollView when a new message is added to the conversation state. We also define an autoScrollEnabled state variable that will be set to false when the user scrolls up more than 100px from the bottom of the ScrollView.

Recent findings suggest that inference Speed Tracking is a feature that tracks the time taken to generate each token and displays under each message generated by the model. This feature is easy to implement because the CompletionResult object returned by the context.completion function contains a timings property which is a dictionary containing many metrics about the inference process. We can use the predicted_per_second metric to track the speed of the model.

Recent findings suggest that the thought process is a feature that displays the thought process of the model like deepseek-qwen-1.5B. The app identifies special tokens like and to handle the model's internal reasoning or "thoughts." When a token is encountered, the app enters a "thought block" where it accumulates tokens that represent the model's reasoning. Once the closing token is detected, the accumulated thought is extracted and associated with the message, allowing people to toggle the visibility of the model's reasoning. To implement this we need to add a thought and showThought property to the Message type. message.thought will store the reasoning of the model and message.showThought will be a boolean that will be set to true when the user clicks on the message to toggle the visibility of the thought.

Recent findings suggest that the app uses the react-native-markdown-display package to render markdown in the conversation. This package allows us to render code in a better format.

We added a checkDownloadedModels function to the App.tsx file that will check if the model is already downloaded on the device, if it's not we will download it, if it is we will load it into the context directly, and we added some elements in the UI to show if a model is already downloaded or not.

We added two notable buttons in the UI, the stop button and the back button. The stop button will stop the generation of the response and the back button will navigate to the model selection screen. For that, We added a handleStopGeneration function to the App.tsx file that will stop the generation of the response by calling context.stop and set the isGenerating state to false. We also added a handleBack function to the App.tsx file that will navigate to the model selection screen by setting the currentPage state to modelSelection.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A jury has found Huawei guilty of bank fraud, wire fraud, money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and violations of the U.S. sanctions against Iran, among others. According to Bloomberg, the verdict was the result of a nearly three-month trial in which a foreign tech giant has been prosecuted by the U.S. Department of Justice. This is a rare occurrence, resulting in a conviction of 10 out of 12 counts, with the Chinese company getting cleared of conspiracy to obstruct justice and racketeering conspiracy.

Sources indicate that “Today’s verdict makes clear that fraud, sanctions evasion, and the theft of intellectual property are not business strategies, they are serious crimes,” James Barnacle, the Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI New York Field Office, which conducted the investigation on the tech firm, told the publication. “Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft, and the FBI will never hesitate to pursue those who profit by breaking the law.”.

In a recent development, huawei has long been in the crosshairs of the U.S., with the manufacturer getting banned from the country in 2018 alongside other Chinese telecommunications hardware manufacturers. It has even sued the U.S. government, claiming that the equipment ban against the company is unconstitutional. Nevertheless, Washington proceeded with the move and built a case against the company as early as 2019. This has been hit by multiple delays, though, owing to the COVID-19 Pandemic, as well as Huawei’s multiple attempts to halt the investigation even before the case went to trial. There was even an allegation that two Chinese intelligence officers offered $61,000 in Bitcoin to a U.S. law enforcement official to get insider information about the case.

It was also in 2018 that the daughter of Huawei founder and manufacturer CFO Meng Wanzhou was arrested in Canada on suspicion of the firm’s attempt to circumvent U.S. sanctions on Iran. Washington even attempted to have her extradited to the U.S., but she was able to return to China in 2019 after admitting to the company’s illegal business in Iran. Aside from that, the U.S. Department of Justice provided other examples of Huawei’s violations, including the theft of T-Mobile’s robotic touch screen testing robot, with a Huawei employee stealing a part of the device from T-Mobile’s controlled lab, the copying of Cisco router source code, another Huawei employee photographing proprietary Fujitsu equipment, and using confidential information gathered through an NDA from Quintel, a U.S. antenna manufacturer, which was subsequently included in Huawei’s patent application.

Sources indicate that on the other hand, the firm’s lead defense attorney, Brian Heberlig, focused on its acquittal on two of the charges. “It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Heberlig told Bloomberg. The racketeering conspiracy “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge.”.

It has been revealed that sentencing hearing for the company is set for September 2027, although it’s still unclear what penalties the U.S. government is seeking. The Chinese Foreign Ministry, on the other hand, said, “The Chinese government firmly opposes the U.S. suppression and containment of Chinese companies and firmly supports Chinese companies in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests.”.

Why isn’t AI changing career advice?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that ask a 17-year-old where their career plan came from and the answer is usually someone at the kitchen table.
  • In a recent development, ask a 17-year-old where their career proposal came from and the answer is usually someone at the kitchen table.
  • Recent findings suggest that the school counselor rarely enters the picture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that ask a 17-year-old where their career plan came from and the answer is usually someone at the kitchen table. A parent, maybe an uncle. These are people who love them and want the best for them. They are also, in most cases, working from a job market map that is 20 or 30 years out of date. The school counselor rarely enters the picture. Most U.S. school counselors spend no more than 20% of their time on career counseling while serving hundreds of students. The available capacity works out to well under an hour per student per year, even before accounting for group programming and administrative responsibilities. Meanwhile, nearly the entire AI and jobs conversation is about what this technology will take away from young workers. That concern is fair. I’ve argued here before that AI will reduce the need for some entry-level white-collar roles, and employers need to plan for that now. But we have become so focused on what AI will do to young workers that we have stopped asking what it can do for them. And there is an irony sitting right in front of us. One of the hardest problems in workforce development is getting accurate, real-time labor market information to the people who need it most. That happens to be the kind of problem AI is unusually good at. THE DATA EXISTS BUT FEW CAN READ IT Labor market data is not scarce. Governments, job boards, and industry groups publish enormous amounts of it every month. The trouble is that it is dense, scattered, and close to illegible for anyone without a statistics background. A 16-year-old is not going to read a state workforce projection. Neither is her dad. So young people make one of the biggest decisions of their lives with the least information. We are preparing them for yesterday’s jobs while tomorrow’s technology sits on the phone in their pocket. They know the system is failing them. In the Broken Marketplace, a Schultz Family Foundation and HarrisX survey of more than 5,700 young Americans ages 16 to 24, more than four in 10 said the education system and the employment resources available to them are broken. Seven in 10 said they learn about career pathways on social media. We know that young people are already asking algorithms for career advice. They are just asking the wrong ones. WHAT A GOOD AI COUNSELOR SOUNDS LIKE At the International Youth Foundation, we’ve been testing this idea with a chatbot called Clara, a partnership we have with the Salesforce Foundation. The premise is straightforward: Take labor market data that would make most people’s eyes glaze over and turn it into a conversation. Picture a young woman who has just finished a technical program and doesn’t know where to apply. Instead of a spreadsheet, she gets something closer to a knowledgeable friend. A chat that says, “Did you know they’re hiring electricians a few miles from you? A couple of things in your background could make you competitive. Let me ask you some questions and see whether it’s worth pursuing.” From there, the tool can explain what training she would need, how long it takes, and whether that field is growing where she lives. That is the guidance a great counselor gives. But most students never get it. Nearly half of career and technical educators say their school’s counselors spend less time on career pathways than on college prep. AI can close that gap at a scale no hiring plan ever could. Substantial data sets, updated in real time, delivered to one person at a time in plain language. That is what these models do best. THE RISK AND FIX ARE REAL To be clear, this is not without risk. General-purpose AI models can sound authoritative while missing the details that matter. When researchers at Renaissance Philanthropy tested leading models on thousands of real career questions from young people, most would have earned a C-minus. For a young person making a first career decision, a confident wrong answer can cost years. That is a reason to build these tools carefully, and to build them now. If AI makes the labor market more volatile, good information becomes increasingly valuable. The work of measuring whether AI gives young people good career advice has barely started, and it deserves far more investment than it is getting. The AI labs should be paying attention, too. Millions of young people are already typing some version of “what job should I go for?” into their products. Making sure those answers are accurate and grounded in real local demand would cost a fraction of what is being spent on the next generation of models. AI can’t save every job. But it could help a young person find the next one. Employers, funders, and the companies building this technology spend a great deal of energy worrying about what AI will do to the next generation of workers. They should spend at least as much making sure it works for them.Christina Sass is president and CEO of the International Youth Foundation.

Industry News: Driving for Thanksgiving? These are the worst times to be on the road this week

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that another Thanksgiving week is upon us, which means tens of millions of Americans will once again travel by plane, train, and automobile to see their loved ones.
  • Sources indicate that another Thanksgiving week is upon us, which means tens of millions of Americans will once again travel by plane, train, and automobile to see their loved ones.
  • “After three years of record highs, the number of travelers is slightly lower partly because of higher travel costs this year,” says Stacey Barber, vice president of AAA travel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that another Thanksgiving week is upon us, which means tens of millions of Americans will once again travel by plane, train, and automobile to see their loved ones. However, this Thanksgiving period will be a little different than in recent years—at least when it comes to transportation. That’s because the American Automobile Association (AAA) claims that, for the first time in several years, fewer Americans will be traveling. “After three years of record highs, the number of travelers is slightly lower partly because of higher travel costs this year,” says Stacey Barber, vice president of AAA travel. “But travelers won’t notice much of a difference on the roads and at the airports, since projected volumes remain near record levels.”  That means that despite fewer travelers, the roads are still expected to be packed at times. With that in mind, here are the best and worst times to travel by car over the 2026 Thanksgiving period. Best times to hit the roads for the Thanksgiving travel period For the 2026 Thanksgiving period, AAA expects 72.9 million people to travel to their holiday destinations by car. That’s down from last year’s 73.1 million automobile travelers, but still a significant amount. AAA defines the 2026 Thanksgiving period as the seven days lasting from Tuesday, November 24 to Monday, November 30, 2026. But despite the expected 72.9 million road travelers, how congested the streets will be depends heavily on when you travel during the period. AAA says these are the best times to be on the road (ie: the times with the expected lowest congestion) over the period, according to transportation data and insights provider INRIX data compiled by the auto organization: Tuesday, November 24: Before 1:00 PM Wednesday, November 25: Before 12:00 PM  Thursday, November 26 (Thanksgiving): Minimal Traffic Impact Expected  Friday, November 27: Before 12:00 PM  Saturday, November 28: Before 11:00 AM  Sunday, November 29: Before 11:00 AM  Monday, November 30: Before 1:00 PM  Worst times to hit the roads for the Thanksgiving travel period INRIX data highlights that the worst days to travel over the Thanksgiving period—that is, the days the congestion is expected to be the highest—are the Tuesday and Wednesday before Thanksgiving, and the Sunday and Monday after. Those are the days when most people choose to travel to and from their holiday destinations. As for the individual times that are expected to be the worst to travel by car, those are: Tuesday, November 24: 2:00 PM to 8:00 PM  Wednesday, November 25: 12:00 PM to 7:00 PM  Thursday, November 26 (Thanksgiving): Minimal Traffic Impact Expected  Friday, November 27: 1:00 PM to 7:00 PM  Saturday, November 28: 12:00 PM to 9:00 PM  Sunday, November 29: 12:00 PM to 8:00 PM  Monday, November 30: 2:00 PM to 7:00 PM  Fewer total travelers are expected over the Thanksgiving 2026 period When combining all modes of transportation—auto, air, and “other,” which includes bus, boat, and train—AAA says 81.48 million people in America are expected to travel over the 2026 Thanksgiving period. That’s about 121,000 fewer than the 81.61 million who traveled during the 2025 Thanksgiving period. Still, 2026’s expected numbers far surpass the 77.78 million people who traveled in 2019, the last year before the pandemic. The expected decline in travelers this year is mainly due to higher travel costs, especially gas prices, AAA says. Besides a decline of about 200,000 car travelers, AAA says there will also be a drop in air travelers by about 0.2% to 5.96 million (versus 5.97 million in 2025). However, more people will travel by “other” modes during this period than last year. “Other” includes travel by bus, train, and cruise. In the 2026 Thanksgiving period, the other travel segment is expected to reach 2.6 million travelers—up 4.1% from 2.49 million in 2025.

#127568. Why the Agent Isn’t the Hard Part: Where Developers Go Wrong With Agentic Workflows

Why the Agent Isn’t the Hard Part: Where Developers Go Wrong With Agentic Workflows

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1417 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial.
  • Recent findings suggest that you can build an AI agent in an afternoon now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sources indicate that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Recent findings suggest that you can build an AI agent in an afternoon now. Pick a model, write a loop, hand it a few tools and watch it book a meeting or open a pull request. The demo works, and everyone in the room is impressed.

Then it meets a real system with real permissions and real customers, and things get quiet. Gartner has predicted that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, citing rising costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Its analyst Anushree Verma described most current projects as early-stage experiments that are driven by hype and often misapplied. A forecast is not a measurement, but the pattern it describes matches what many teams report: the agent is rarely what breaks. The workflow around it is.

According to recent reports, this article covers where that workflow tends to fail, with a focus on permissions, tool connections and human approval. It includes a small, runnable policy gate in JavaScript, compares the main safeguards and notes their limits. Standards and guidance change promptly in this area, so check the linked sources for the current versions.

A year or two ago the model was often the differentiator. Today many teams can reach the same frontier models through the same kinds of APIs, so if the intelligence is similar, the advantage has to come from somewhere else.

Anthropic’s guide to building effective agents reached a similar conclusion after working with teams building agents. It reports that the most successful implementations were not using complex frameworks or specialized libraries, and were building with simple, composable patterns instead. It also separates workflows, where code paths are predefined, from agents, where the model chooses its own steps, and advises using the simplest approach that works and adding complexity only when measurement shows it helps.

That should change where developers spend their time. Frameworks matter, but three less glamorous questions matter more: what can the agent touch, when does it stop, and who checks its work?

Industry observers note that the OWASP guidance on Excessive Agency names what goes wrong here. It covers agents that can do more than they need to, and it traces the problem to three root causes: excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy.

According to recent reports, in practice this looks familiar. An agent that only needs to read tickets is given a token that can also close them. A summarization tool connects with an admin account because that was quicker to set up. A generic “run shell command” tool is exposed when the agent only ever needs to write one file.

It has been revealed that the fix is ordinary engineering discipline applied to a new kind of caller. OWASP’s recommendations include giving each tool only the functions and permissions it needs, preferring narrow tools over open-ended ones, running actions under the user’s own scoped identity, requiring human approval for high-impact actions and enforcing authorization in the downstream system rather than letting the model decide. The last point is the key one: a model can be talked out of a rule written in a prompt, but an API that checks scopes cannot.

Make the risky properties of a tool explicit in its definition so your orchestration layer can act on them:.

In a recent development, nothing clever is happening there, which is the point. The decision about what needs a human is made by a developer at design time, not by a model at runtime.

The definitions above only help if something enforces them. The sketch below is a policy gate that sits between the model and your tools. It checks that the tool exists, that the caller was granted the scope, and whether the action is reversible, and it records each decision. It runs on Node.js 18 or later with no dependencies.

Recent findings suggest that A short test file shows the behavior. Unknown tools and missing scopes are denied, reads run, and the irreversible send waits for a person:.

This is deliberately minimal. A real system would load scopes from the user’s actual session, enforce the same scopes again in the downstream API, and store the audit log somewhere durable. The gate is a second line of defense, not a replacement for authorization in the systems the agent calls.

According to recent reports, the Model Context Protocol has become a common way to connect agents to tools. Anthropic donated MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation, in December 2025. Block contributed goose and OpenAI contributed AGENTS.md as founding projects, which shows how central the ecosystem has become.

A standard protocol is good news. It also means you can install a tool server in minutes and expose every endpoint of your glitch tracker, repository or CRM to your agent, whether it needs them or not. Easy connection quietly pushes more power to the agent.

Recent findings suggest that the protocol’s own security best practices document covers several relevant risks, including confused deputy problems in proxy servers, token passthrough, local server compromise and scope minimization. For scopes, it recommends starting with a minimal set and elevating only when a privileged operation is first attempted, and it lists wildcard or omnibus scopes as a common mistake.

Industry observers note that A sensible rule is to treat every tool server like a third-party dependency running with production credentials. Review the tools it exposes, switch off the ones the workflow does not use, pin versions and log every call. If you would not let a newly introduced contractor do it on day one, the agent should not do it either.

Human-in-the-loop design is often implemented as “approve everything”. That fails in a predictable way: people click approve forty times a day and stop reading by lunchtime.

According to recent reports, A better rule is to gate on reversibility. Reads run freely, reversible writes run and get logged, and irreversible actions such as sending, paying or deleting wait for a person. Everything leaves a trace that a developer can replay when something looks odd. The gate above implements exactly this split.

Some teams build these pieces themselves, and others buy them. Elsewhen, a London-based consultancy that works on agentic operations for enterprise teams, describes its own service in similar terms. Its page lists approval gates where people sign off consequential decisions, an audit trail of what each agent read and which systems it touched, and a shared layer of permissions and guardrails that is reused across workflows. Elsewhen also claims its Planet Agent report found that agents tend to start at the edges of an organization, where tasks are repeatable and mistakes are cheap, and then move toward the core. Treat that as the vendor’s own finding, and ask for the underlying evidence before relying on it.

According to recent reports, the same logic applies outside engineering. The first question worth asking any AI partner is what they have actually put into production, and developers can ask the same of their own work.

Recent findings suggest that no single control is enough. The table summarizes what each safeguard does well and where it falls short.

It is the OWASP term for an agent that can do more than it needs to, caused by excessive functionality, permissions or autonomy.

A prompt rule can be bypassed or ignored, while a scope check in the downstream API is enforced regardless of what the model says.

Usually not. Gating on reversibility keeps humans focused on actions such as sending, paying and deleting, and avoids approval fatigue.

Treat them like any third-party dependency. Review the tools they expose, limit scopes, pin versions and log calls.

In a recent development, the agentic projects that survive the next two years will probably not be the ones with the most ambitious autonomy. They will be the ones where someone sat down early and decided what the agent could touch, what it had to ask about and how anyone would know what it did.

That work does not demo well and it will not trend on social media. It is still the part that decides whether your agent becomes infrastructure or ends up among the projects that get cancelled.

According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

#127567. Breaking: LeRobot goes to driving school: World’s largest open-source self-driving dataset

📅 11 Mar 2025 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1920 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: LeRobot goes to driving school: World’s largest open-source self-driving dataset

📅 11 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1920 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR of L2D, the world's largest self-driving dataset!
  • State-of-the art Vision Language Models and Large Language Models are trained on open-source image-text corpora sourced from the internet, which spearheaded the recent acceleration of open-source AI.
  • Industry observers note that table 1: Open source self-driving datasets (*excluding lidar and radar).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR of L2D, the world's largest self-driving dataset!

State-of-the art Vision Language Models and Large Language Models are trained on open-source image-text corpora sourced from the internet, which spearheaded the recent acceleration of open-source AI. Despite these breakthroughs, the adoption of end-to-end AI within the robotics and automotive community remains low, primarily due to a lack of high quality, large scale multimodal datasets like OXE. To unlock the potential for robotics AI, Yaak teamed up with the LeRobot team at 🤗 and is excited to announce Learning to Drive (L2D) to the robotics AI community. L2D is the world’s largest multimodal dataset aimed at building an open-sourced spatial intelligence for the automotive domain with first class support for 🤗’s LeRobot training pipeline and models. Drawing inspiration from the best practices of source version control, Yaak also invites the AI community to search and discover novel episodes in our entire dataset (> 1 PetaBytes), and queue their collection for review to be merged into future release (R5+).

Industry observers note that table 1: Open source self-driving datasets (*excluding lidar and radar). Source.

L2D was collected with identical sensor suites installed on 60 EVs operated by driving schools in 30 German cities over the span of 3 years. The policies in L2D are divided into two groups — expert policies executed by driving instructors and student policies by learner drivers. Both the policy groups include natural language instructions for the driving task. For example, “When you have the right of way, take the third exit from the roundabout, carefully driving over the pedestrian crossing”.

Fig 1: Visualization: Nutron (3 of 6 cameras shown for clarity) Instructions: “When you have the right of way, drive through the roundabout and take the third exit”.

Expert policies have zero driving mistakes and are considered as optimal, whereas student policies have known sub optimality (Fig 2).

Fig 2: Student policy with jerky steering to prevent going into lane of the incoming truck.

Sources indicate that both groups cover all driving scenarios that are mandatory for completion to obtain a driving license within the EU (German version), for example, overtaking, roundabouts and train tracks. In the release (See below R3+), for suboptimal student policies, a natural language reasoning for sub-optimality will be included. F.ex “incorrect/jerky handling of the steering wheel in the proximity of in-coming traffic ” (Fig 2).

L2D (R2+) aims to be the largest open-source self-driving dataset that empowers the AI community with unique and diverse ‘episodes’ for training end-to-end spatial intelligence. With the inclusion of a full spectrum of driving policies (student and experts), L2D captures the intricacies of safely operating a vehicle. To fully represent an operational self-driving fleet, we include episodes with diverse environment conditions, sensor failures, construction zones and non-functioning traffic signals.

Industry observers note that both the expert and student policy groups are captured with the identical sensor setup detailed in the table below. Six RGB cameras capture the vehicle’s context in 360o, and on-board GPS captures the vehicle location and heading. An IMU collects the vehicle dynamics, and we read speed, gas/brake pedal, steering angle, turn signal and gear from the vehicle’s CAN interface. We synchronized all modality types with the front left camera (observation.images.front_left) using their respective unix epoch timestamps. We also interpolated data points where feasible to enhance precision (See Table 2.) and finally reduced the sampling rate to 10 hz.

Fig 3: Multimodal data visualization with Visualization: Nutron (only 3 of 6 cameras shown for clarity).

Table 2: Modality types, LeRobot v3.0 key, shape and interpolation strategy.

L2D follows the official German driving task catalog (detailed version) definition of driving tasks, driving sub-tasks and task definition. We assign a unique Task ID and natural language instructions to all episodes. The LeRobot:task for all episodes is set to “Follow the waypoints while adhering to traffic rules and regulations”. The table below reveals a few sample episodes, their natural language instruction, driving tasks and subtasks. Both expert and student policies have an identical Task ID for similar scenarios, whereas the instructions vary with the episode.

Table 3: Sample episodes in L2D, their instructions and Task ID derived from EU driving task catalog.

It has been revealed that we automate the construction of the instructions and waypoints using the vehicle position (GPS), Open-Source Routing Machine, OpenStreetMap and a Large Language Model (LLM) (See below). The natural language queries are constructed to closely follow the turn-by-turn navigation available in most GPS navigation devices. The waypoints (Fig 4) are computed by map-matching the raw GPS trace to the OSM graph and sampling 10 equidistant points (orange) spanning 100 meters from the vehicles current location (green), and serve as drive-by-waypoints.

Fig 4: L2D 6x RGB cameras, waypoints (orange) and vehicle location (green) Instructions: drive straight up to the stop stop sign and then when you have right of way, merge with the moving traffic from the left.

We collected the expert and student policies with a fleet of 60 KIA E-niro driving school vehicles operating in 30 German cities, with an identical sensor suite. The multimodal logs collected with the fleet are unstructured and void of any task or instructions information. To search and curate for episodes we enrich the raw multimodal logs with information extracted through map matching the GPS traces with OSRM and assigning node and way tags from OSM (See next section). Coupled with a LLM, this enrichment step enables searching for episodes through the natural language description of the task.

Sources indicate that for efficiently searching relevant episodes, we enrich the GPS traces with turn information obtained by map-matching the traces using OSRM. We additionally use the map-matched route and assign route features, route restrictions and route maneuvers, collectively referred to as route tasks, to the trajectory using OSM (See sample Map). Appendix A1-A2 provides for more details on the route tasks we assign to GPS traces.

Fig 5: Driving tasks assigned to raw GPS trace (View map).

The route tasks which get assigned to the map-matched route, are assigned the beginning and end timestamps (unix epoch), which equates to the time when the vehicle enters and exits the geospatial linestring or point defined by the task (Fig 6).

Fig 6: Pink: GNSS trace, Blue: Matched route, tasks: Yield, Train crossing and Roundabout (View Map).

We perform semantic spatiotemporal indexing of our multimodal data with the route tasks as described in Fig 5. This step provides a rich semantic overview of our multimodal data. To search within the semantic space for representative episodes by instructions, for example, “drive up to the roundabout and when you have the right of way turn right”, we built a LLM-powered multimodal natural language search, to search within all our drive data (> 1 PetaBytes) and retrieve matching episodes.

Sources indicate that we structured the natural language queries (instructions) to closely resemble turn-by-turn navigation available in GPS navigation devices. To translate instructions to route tasks, we prompt the LLM with the instructions and steer its output to a list of route features, route restrictions, route maneuvers and retrieve episodes assigned to these route tasks. We perform a strict validation of the output from the LLM with a pydantic model to minimize hallucinations. Specifically we use llama-3.3-70b and steer the output to the schema defined by the pydantic model. To further improve the quality of the structured output, we used approx 30 pairs of known natural language queries and route tasks for in-context learning. Appendix A. 2 provides details on the in-context learning pairs we used.

Instructions: Drive up to the roundabout and when you have the right of way turn right.

Industry observers note that L2D on 🤗 is converted to LeRobotDataset v2.1 and LeRobotDataset v3.0 format to fully leverage the current and future models supported within LeRobot. The AI community can now build end-to-end self-driving models leveraging the state-of-the-art imitation learning and reinforcement learning models for real world robotics like ACT, Diffusion Policy, and Pi0.

Existing self-driving datasets (table below) focus on intermediate perception and planning tasks like 2D/3D object detection, tracking, segmentation and motion planning, which require high quality annotations making them difficult to scale. Instead L2D is focused on the development of end-to-end learning which learns to predict actions (policy) directly from sensor input (Table 1.). These models leverage internet pre-trained VLM and VLAM.

Robotics AI models’ performances are bounded by the quality of the episodes within the training set. To ensure the highest quality episodes, we plan a phased release for L2D. With each new release we add additional information about the episodes. Each release R1+ is a superset of the previous releases to ensure clean episode history.

In a recent development, 1. instructions: Natural language instruction of the driving task 2. task_id: Mapping of episodes to EU mandated driving tasks Task ID 3. observation.state.route : Information about lane count, turn lanes from OSM 4. suboptimal: Natural language description for the cause of sub-optimal policies.

The entire multimodal dataset collected by Yaak with the driving school fleet is 5x larger than the planned release. To further the growth of L2D beyond R4, we invite the AI community to search and uncover scenarios within our entire data collection and build a community powered open-source L2D. The AI community can now search for episodes through our natural language search and queue their collection for review by the community for merging them into the upcoming releases. With L2D, we hope to unlock an ImageNet moment for spatial intelligence.

Fig 7: Searching episodes by natural language instructions.

It has been revealed that for R0, R1 we recommend using LeRobotDataset, with revision=[R0|R1], which can be used directly from the pypi release of LeRobot. For R2+, please follow installation outlined here or install from main as below, as we recommend using StreamingLeRobotDataset as R3 is is Dataset v3.0 format.

Industry observers note that for real world testing of the AI models trained with L2D and LeRobot, we invite the AI community to submit models for closed loop testing with a safety driver, starting summer of 2025. The AI community will be able to queue their models for closed loop testing, on our fleet and choose the tasks they’d like the model to be evaluated on and, for example, navigating roundabouts or parking. The model would run in inference mode (Jetson AGX or similar) on-board the vehicle. The models will drive the vehicle with LeRobot driver in two modes.

Industry observers note that list of route restrictions. We consider route tags from OSM a restriction if it imposes restrictions on the policy, for example speed limit, yield or construction. Route features are physical structures along the route, for example inclines, tunnels and pedestrian crossing. Route maneuvers are different scenarios which a driver encounters during a normal operation of the vehicle in an urban environment, for example, multilane left turns and roundabouts.

OSM = Openstreetmap, VLM= Vision Language Model, derived: Hand crafted rules with OSM data.

Prompt template and pseudo code for configuring the LLM using groq to parse natural language queries into structured prediction for route features, restrictions and maneuvers with a pydantic model. The natural language queries are constructed to closely follow the turn-by-turn navigation available in most GPS navigation devices.

Example pairs (showing 3 / 30) for in-context learning to steer the structured prediction of LLM, where ParsedInstructionModel is a pydantic model.

Onboard compute: NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier.

Table 6: Information on hardware kit used for data collection.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Streaming in 1080p will be the default in Google Meet, regardless of whether you pay for Google Workspace. That includes personal Google Accounts.

Google says people will default to sending and receiving 1080p video, at the minimum. Previously, Google Meet made 720p the standard for streaming, and a higher resolution had historically been locked behind the Google One 2TB plan. That’s been true since 1080p streaming was rolled out in 2023.

Industry observers note that the upgrade will roll out to everyone, including those with Google Workspace accounts and personal Google Accounts. The only requirement to stream your own 1080p video in Google Meet for web will be hardware-based. Google’s press release states that devices with cameras capable of streaming in high definition will do so, and the feature will be turned on automatically.

According to recent reports, it can be disabled, though. Consumers can head to Settings > Video in Google Meet for web. Video will also appear in a lower resolution if the user’s video tile is shrunk down on-screen.

It has been revealed that the revision appears to be centered on web-only instances of Google Meet, and might not include the app on Android or iOS. For the time being, those versions may still be limited to streaming in 720p for those who don’t have an active Google One subscription.

Google Meet started its extended rollout of 1080p streaming to everyone earlier this month, so it shouldn’t be much longer until the change has taken place completely.

#127565. Breaking: The state of China's memory industry in 2026

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2807 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The state of China's memory industry in 2026

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2807 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that china’s homegrown memory comes largely from two companies, CXMT for DRAM and YMTC for 3D NAND, and both are booming.
  • Industry observers note that both are expanding and adding fabs, and each is edging into the other’s products.
  • In a recent development, memory is a commodity, so the story is in the wafers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that china’s homegrown memory comes largely from two companies, CXMT for DRAM and YMTC for 3D NAND, and both are booming. CXMT’s Oct. 30 quarterly report shows a nine-month net profit of ¥132.0 billion ($19.6 billion), against a ¥5.28 billion ($785 million) loss a year earlier, on revenue more than eight times as high, at ¥269.0 billion ($40.0 billion). YMTC’s numbers, just for Q1, are at ¥47.04 billion ($7.0 billion) in revenue and ¥33.38 billion ($5.0 billion) in profit attributable to shareholders, more than double 2025.

Industry observers note that both are expanding and adding fabs, and each is edging into the other’s products. No Chinese manufacturer can yet produce high-bandwidth memory (HBM) in volume, though. HBM is the stacked DRAM that AI accelerators depend on, and at the moment the U.S. bars Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron from selling it into China. CXMT’s prospectus lists no HBM project, though its HBM3E is reportedly in risk production, an early run before the process is fully qualified. Huawei designs its own HBM but doesn’t say who makes it.

In a recent development, memory is a commodity, so the story is in the wafers. We cover the companies running memory fabs in China: CXMT, YMTC, a handful of smaller Chinese fabs, and Samsung and SK hynix, which run some of their biggest plants there. Huawei makes the cut for its HBM program, though it has no memory fab. Fabless designers, module makers, and NOR flash producers are left out, except XMC for its HBM line. Fab counts, products, and financials come from filings and company statements; capacities, planned fabs, and the HBM progress that remains the major question mark rest largely on anonymous reporting. Let's dive into the current state of the Chinese DRAM industry.

CXMT, short for ChangXin Memory Technologies, is China’s biggest homegrown DRAM maker. It operates two 12-inch fabs in Hefei and one in Beijing, each able to produce around 100,000 wafers a month. It is also building fabs in Shanghai and Hefei and is in funding talks for a second Beijing fab, which together could take it past 600,000 wafers a month. The Shanghai fab is expected to have two to three times the capacity of the Hefei base, with tools going in during the second half of 2026 and volume in 2027.

CXMT is now the fourth-largest DRAM maker worldwide, with 9.5% of DRAM revenue in Q2, according to TrendForce. CXMT says LPDDR6 is in mass production for Xiaomi, and its president says the first 4F² product, a server DDR5 RDIMM, is due by year-end. This comes after record first-half revenue of ¥150.3 billion ($22.4 billion), net profit of ¥77.6 billion ($11.5 billion), an 84.84% gross margin on its main business, and a listing on Shanghai’s STAR Market on July 27. Third-quarter profit alone was ¥54.4 billion ($8.1 billion).

Industry observers note that the primary products are DDR5 rated up to 8,000 MT/s with 24Gb dies, and LPDDR5X rated up to 10,667 MT/s. CXMT says its fifth-generation G5 platform reaches 11.95nm active-area half-pitch with quadruple patterning for 24Gb LPDDR5X, and gets at least 50% more dies out of each wafer than G4, counted as 8Gb dies. CXMT says a DRAM product on its sixth-generation platform has also completed engineering-sample validation. Jeongdong Choe, Senior Technology Fellow at TechInsights, told Tom’s Hardware Premium that the firm measured the smallest active half-pitch on CXMT’s G4 at 14.8nm and hasn’t analyzed G5 yet.

Recent findings suggest that CXMT lists no GDDR or 3D NAND among its products and is limited to nodes made without extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography as it lacks the tooling. CXMT’s second Beijing fab, however, is planned to include a 3D NAND R&D line, which could shake things up. The growth picture for now is capacity and price, with the tests of scaling without EUV lying with the RDIMM and Shanghai fab.

Sources indicate that YMTC, short for Yangtze Memory Technologies Co., has two fabs of its own in Wuhan, which can produce about 200,000 wafers a month together. A third fab in the Xinzhou district, registered in September last year, is expected to produce about 50,000 wafers a month by 2027 and eventually 100,000 at full capacity. While YMTC is known for its NAND flash, roughly half of Fab 3’s output is earmarked for DRAM. The manufacturer also makes enterprise SSDs and UFS and eMMC parts, and sells consumer SSDs under its ZhiTai brand. YMTC filed its own STAR Market prospectus, to match CXMT’s, on Aug. 21.

According to recent reports, NAND flash was, until recently, the star of the show for Chinese memory, and YMTC’s Xtacking technology is one reason why. Its fifth-generation Xtacking 4.0 die, used in 1Tb TLC and 2Tb QLC parts, has 294 gates, and Choe told us 267 of them are active word lines. Most of what YMTC ships, however, is still 160- and 232-layer NAND. Samsung licensed YMTC’s Xtacking bonding patents in February 2025, so the technology could be considered both proven and valuable.

Omdia data put YMTC at 38.5% of China’s NAND market in Q2, ahead of Samsung’s 33.5%. Globally, YMTC ranked third in NAND shipments in Q2, according to Counterpoint Research, and its share of NAND revenue rose from 9% to 14% between Q1 2025 and Q1 2026. YMTC’s stated long-term targets are about 20% of global NAND supply and about 500,000 wafers a month, DRAM included.

For DRAM, YMTC’s Fab 2 is running about 5,000 wafers a month of 16Gb LPDDR5, still in R&D and testing, with no proposal for mass production. However, a 9,600 MT/s part on a vertical channel transistor (VCT) 4F² cell is slated for mass production at Fab 3 if it passes qualification. XMC, YMTC’s former foundry unit, left its control in July.

Two smaller fabs worthy of note are Fujian Jinhua and SwaySure. The former has a 12-inch fab in Jinjiang, which produces custom DDR4 on 25nm, at 40,000–50,000 wafers a month, with about 90% going to Huawei. DDR4 prices have surged this year, by as much as 50% in the first quarter alone, as the big suppliers wind DDR4 down in favor of server and HBM parts and enterprise buyers stock up.

SwaySure, a Shenzhen manufacturer founded in March 2022 with state-owned investment, is building a 28nm 12-inch DRAM line and is reportedly backed by Huawei. Analyst Jim Handy of Objective Analysis doubts the 28nm line could make HBM. Neither company responded to our requests for additional information.
