Not every AI chip needs HBM. Inference hardware can get by on LPDDR5X, as Axera’s AX8860P does in Sipeed’s MaixStation, or on DRAM bonded straight onto the processor, the approach PieceMakers is betting on. Training-class accelerators like Huawei’s Ascend series still need HBM, though, and since the U.S. banned the export of HBM as of Dec. 2, 2024, China can’t buy it from the massive three memory makers.

In a recent development, even those who can get HBM are seeing heat and yield concerns with larger memory stacks, specifically 12-high. SK hynix said on its Q3 2026 earnings call that some customers’ spec changes show “demand is indeed overwhelming supply,” and that lowering the stack is “a strategy to increase the number of cubes that can be obtained for the same capacity.” This mirrors other indicators, including potential Nvidia Rubin Ultra decisions, and it suggests that HBM is in short enough supply that even easier-to-build stacks are in high demand.

CXMT has sampled HBM with Tongfu, and HBM3 built on its 16nm-class G4 node to Huawei. Its HBM3E has now gone to several domestic AI chip designers as samples, with limited production due by the end of 2026, and an expansion expected in 2027. Yields are only about 20% to 30%, though, against about 70% at SK hynix, and in testing the chips performed closer to SK hynix’s HBM3 than to its HBM3E. An HBM packaging plant in Shanghai worth at least ¥17.1 billion ($2.5 billion) is targeted for year-end, with capacity for about 30,000 units a month.

Tongfu reportedly sampled HBM2, but its own filings mention only DRAM and flash packaging. Huawei mentioned last year that “we will offer two proprietary HBMs.” It launched the Atlas 350 card in March, built on the Ascend 950PR, which carries 112GB of HBM. XMC has had a 3,000-wafer-a-month HBM line under construction since early 2024, but no production has been confirmed. At this time, YMTC, Jinhua, and SwaySure don’t appear to make HBM, though reports say YMTC is developing the through-silicon via (TSV) stacking it would need, and Jinhua was named in a Huawei-led HBM group in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that huawei noted in 2025 that the 950PR would use HiBL 1.0, its own “low-cost HBM”; TechInsights told us it hasn’t analyzed HiBL 1.0 yet. However, Huawei’s 2025 roadmap specced out the 950PR's 128GB of HBM at 1.6TB/s. Huawei said that its 950PR is “optimized for the prefill stage of inference,” which is compute-heavy with “lower demand for memory access bandwidth,” and that using HiBL 1.0 is “more cost-effective than HBM3E and HBM4E” for that workload. The higher-end HiZQ 2.0, for the 950DT, is due in Q4 and, by Huawei’s figures, brings 144GB at 4TB/s. In both cases, Huawei’s supplier remains in doubt, and the organization did not respond to our requests for comment.

HBM3 samples to Huawei; HBM3E sampling, with limited production by year-end at 20–30% yields.

Barred by the U.S. rule of Dec. 2, 2024.

Industry observers note that of the companies from outside China, Samsung and SK hynix both run large memory fabs on Chinese soil, and both are now upgrading their NAND lines there. Samsung’s Xi’an handles about 40% of the company’s NAND, including 236-layer, or V8, in volume, with X2 converting to 286-layer, or V9, this year, slated to reach 5,000 V9 wafers a month in December and 40,000 by December 2027. A Samsung spokesperson told Tom’s Hardware Premium that the company “has been transitioning its existing manufacturing operations in Xi’an to 9th-generation V-NAND in compliance with U.S. export regulations and in close communication with the U.S. government.”.

It has been revealed that SK hynix’s Wuxi produces 30–40% of its DRAM and has moved from 1z to 1a, with the EUV layers done in Korea. Dalian turns out about 100,000 wafers a month of 192-layer floating-gate NAND and is moving to 240 layers, the most SK hynix is authorized to make there.

SK hynix, which already sells NAND with up to 321 layers elsewhere, told us it needs a U.S. license every year and declined to give product details or capacities for individual fabs. The firm said that it intends for its 321-layer flash to be “over 50% of domestic (Korean) capacity in the fourth quarter,” which puts the Dalian lag into relief.

According to recent reports, SK hynix also has “Mod B,” a second fab at its Dalian site that was completed in 2023. The firm has reportedly tied a latest U.S. NAND fab to Washington, letting it ship more U.S. tools there: Dalian’s 2026 license capped its equipment, no 2027 license had been issued as of mid-October, and its U.S.-based Solidigm unit has applied for an export license to buy more tools for Mod B. SK hynix told Tom’s Hardware that “no capacity expansion is being sought for the Dalian Mod B” and has been installing equipment at its Dalian factory.

Solidigm is now reportedly in talks with the U.S. Commerce Department over a $45 billion chip plant in the U.S., but wants Washington’s approval to ship equipment to upgrade the Dalian plant first, arguing that the upgrade would help finance the new site. However, SK hynix denied an earlier report of such a deal and claims no specific intends have been finalized.

As for its Chongqing packaging plant, SK hynix told us it is “exploring various strategic options to enhance our packaging competitiveness,” though nothing is final. Elsewhere in China, Samsung’s Suzhou plant handles assembly and testing, and Micron’s Xi’an site handles packaging and testing.

All of this plays out inside a U.S.-China fight over chips that AI has only sped up. CXMT isn’t presently on the Commerce Department’s Entity List, which bars U.S. suppliers from shipping to listed companies without a license; YMTC, Jinhua, and SwaySure are. Jinhua has been on the list since 2018; SwaySure joined in December 2024 over its Huawei links, and YMTC was added in December 2022.

In a recent development, CXMT is, however, on the Pentagon’s 1260H list of Chinese military companies, which it is suing over. It’s been on the list since January 2025 and stayed on with the June revision. For Samsung and SK hynix, the validated end-user status that let both firms ship in U.S. tools was revoked as of Dec. 31, 2025. Annual licenses are now required, and the Commerce Department has said it doesn’t intend to license capacity expansions or technology upgrades. Meanwhile, both companies say upgrades are under way, which sits uneasily with that policy.

In a recent development, china, for its part, has been weighing broader technology export controls and has now proposed adding 40 technologies, reportedly including some memory-chip design technologies, to its Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited and Restricted from Export. The draft, Announcement 48 from China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology, is open for comment until Nov. 15, and anyone exporting a listed technology must register first.

3D NAND: 236-layer V8; V6 ended.

About 40% of Samsung’s NAND (both Xi’an fabs).

3D NAND, converting to 286-layer V9.

Converting to V9; 5,000 V9 wafers a month in December 2026, 40,000 by December 2027.

DRAM, mostly 1a; EUV layers done in Korea.

Floating-gate 3D NAND, 192-layer, moving to 240.

About 100,000 wafers a month; 30% to 40% of SK hynix’s NAND.

Producing; upgrading, authorized up to 240 layers.

Built in 2023; SK hynix claims no expansion is sought; no 2027 license yet.

It has been revealed that currently, China’s homegrown memory hinges on two manufacturers that are, admittedly, booming at the moment, although the memory industry worldwide has seen a massive surge since spring 2025. SK hynix said that “our DRAM and HBM volume for the next three years through 2029 are effectively sold out” with supply failing to keep up with demand as “a constraint projected to continue through 2030.” Its average selling prices rose from Q2 by mid-20% for NAND and high-20% for DRAM.

According to recent reports, there may be some signs of at least temporary cooling in China’s consumer channel, though, as China Flash Market reports that SSD prices fell across the board this week, with most spot NAND wafers trading more than 30% below suppliers’ official prices. It looks like supply will remain a hot topic and China’s production capabilities are front and center.

CXMT and Huawei both have HBM milestones due by year-end: CXMT’s limited HBM3E production and Shanghai packaging plant, and Huawei’s 950DT with HiZQ 2.0. YMTC’s Fab 3 is due in late 2026 or 2027, and CXMT’s HBM3E expansion is expected in 2027. That leaves little time to ramp within 2027, especially at CXMT’s current yields, so we’re skeptical of volume HBM from a Chinese fab, whether measured against domestic demand or global supply, before 2028. Samsung and SK hynix, meanwhile, still need U.S. licenses for next year to keep tooling their Chinese fabs.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

6 tips to use this Thanksgiving when family asks about your career

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Evan Reece has a few strategies for handling unwelcome questions about his career when he gathers with family. He founded and ran a ski lift ticket platform for 15 years, but it went out of business during the COVID-19 pandemic. Reece then started a career management platform. He’s its sole employee and earns less than he did before.At family parties, he sometimes feels pressure to explain why he doesn’t get a full-time job working for someone else. When he’s asked such questions, he reminds himself that people usually ask because they care.“Oftentimes, if we’re stressed about something that we don’t have an answer to, the question feels like an interrogation, when that’s rarely the intention of the person asking the question,” mentioned Reece, 48, who runs the career management platform Truest.me.A simple “How’s your job going?” can feel like an ambush when you’re unemployed, underemployed or working in jobs your friends and relatives don’t understand or may regard as frivolous. These queries can bring up painful experiences like layoffs. Advice can sound like criticism to recent graduates in a seemingly impenetrable job market, while curiosity about someone’s income can feel like judgment.Even inquiries motivated by a genuine desire to connect can come across as invasive or awkward in a group setting.With holiday gatherings approaching, here are some tips and potential scripts to help you handle tricky career conversations with relatives and feel less defensive. The same strategies can be applied when faced with scrutiny about getting married or having children. Anticipate questions and strategy responses in advance Have a short, confident response or two ready for the job-related queries you think might come up, said Melody Wilding, an executive coach and author of “Managing Up.”For example, if you’re unemployed, you could say, “I’m taking time to find the right fit and not rushing into something latest.” Or if you’ve made an unconventional career move, say, “I know it’s not what everyone would choose, but I’m excited about it,” Wilding said.“Then redirect the conversation nicely. You might say, ‘Tell me about you,’ or ‘I’d love to hear about your recent trip,'” she added. Be a boomerang when fielding questions Turning the inquiries around on the questioner can deflect attention and be entertaining.“If someone is willing to ask you a question that requires tremendous vulnerability out of you, then they should be willing to answer one too,” Reece said.When a relative asks if you’re “still job searching” or “Why did you leave a good job?” get curious before you get defensive, Wilding suggested. Instead of immediately responding to their question, try to understand the motivation behind it by countering, “Why do you ask?” or “What makes you say that?” Wilding said.“Maybe they’re just making conversation, which saves you from launching into a full defense of your choices,” she said. Turn it into a game If someone asks about an unstable job or recent layoff, you can say it’s been challenging and then suggest, “Let’s play a game. Everybody tell a story about the worst job they ever had,” Reece said. “Anybody who’s ever worked has a story. And they’re usually amazing.”For recent graduates or those who are trying to figure out what’s next, you could be honest about your uncertainty and reply, “Everybody go around and talk about a time in their career when they weren’t sure what to do next and what you did,” Reece suggested. Let others take the spotlight Hope Bond, 53, spent a decade working as an editor in the magazine industry. She left the field for a few years to raise her young children, then did some freelance editing jobs. When she sought to return to full-time work in 2020, she couldn’t find a position. Bond began working as a site manager for a movie production location in 2024.She loves the job, despite its erratic hours, instability and hourly pay. But at gatherings with her family of lawyers and bankers, she often felt singled out by probing questions about her work.After years of answering their questions, she now redirects them and encourages others to be the star of the conversation, especially her children.“I stay on the periphery. The younger generations are the ones who are bringing the great energy, so I like them to have the floor,” Bond said. “I don’t insert myself into conversation if we’re talking about career or money. Those are my two boundaries. Even with a family that is loving and supportive and wants the best for me, it is just awkward.” Share context about the job market When people feel scrutinized after layoffs or extended unemployment, Avigail Lev, a psychologist at the Bay Area CBT Center in San Francisco, suggests explaining to family members how the job market has changed and how artificial intelligence has impacted their fields.“The first thing you need to say is to speak to the context that things are different, and the decisions about work are very different right now,” Lev said.Many of Lev’s clients work in technology or at AI companies and worry about losing their jobs, while some have already been laid off, she said.“Some people are very depressed right now about not having work or not knowing what’s next. And having a relative blame you for something that’s not in your control is the last thing that you need right now,” Lev said. Choose what you reveal One way to avoid unnecessary judgment is to choose whom you share details about your professional life with.Rishabh Dutta, 25, of Mumbai, India, quit his marketing job for Bollywood movies after stress and long hours led to hair loss. For the next few months, “everyone was constantly asking me what I was doing, if I had found something else,” he said.The next time Dutta left a job, he kept it to himself for a few months. “I just decided not to tell them, and honestly I don’t regret it,” he said. Share your stories and questions about workplace wellness at cbussewitz@ap.org. Follow AP’s Be Well coverage, focusing on wellness, fitness, diet and mental health at https://apnews.com/hub/be-well. —Cathy Bussewitz, AP Business Writer.

That’s admittedly more than the price of a Picco, but if you were already in the market for an Android-powered e-reader and looking for a deal, the rest of its lineup is worth recommending if a gifted add-on is worth it to you. The 10-person board that voted to reinstate Nvidia’s CEO is also now under scrutiny

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that jensen Huang has been under a spotlight for weeks, but after the 11-day period of disorder that included the resignation and reinstatement of the Nvidia executive, the manufacturer’s board is joining him at the center of scrutiny.The 10-person board voted unanimously to rehire Huang as Nvidia’s president, CEO and a fellow board member, writing in an announcement Monday that the decision emerged after discussions with Huang and “input from senior levels of the United States government.” President Donald Trump said he believes his intervention was crucial to the reinstatement.Just six days earlier, the board was singing a different tune. Board members had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation following his admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The board did not intend to reinstate him, Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of a quarterly earnings call.“To bow to pressure to bring someone back who has hurt the reputation of the company is crazy,” said Kathleen Day, a lecturer at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School.The board’s stunning reversal has spurred questions about its independence and what Trump’s role means for the meeting of business and politics. Concerns swirl about corporate governance and Trump’s intervention Nvidia’s board includes both business leaders with longstanding ties to the company and a group of more recent additions who have experience at significant-name companies including Taco Bell, PepsiCo and Eli Lilly.Some experts have called for the board to resign in the wake of the havoc.Day, who has expertise in financial crises and corporate governance, emphasized that the board has a duty to represent shareholders, not the CEO.“The shareholders should demand a new board,” she said.Corporate governance experts say long tenures for board members can compromise their independence. Under the rules of the New York Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq, companies are required to have a majority of directors who are independent.“Traditionally, it’s a good practice” to limit how long people can sit on a board, said Nada Kakabadse, professor of policy, governance and ethics at the University of Reading’s Henley Business School. “They should be eight years maximum. Four years, plus another four years if they’re performing well. But beyond that, they really become not independent anymore, right?”It’s not unusual for U.S. tech bosses to stuff their boards with allies or high-profile figures who might not be aware of what’s happening at the company, Kakabadse said.American business has a culture of “leader heroes” — entrepreneurs who founded companies and are seen as the only ones who can steer them through tough times, she said. But at some point, the companies can get so big that “you need proper corporate structure, you need proper governance.”Many people are also questioning what “input” the company received from senior government leaders and why it persuaded the board to make a complete turnaround.“The board should have listened to the president’s request and stuck to its position that it was time to find a new CEO,” said Peter Cohan, an associate professor of management practice at Babson College. “In my opinion, by giving in to Trump, the board is endangering the company. That’s because Huang has seen that he can do anything he wants, and he will get away with it.”The idea of an independent board of experts looking out for the long-term interests of the company and its shareholders “sort of goes out the window” if the sitting president “essentially tells them what to do,” said Daniel Kinderman, a professor of political science and international relations at the University of Delaware.“This is really the mark of crony capitalism, right?” he said.Kinderman said the episode might “open the door a little bit more for more aggressive actions on behalf of elected representatives” in their relationships with businesses. Lawmakers call for accountability from the board The Nvidia saga has made waves in Washington, particularly in conversations around export controls. Huang’s affair raised questions about Nvidia’s compliance with those restrictions. The reinstatement has renewed fervor on Capitol Hill for more transparency from both Huang and the board.Elected officials from both parties were quick to respond to the reinstatement with criticism and skepticism.Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, said the decision to bring Huang back was “reckless.” She wrote in a statement Monday that it does not change the fact that Huang, Nvidia executives and the company’s board “still owe Congress answers.”Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, a New York Democrat, called for both Huang and the board to testify publicly to Congress. “A boardroom vote does not resolve a national security risk,” she said in a statement Monday.California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who is investigating Nvidia in connection with Huang’s affair, said Tuesday in an interview with CNBC that the president’s intervention “does not bode well for enforcement of the law by the federal government without fear, without favor.”The California Department of Justice said Thursday that it is asking Nvidia whether its advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public. Some members joined the Nvidia board in the 1990s Two board members, Mark Stevens and Tench Coxe, joined the board in 1993 when Nvidia was founded. Stevens and Coxe were both previously venture capitalists who made early investments in Nvidia.Two other long-serving board members, Jones and Brooke Seawell, are the former chief executive and chief financial officer, respectively, of Synopsys, which makes chip-design software and counted Nvidia as its first customer. Jones joined Nvidia’s board in 1993, while Seawell joined four years later.Stephen Neal, who’s designated as the board’s “lead independent director,” joined in 2019. He’s the chairman emeritus of Cooley LLP, Nvidia’s longtime law firm, and has advised the company in “various governance matters,” according to his bio.Other board members have less of a direct link to Nvidia.Melissa Lora, former president of Taco Bell International, spent 31 years at the fast food company and joined Nvidia’s board in 2023. Aarti Shah, formerly a senior vice president and chief digital officer at pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly, joined in 2020.John Dabiri, an engineering professor at the California Institute of Technology whose lab researches fluid mechanics, was added to the board in 2020. Dawn Hudson was the NFL’s chief marketing officer and a former CEO of Pepsi-Cola’s North American division who’s been on the board since 2013. Suzanne Nora Johnson was a vice chairman at Goldman Sachs who joined the board in July.None of the board members provided comment in response to requests from The Associated Press. This story corrects that Shah joined the Nvidia board in 2020, not 2021. —Kaitlyn Huamani and Kelvin Chan, Associated Press.

The board did not intend to reinstate him, Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of a quarterly earnings call.“To bow to pressure to bring someone back who has hurt the reputation of the company is crazy,” said Kathleen Day, a lecturer at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School.The board’s stunning reversal has spurred questions about its independence and what Trump’s role means for the meeting of business and politics.

Nvidia’s board includes both business leaders with longstanding ties to the firm and a group of more recent additions who have experience at big-name companies including Taco Bell, PepsiCo and Eli Lilly.Some experts have called for the board to resign in the wake of the havoc.Day, who has expertise in financial crises and corporate governance, emphasized that the board has a duty to represent shareholders, not the CEO.“The shareholders should demand a new board,” she remarked.Corporate governance experts say long tenures for board members can compromise their independence. Under the rules of the New York Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq, companies are required to have a majority of directors who are independent.“Traditionally, it’s a good practice” to limit how long people can sit on a board, said Nada Kakabadse, professor of policy, governance and ethics at the University of Reading’s Henley Business School. “They should be eight years maximum. Four years, plus another four years if they’re performing well. But beyond that, they really become not independent anymore, right?”It’s not unusual for U.S. tech bosses to stuff their boards with allies or high-profile figures who might not be aware of what’s happening at the company, Kakabadse said.American business has a culture of “leader heroes” — entrepreneurs who founded companies and are seen as the only ones who can steer them through tough times, she said. But at some point, the companies can get so big that “you need proper corporate structure, you need proper governance.”Many people are also questioning what “input” the company received from senior government leaders and why it persuaded the board to make a complete turnaround.“The board should have listened to the president’s request and stuck to its position that it was time to find a new CEO,” said Peter Cohan, an associate professor of management practice at Babson College. “In my opinion, by giving in to Trump, the board is endangering the company. That’s because Huang has seen that he can do anything he wants, and he will get away with it.”The idea of an independent board of experts looking out for the long-term interests of the company and its shareholders “sort of goes out the window” if the sitting president “essentially tells them what to do,” said Daniel Kinderman, a professor of political science and international relations at the University of Delaware.“This is really the mark of crony capitalism, right?” he said.Kinderman said the episode might “open the door a little bit more for more aggressive actions on behalf of elected representatives” in their relationships with businesses.

Sources indicate that the Nvidia saga has made waves in Washington, particularly in conversations around export controls. Huang’s affair raised questions about Nvidia’s compliance with those restrictions. The reinstatement has renewed fervor on Capitol Hill for more transparency from both Huang and the board.Elected officials from both parties were quick to respond to the reinstatement with criticism and skepticism.Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, stated the decision to bring Huang back was “reckless.” She wrote in a statement Monday that it does not change the fact that Huang, Nvidia executives and the manufacturer’s board “still owe Congress answers.”Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, a Fresh York Democrat, called for both Huang and the board to testify publicly to Congress. “A boardroom vote does not resolve a national security risk,” she said in a statement Monday.California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who is investigating Nvidia in connection with Huang’s affair, said Tuesday in an interview with CNBC that the president’s intervention “does not bode well for enforcement of the law by the federal government without fear, without favor.”The California Department of Justice said Thursday that it is asking Nvidia whether its advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public.

In a recent development, two board members, Mark Stevens and Tench Coxe, joined the board in 1993 when Nvidia was founded. Stevens and Coxe were both previously venture capitalists who made early investments in Nvidia.Two other long-serving board members, Jones and Brooke Seawell, are the former chief executive and chief financial officer, respectively, of Synopsys, which makes chip-design software and counted Nvidia as its first customer. Jones joined Nvidia’s board in 1993, while Seawell joined four years later.Stephen Neal, who’s designated as the board’s “lead independent director,” joined in 2019. He’s the chairman emeritus of Cooley LLP, Nvidia’s longtime law firm, and has advised the organization in “various governance matters,” according to his bio.Other board members have less of a direct link to Nvidia.Melissa Lora, former president of Taco Bell International, spent 31 years at the fast food company and joined Nvidia’s board in 2023. Aarti Shah, formerly a senior vice president and chief digital officer at pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly, joined in 2020.John Dabiri, an engineering professor at the California Institute of Technology whose lab researches fluid mechanics, was added to the board in 2020. Dawn Hudson was the NFL’s chief marketing officer and a former CEO of Pepsi-Cola’s North American division who’s been on the board since 2013. Suzanne Nora Johnson was a vice chairman at Goldman Sachs who joined the board in July.None of the board members provided comment in response to requests from The Associated Press.

This story corrects that Shah joined the Nvidia board in 2020, not 2021.

—Kaitlyn Huamani and Kelvin Chan, Associated Press.

Open R1: Update #3

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the last few weeks, we have focused our efforts on reproducing the competitive programming (code reasoning) aspects of the DeepSeek-R1 recipe.
  • Here’s an overview of how the OlympicCoder models stack up against various instruction fine-tuned and reasoning models.
  • Read on to learn how we built the dataset, benchmark and models!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the last few weeks, we have focused our efforts on reproducing the competitive programming (code reasoning) aspects of the DeepSeek-R1 recipe.

In this post, we are excited to share:.

Here’s an overview of how the OlympicCoder models stack up against various instruction fine-tuned and reasoning models. We find that training models on CodeForces-CoTs produces top-tier performance, with OlympicCoder-32B outperforming all open-weight models we tested, including some that are over 100x larger 🤯.

Read on to learn how we built the dataset, benchmark and models!

International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI).

Sources indicate that codeForces is one of the most popular websites among competitive programmers, hosting regular contests where participants must solve challenging algorithmic optimization problems. The challenging nature of these problems makes them an interesting dataset to improve and test models’ code reasoning capabilities.

According to recent reports, while previous efforts such as DeepMind’s CodeContests dataset have compiled a large number of CodeForces problems, today we are releasing our own open-r1/codeforces dataset, with more than 10k problems covering the very first contests all the way to 2025, ~3k of which were not included in DeepMind’s dataset. Additionally, for around 60% of the problems, we have included the editorial, which is an explanation, written by the contest organizers, explaining the correct solution. You will also find 3 correct solutions per problem extracted from the official website.

Furthermore, we are releasing open-r1/codeforces-cots, which contains chain of thought generations produced by DeepSeek-R1 on these problems, where we asked the model to produce solutions in C++ (the main language used in competitive programming) and Python, totaling close to 100k samples.

We fine-tuned Qwen2.5 Coder Instruct 7B and 32B on this dataset, resulting in our OlympicCoder-7B and OlympicCoder-32B models. You will find more details on these models further along in the blogpost.

While datasets like DeepMind’s contests and others containing competitive programming problems include test cases and claim to be verifiable, these test cases are often a small subset of the full suite used on contest websites. CodeForces, in particular, caps displayed test cases at ~500 characters, which means that these datasets only contain the shorter, easier test cases that fit into this limit.

As an example, we took 7 problems for which the R1 generated solution passed all the public test cases and tried submitting them to the CodeForces platform:.

Recent findings suggest that although they passed the shorter tests, every single one of these solutions failed on the full test set. This underscores the need for latest fully verifiable competitive programming dataset. While we plan to try model-based solutions to generate and validate additional challenging tests that may be added to our CodeForces dataset in the future, for now we went looking for fully available problem data elsewhere.

The International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) is one of five international science olympiads (if you are familiar with AIME, IOI is the programming equivalent of IMO, for which the very best students who take part in AIME are invited) and tests a very select group of high school students (4 per country) in complex algorithmic problems.

It has been revealed that the problems are extremely challenging, and the full test sets are available and released under a permissive (CC-BY) license. This means that IOI is the perfect dataset to test a model's code reasoning capabilities.

It has been revealed that in IOI, each problem has several subtasks, each with different input constraints. To solve a subtask, a submission needs to pass all of its test cases within the (strict) time limits. While the final subtask is usually the “full problem”, some subtasks effectively describe a much easier (more constrained) problem, and contestants very often target specific subtasks to get partial scores instead of just trying to solve the full problem (perfect scores are relatively rare).

Industry observers note that following a recent OpenAI paper where o1 live competed at IOI’2024 (the last iteration), we similarly processed all problems from IOI’2024 (as well as previous IOIs up until 2020), and split them into their subtasks, such that each prompt would ask models to solve one specific subtask. We release the processed problem statements, as well as all grading/checker files required to run them and test cases in open-r1/ioi and open-r1/ioi-test-cases.

We created custom code to run solutions (many problems have complicated setups, requiring a “manager” process communicating with several processes running the user submission and special checkers to validate solutions) and to grade according to IOI rules, which is available at https://github.com/huggingface/ioi, and evaluated over 40 leading reasoning models on IOI’2024.

At IOI, contestants have a 50 submission limit per problem. We generated 50 submissions for each subtask and then applied a selection strategy similar to the one used by OpenAI to get scores under contest conditions for each problem. Results can be found below, where the horizontal lines represent the threshold for bronze, silver and gold models from real contest data. While o1 comes very close to bronze, ultimately no model would reach the medal threshold (50th percentile of contestants).

Our OlympicCoder models (in red), do fairly well compared to other frontier models, even surpassing some closed source models (in gold) such as claude-3.7-sonnet-thinking, and OlympicCoder-32B even outperforms o1-mini and DeepSeek-R1, the model we distilled from, on the 50 submission limit setting.

It has been revealed that an vital note is that our submission strategy may penalize non reasoning models, such as Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, OlympicCoder-32B’s base model. To simulate real contest conditions, in which a submission’s score is only known after it is actually submitted, we employed a round robin submission strategy similar to the one employed by OpenAI for o1-ioi: we start by submitting a solution that targets the last subtask of the problem, then one targeting the second to last, and so on, only evaluating a solution when it is picked for submission. We skip over submissions targeting subtasks that have already been solved by previously selected submissions, and within each targeted subtask we prefer submissions from longer generations — which is a criteria that makes sense for reasoning models, but less so for other models.

If we remove the 50 submission limit (which would place us outside the contest conditions), and evaluate all submissions we generated (50 per subtask), we obtain the following results:.

While creating the OlympicCoder models, we ran a large number of SFT experiments to understand the role of various filters applied to the CodeForces dataset. We found the following subsets of open-r1/codeforces-cots gave the best overall performance:.

Note that we only focused on the C++ solutions, but blending in the Python solutions would likely boost performance even further.

In a recent development, we used LiveCodeBench as a test bed for our models and then ran the best performing checkpoints through the much harder IOI benchmark. We tested various hyperparameter configurations to train our models and settled on the following:.

Below we share some lessons we learned from tuning the Qwen2.5 Coder models on R1 reasoning traces.

Sample packing is a widely used method to efficiently process variable-length sequences and accelerate training. As shown in the figure below, the way this works concatenating training samples (coloured) into equal sized chunks that removes the need to use padding tokens (gray) across batches:.

With packing, samples can overlap across the boundaries of each chunk, but in practice this doesn’t matter too much if most of the samples are much smaller than the chunk size.

However, for the reasoning traces we distilled from R1, we wondered whether packing could hurt performance because many traces are long and the fraction of clipped answers could be high. This means it may be difficult to train the model to attend to long context information, particularly when the question and answer have been packed into different chunks.

As shown in the striking figure below, we found that packing substantially hurts the model’s performance: with packing, the model is barely able to solve problems from LiveCodebench, but without packing, the performance improves over several epochs before plateauing out:.

Industry observers note that we suspect this stark difference is accentuated by the fact that our training sets only consist of C++ solutions, while LiveCodeBench only evaluates performance on Python. Nevertheless, we found that across all datasets we ablated, packing was consistently worse.

For most SFT experiments that we’ve run with Qwen models, a learning rate of 2e-5 is typically good enough to get strong performance. However, when applying SFT with reasoning data to an existing instruct model, we found that significant performance gains could be had by using a much larger learning rate of 4e-5. As shown in the figure below, the difference across each doubling of the learning rate amounted to almost 10 points improvement on LiveCodeBench!

In a recent development, when we created the solutions_w_editorials subset of open-r1/codeforces-cots, our intuition was that by providing R1 with the problem and solution, we would obtain better reasoning traces. Surprisingly, this intuition was not borne out during evaluation, with the naive sampling from problem statements giving a modest, yet consistent boost during training:.

In a recent development, while vibe testing some of our models, we encountered a peculiar phenomenon: if prompted with in-domain queries (like competitive coding), the model would emit the expected long CoT within and tokens, followed by the final answer. However, for out-of-domain queries like “What is the capital of Switzerland”, the model would revert back to the behaviour of the original instruct model!

Here’s an example of a simple query failing to return the long CoT:.

Assistant: 2. It is one of the simplest mathematical addition problems. 1 + 1 equals 2. This problem is often used as a riddle or puzzle, particularly in job interviews or online tests to determine a candidate's ability to solve problems swiftly. While it may seem obvious to most people, it can be a useful question for employers to assess critical thinking and problem-solving skills. Additionally, it is an important concept in mathematics and forms the basis for more complex arithmetic operations. So next time someone asks you what 1+1 is, you can confidently state that it is 2!

In a recent development, in this solution, we define a function add_numbers that takes two parameters a and b and returns their sum. We then call this function with 1 and 1, storing the result in the variable result, which is then printed. This demonstrates a straightforward way to compute and display the sum of two integers. The example serves as a simple yet effective illustration of basic arithmetic operations in Python.

However, if we prefill the assistant's response with the desired behaviour emerges:.

Assistant: Okay, I need to answer the question "What is 1+1?" Let's see. Oh right, 1 plus 1 equals 2. But wait, maybe there's more to it. Like, what if someone asks in a different way? Or perhaps considering other number bases? Like in base 10 it's 2, but in binary it's 10. Hmm, but the question is straightforward. The user probably expects the simple answer. So the correct answer here is 2. Should I just state that? Yes, 1 + 1 is equal to 2. Is there anything else you'd like to know about this calculation?

This suggests that when distilling reasoning traces into an existing post-trained model, one should enforce prefilling by default in the final model’s chat template. Incidentally, this is also what DeepSeek does with their distilled models and the behaviour above may be the reason why. (It is also amusing to speculate whether hitting the “think” button on popular chat UIs is simply prefilling the assistant response 🙂).

Combining all these lessons produced OlympicCoder-7B, which matches the performance of DeepSeek’s distilled model and significantly improves on the base Qwen2.5-Coder one:.

In a recent development, throughout the training of OlympicCoder-7B, we found DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 was sufficient to train each model with 32k context on a single node of 8 x H100s. However, when we tried scaling up our recipe to 32B, we ran into a host of memory problems. In particular, our runs would OOM once the context was scaled beyond 20k tokens, even on 16 nodes 😢. This wasn’t ideal as 20% of the CodeForces-CoTs traces are larger than 20k tokens, which means they would get truncated during training.

The root of the problem is that transformers and trl do not yet support context parallelism, although see this matter to track progress.

In the meantime, we explored a variety of memory saving techniques and found that combining FSDP with the paged_adamw_8bit optimizer allowed us to scale the context to 22,528 tokens: still not ideal, but only 9% of the data was truncated.

Recent progress has been made to improve the implementation of GRPO in TRL, bringing enhancements that further boost efficiency, scalability, and resource utilization. Here’s a summary of the most crucial changes since the last update:.

One of the main bottlenecks of GRPO is the same as for any online method: generation takes time. A key way to make GRPO more sample-efficient is to reuse generated samples multiple times during optimization instead of discarding them after a single use. This technique was actually introduced a long time ago with PPO.

For GRPO, the number of times a sample is reused is denoted as μ.

It is now possible to reuse generated samples multiple times, significantly speeding up the process.

According to recent reports, however, be cautious—if μ is too large, it can negatively impact learning. Based on our experience, a good balance is between 2 and 4.

It has been revealed that when training a model, not all rewards are equally crucial. For example, we may want the model to prioritize correctness over formatting, rather than treating both aspects equally.

In a recent development, to address this, it is now possible to assign different weights to different rewards, allowing finer control over the optimization process. By adjusting these weights, we can guide the model to focus more on the aspects that matter most for a given task.

Several smaller but impactful improvements have been made to GRPO:.

Next Steps and Work in Progress.

The current focus is on two key areas:.

According to recent reports, we have further enriched our previously released OpenR1-Math-Raw dataset with latest metadata to enable more informed decision-making during filtering and verification. Specifically, we have added the following columns:.

To help the community understand the impact of verification-based filtering on math datasets for SFT distillation, we conducted several ablation experiments. Starting with a randomly selected pool of 200k samples, we created six distinct SFT datasets based on the following filtering rules:.

For filtering in data-constrained settings, both precision and recall are notable considerations. Therefore, we didn't run each experiment with the same token budget but rather trained on single epoch over all data. For the model, we chose Qwen7B-Instruct and fine-tuned it with RoPE extension to a 32k context length and cosine schedule. To track performance progression, we evaluated the models at every 40th step on AIME-24, AIME-25, and MATH-500 using lighteval. The results are summarized below:.

Based on our findings, the optimal filtering method depends heavily on the training token budget. For shorter runs, stricter verification methods offer significant advantages. As a general recommendation, we recommend combining llama verification with math_verify—as done in the LorMV dataset.

The Hugging Face learn team are working on accessible material on Reinforcement Learning, GRPO, and training reasoning models with TRL. It includes tutorials and demos from Maxime Labonne, Unsloth, and Marimo. Check out the reasoning course if you’re looking for a good place to get started in this fast moving field!

The last few weeks have seen continued exploration of GRPO across a wide variety of tasks, along with several new reasoning datasets that target domains that are broader than math and code. Here’s some of the releases we found especially exciting:.

Welcome Gemma 3: Google's all newly introduced multimodal, multilingual, long context open LLM

📅 12 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today Google releases Gemma 3, a latest iteration of their Gemma family of models.
  • All the models are on the Hub and tightly integrated with the Hugging Face ecosystem.
  • According to recent reports, both pre-trained and instruction tuned models are released.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today Google releases Gemma 3, a latest iteration of their Gemma family of models. The models range from 1B to 27B parameters, have a context window up to 128k tokens, can accept images and text, and support 140+ languages.

Try out Gemma 3 now 👉🏻 Gemma 3 Space.

All the models are on the Hub and tightly integrated with the Hugging Face ecosystem.

According to recent reports, both pre-trained and instruction tuned models are released. Gemma-3-4B-IT beats Gemma-2-27B IT, while Gemma-3-27B-IT beats Gemini 1.5-Pro across benchmarks.

Recent findings suggest that gemma 3 is Google's latest iteration of open weight LLMs. It comes in four sizes, 1 billion, 4 billion, 12 billion, and 27 billion parameters with base (pre-trained) and instruction-tuned versions. Gemma 3 goes multimodal! The 4, 12, and 27 billion parameter models can process both images and text, while the 1B variant is text only.

Industry observers note that the input context window length has been increased from Gemma 2’s 8k to 32k for the 1B variants, and 128k for all others. As is the case with other VLMs (vision-language models), Gemma 3 generates text in response to the user inputs, which may consist of text and, optionally, images. Example uses include question answering, analyzing image content, summarizing documents, etc.

Sources indicate that while these are multimodal models, one can use it as a text only model (as an LLM) without loading the vision encoder in memory. We will talk about this in more detail later in the inference section.

The three core enhancements in Gemma 3 over Gemma 2 are:.

Industry observers note that in this section, we will cover the technical details that lead to these enhancements. It is interesting to start with the knowledge of Gemma 2 and explore what was necessary to make these models even better. This exercise will help you think like the Gemma team and appreciate the details!

Sources indicate that scaling context length to 128k tokens could be achieved efficiently without training models from scratch. Instead, models are pretrained with 32k sequences, and only the 4B, 12B, and 27B models are scaled to 128k tokens at the end of pretraining, saving significant compute. Positional embeddings, like RoPE, are adjusted—upgraded from a 10k base frequency in Gemma 2 to 1M in Gemma 3—and scaled by a factor of 8 for longer contexts.

It has been revealed that KV Cache management is optimized using Gemma 2’s sliding window interleaved attention. Hyperparameters are tuned to interleave 5 local layers with 1 global layer (previously 1:1) and reduce the window size to 1024 tokens (down from 4096). Crucially, memory savings are achieved without degrading perplexity.

Gemma 3 models use SigLIP as an image encoder, which encodes images into tokens that are ingested into the language model. The vision encoder takes as input square images resized to 896x896. Fixed input resolution makes it more difficult to process non-square aspect ratios and high-resolution images. To address these limitations during inference, the images can be adaptively cropped, and each crop is then resized to 896x896 and encoded by the image encoder. This algorithm, called pan and scan, effectively enables the model to zoom in on smaller details in the image.

Sources indicate that similar to PaliGemma, attention in Gemma 3 works differently for text and image inputs. Text is handled with one-way attention, where the model focuses only on previous words in a sequence. Images, on the other hand, get full attention with no masks, allowing the model to look at every part of the image in a bidirectional manner, giving it a complete, unrestricted understanding of the visual input.

In a recent development, one can see in the figure below that the image tokens are provided with bi-directional attention (the entire square is lit up) while the text tokens have causal attention. It also indicates how attention works with the sliding window algorithm.

Industry observers note that to make a LLM multilingual, the pretraining dataset incorporates more languages. The dataset of Gemma 3 has double the amount of multilingual data to improve language coverage.

To account for the changes, the tokenizer is the same as that of Gemini 2.0. It is a SentencePiece tokenizer with 262K entries. The upcoming tokenizer significantly improves the encoding of Chinese, Japanese and Korean text, at the expense of a slight increase of the token counts for English and Code.

For the curious mind, here is the technical report on Gemma 3, to dive deep into the enhancements.

It has been revealed that the LMSys Elo score is a number that ranks language models based on how well they perform in head-to-head competitions, judged by human preferences. On LMSys Chatbot Arena, Gemma 3 27B IT reports an Elo score of 1339, and ranks among the top 10 best models, including leading closed ones. The Elo is comparable to o1-preview and is above other non-thinking open models. This score is achieved with Gemma 3 working on text-only inputs, like the other LLMs in the table.

Gemma 3 has been evaluated across benchmarks like MMLU-Pro (27B: 67.5), LiveCodeBench (27B: 29.7), and Bird-SQL (27B: 54.4), showing competitive performance compared to closed Gemini models. Tests like GPQA Diamond (27B: 42.4) and MATH (27B: 69.0) highlight its reasoning and math skills, while FACTS Grounding (27B: 74.9) and MMMU (27B: 64.9) demonstrate strong factual accuracy and multimodal abilities. However, it lags in SimpleQA (27B: 10.0) for basic facts. When compared to Gemini 1.5 models, Gemma 3 is often close—and sometimes better—proving its value as an accessible, high-performing option.

Tech Report: Xet is on the Hub

📅 18 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1372 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Click here to read about joining the Xet waitlist (or head over to join immediately).
  • Over the past few weeks, Hugging Face’s Xet Team took a major step forward by migrating the first Model and Dataset repositories off LFS and to Xet storage.
  • Recent findings suggest that this marks one of many steps to fulfill Hugging Face’s vision for the Hub by empowering AI builders to build, iterate, and collaborate more effectively on massive models and datasets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Click here to read about joining the Xet waitlist (or head over to join immediately).

Over the past few weeks, Hugging Face’s Xet Team took a major step forward by migrating the first Model and Dataset repositories off LFS and to Xet storage.

Recent findings suggest that this marks one of many steps to fulfill Hugging Face’s vision for the Hub by empowering AI builders to build, iterate, and collaborate more effectively on massive models and datasets. If you're interested in deeper dives on the technology itself, check out the following posts:.

It has been revealed that but this post isn't about the core technology. It's a behind-the-scenes view of getting Xet on the Hub; taking you through our proof-of-concept to the first migration of repositories.

The migration shifted ~6% of the Hub’s download traffic onto Xet infrastructure, validating several integral components and testing integrations with the myriad of ways repositories are accessed (e.g., via local development environments, different libraries, CI systems, cloud platforms, etc.). With nearly two million developers working on over two million public repositories, it’s real-world usage that’s the ultimate proving ground. Engineering a complex system like Xet storage is a balancing act. You proposal for scale, performance, and reliability, but once bytes start moving, challenges emerge. The trick is knowing when to move from design and theory to practice.

Recent findings suggest that LFS, the storage system behind repositories today, stores large files in a separate object storage outside of the repository. LFS deduplicates at the file level. Even tiny edits create a fresh revision to upload in full; painful for the multi-gigabyte files found in many Hub repositories.

According to recent reports, in contrast, Xet storage uses content-defined chunking (CDC), to deduplicate at the level of bytes (~64KB chunks of data). If you edit one row in a Parquet file or tweak a small piece of metadata in a GGUF model, only those changed chunks are sent over the wire.

This provides significant benefits to large file transfers. For example, the Xet team keeps an internal ~5 GB SQLite database that powers a metrics dashboard. With LFS, appending 1 MB (around the average update right now) requires re-uploading the entire 5 GB file. With Xet storage, we push only the new data.

This means uploads for the dashboard take a tenth of a second (at 50Mb/s) instead of the 13 minutes if the database were backed by LFS.

Making this work requires coordination between the following components:.

Before moving to production, the system was released into an ephemeral environment, where we built a steel thread of functionality to enable uploading and downloading via the huggingface_hub. The video below reveals our progress one month in:.

It has been revealed that after the heady highs of a quick proof-of-concept, the team settled into battling gnarly integration points (privacy, backward compatibility, fragmentation, etc) with the complex ecosystem that is the Hub. Eventually, the infrastructure moved into production for Hugging Face team members. With real usage now rolling in, we moved forward with the first large-scale migration.

In a recent development, on February 20th at 10 a.m., it was all hands on deck. In the weeks prior the team had built the internal tooling to migrate files from LFS to Xet and, just as importantly, roll back a repository to LFS if necessary. Now it was time to put it to the test. Grafana and Kibana lit up with latest logs and metrics, showing the load shift in real time.

The picture is the same in Kibana, only here you can tell when we took a lunch break:.

Recent findings suggest that by the end of the day, we had successfully migrated all target repositories for a total of 4.5 TB into Xet storage. Downloads from each repository were now served by our infrastructure.

No launch is without its lessons. The system handled the load smoothly and migrations went off without any major disruptions, but as the bytes flowed through various components we began to see some trends.

Reviewing network throughput post-migration, we saw that CAS was downloading four times more data than it was returning to clients:.

Recent findings suggest that upon further investigation we found the vast majority of requests to CAS were for 10MB ranges of data within files. These requests come from users that are using hf_transfer to accelerate their downloads of large files. The requested ranges do not align on block boundaries and the block format doesn’t provide uncompressed chunk lengths to facilitate skipping directly to the data within the block. Instead, CAS streams the block starting at the beginning and reads until it finds the requested data.

Given a block with an average size of 60MB and multiple partial requests to ranges within that block, the overhead accumulates. CAS reads 210MB for just 60MB delivered, a ratio of 3.5 bytes downloaded : 1 byte sent to the client. At scale across blocks of irregular sizes and ranges that can span several blocks, the 4 bytes downloaded : 1 byte sent ratio is matched.

As usual, an image is worth a thousand words:.

To fix this, we updated the block format to store chunk-length metadata, enabling CAS to download only what each request actually needs. This format change required coordinated updates across:.

All of which were undertaken without downtime. Not only did this result in a balanced ratio in CAS downloads to returned data, but also reduced GET latency by ~35% across the board.

Sources indicate that at the same time, we also saw an unexpected load imbalance across our CAS cluster. One pod would spike to hundreds of active uploads while other pods chugged along at single digits. Swapping the load balancer’s routing algorithm (from round-robin to least outstanding requests) and adding more nodes made little difference in the moment.

Digging deeper we realized that during uploads, CAS writes to a temporary file for validation before uploading without calling fsync, allowing the OS to buffer writes in the page cache. When a spike of uploads comes in, the unflushed page cache leads to increased memory pressure.

Sources indicate that as the OS tries to flush the page cache to disk, the pod experiences throughput throttling from block storage, causing increased latency on uploads. While uploads slowly process, newly introduced requests continue to come in, pushing more to the disk. This creates a vicious cycle, leading to a backlog of uploads and the imbalance that we saw during the migration:.

To keep a pod from getting in this state, we put a limit to the number of concurrent uploads each machine accepts before rejecting requests that, when reached, pushes requests on to other pods in the cluster. If all pods in the cluster get in this state, then our autoscaling policies kick in. Longer-term solutions might include forcing disk syncs, removing the on-disk buffering, or switching to ephemeral storage with better throughput.

Industry observers note that these two concerns led to important architectural improvements, but they weren’t the only challenges the team tackled in the weeks following the migration. We also addressed other performance issues, a memory leak (which we fixed but still can't definitively root cause), and on advice from AWS to migrate the LFS Bridge from an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to a Network Load Balancer (NLB) to improve scalability during bursts of traffic.

It has been revealed that in short, real-world load was essential for exposing these challenges, and incremental migrations let us tackle them safely. That’s how we’re ensuring Xet-backed repositories scale reliably for the entire Hugging Face community with faster uploads, fewer bottlenecks, and minimal disruption all the way.

With the initial migration complete, Xet is now on the Hugging Face Hub.

Recent findings suggest that we’re finalizing an official integration with the huggingface_hub that will mean you get the benefits of Xet without any significant changes to your current workflow. To get going:.

It has been revealed that if you have any questions, drop us a line in the comments 👇 or open a discussion on the Xet team page. And stay tuned as we roll out more pieces (faster web uploads, faster Git workflows), bringing faster big-file collaboration to every AI builder on Hugging Face!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that at its annual GTC conference, NVIDIA has unveiled a trio of groundbreaking open-source releases aimed at accelerating physical AI development. Release of a upcoming suite of world foundation models (WFMs) with multicontrols called Cosmos Transfer, a highly curated Physical AI Dataset, and the first open model for general humanoid reasoning called NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1 - represent a significant leap forward in physical AI technology, offering developers powerful tools and resources to advance robotics systems, and enhance autonomous vehicle technology.

Cosmos Transfer, the latest addition to NVIDIA's Cosmos™ world foundation models (WFMs), introduces a new level of control and accuracy in generating virtual world scenes.

Available in 7 billion parameter size, the model utilizes multicontrols to guide the generation of high-fidelity world scenes from structural inputs, ensuring precise spatial alignment and scene composition.

The model is built by training individual ControlNets separately for each sensor modality used to capture the simulated world.

Input types include 3D bounding box map, Trajectory map, Depth map, Segmentation map.

Outputs from Cosmos Transfer varying environments and weather conditions.

Sources indicate that cosmos Transfer coupled with the NVIDIA Omniverse platform is driving controllable synthetic data generation for robotics and autonomous vehicle development at scale. Find more Cosmos Transfer Examples on GitHub.

Cosmos Transfer samples built using post-training base model are also available for autonomous vehicles.

NVIDIA has also released Physical AI Dataset, an open-source dataset on Hugging Face for developing physical AI. This commercial-grade, pre-validated dataset consists of 15 terabytes of data representing more than 320,000 trajectories for robotics training, plus up to 1,000 Universal Scene Description (OpenUSD) assets, including a SimReady collection.

The dataset is designed for post-training foundation models like Cosmos Predict world foundation models, providing developers with high-quality, diverse data to enhance their AI models.

Sources indicate that another exciting announcement is the release of NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1, the world's first open foundation model for generalized humanoid robot reasoning and skills. This cross-embodiment model takes multimodal input, including language and images, to perform manipulation tasks in diverse environments. The NVIDIA Isaac GR00T-N1-2B model is available on Hugging Face.

It has been revealed that isaac GR00T N1 was trained on an expansive humanoid dataset, consisting of real captured data, synthetic data generated using components of the NVIDIA Isaac GR00T Blueprint, and internet-scale video data. It is adaptable through post-training for specific embodiments, tasks and environments.

Sources indicate that isaac GR00T N1 uses a single model and set of weights to enable manipulation behaviors on various humanoid robots, such as the Fourier GR-1 and 1X Neo. It demonstrates robust generalization across a range of tasks, including grasping and manipulating objects with one or both arms, as well as transferring items between arms. It can also execute complex, multi-step tasks that require sustained contextual understanding and the integration of diverse skills. These capabilities make it well-suited for applications in material handling, packaging, and inspection.

Isaac GR00T N1 features a dual-system architecture inspired by human cognition, consisting of the following complementary components:.

Post-training is the path forward to advancing autonomous systems, creating specialized models for downstream physical AI tasks.

It has been revealed that check out GitHub for Cosmos Predict and Cosmos Transfer inference scripts. Explore the Cosmos Transfer research paper for more details.

It has been revealed that the NVIDIA Isaac GR00T-N1-2B model is available on Hugging Face. Sample datasets and PyTorch scripts for post-training using custom user datasets, which is compatible with the Hugging Face LeRobot format are available on GitHub. For more information about the Isaac GR00T N1 model, see the research paper.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.﻿.

AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.﻿.

According to recent reports, if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Chess.com is ready to go a lot bigger than chess. After launching Gambit, a gambling-free poker site, earlier this year, the company is now adding 10 more games: backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble alternative called word. They’re all part of Chess’s latest Classic Games platform, which is launching its public beta on Saturday on the web and through a new app for iOS and Android.

“Our cofounders have had many people come up to them and say, ‘Hey, I run a mahjong night on Wednesdays’ or ‘I go to this local bar in Chicago with like five people, and we love playing go, but we lack a Chess.com,’” chief growth officer Albert Cheng says in an interview with The Verge. “The way that Chess.com has grown this community of almost 300 million members has not really happened for a lot of these other types of classic games.”.

Classic Games is aimed at filling that gap. Some of the new games, like shoji or xiangqi, are strategy games similar to chess while others are further afield, like sudoku, solitaire, and word. The Classic team chose the new games through “a mix of community feedback, market research, and then just our own confidence in our ability to serve that game well,” Cheng notes. It’s focused on classics that “have some sort of lifelong journey of learning and a community.”.

According to recent reports, classic Games will feel familiar if you’ve ever played a match on Chess.com. Each game has lessons, leaderboards, and a rating system. Multiplayer games like checkers or mahjong have options for matches against other players or bots, and they use the same bot characters that Chess.com has. (Martin remains the lowest-rated bot across the board, whether it’s on Chess, Gambit, or Classic.) Not all of the games have the same play modes — word and mahjong have puzzles like chess, while sudoku has a set of daily grids and solitaire has daily deals.

It has been revealed that the expansion hasn’t put Chess.com itself on the back burner, according to Cheng. If anything, it’s never been better. “Chess is more and more so in the public zeitgeist than I’ve ever seen it, frankly, during my time here,” Cheng claims. “Our daily active consumers are higher than they’ve ever been during the manufacturer’s history.” He declined to share exactly how many daily users Chess.com presently has but said the site is “doing amazingly well.”.

According to recent reports, so, while the company is expanding beyond its domain name, chess remains its primary focus. “The amount of folks that are fully dedicated toward building fresh games is less than 1 percent of the company,” according to Cheng.

According to recent reports, AI played a key role in helping Chess.com launch 11 newly introduced games in a matter of months with a team of only a few people. Earlier this year, Cheng told The Verge his team built Gambit with the help of AI, mainly for coding tasks. He states they used “almost entirely the same approach” for Classic, with AI helping to speed up the coding process again.

“Because these games are built on top of the Chess.com code base and design system and bot characters and rating systems, it’s a huge advantage and allows us to move very rapidly alongside AI to bring these types of games to market with a very small team,” Cheng states. “As we create more and more games, the adjacent games that can be created to it just happen much faster because the infrastructure is there, as opposed to standing everything up from scratch.”.

Industry observers note that AI wasn’t used for Classic Games’ art and design, Cheng says. “The look and feel of it is very carefully crafted by humans, and we’re proud of that,” he says. “The truth is, it really is a blend. It’s a small team of really talented folks that have good product and design judgment, and they’re leveraging AI.”.

“We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years.”.

Chess.com’s comfort with AI may come from the fact that human chess players have now spent decades playing and learning alongside machines. “We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years,” Cheng notes, calling back to Garry Kasparov’s 1996 chess match against IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer. “Even before the tech giant was founded 20 years ago, the idea that AI was super powerful at the game of chess was embedded in how the cofounders thought about the company.”.

Elsewhere in the games industry, there’s been increasing tension over the use of AI. Cheng states that while Chess.com may be using AI to “accelerate” coding tasks, the creative side of things has become more important. “On the art and the design side, the ratios are shifting a decent amount, where we’re hiring more of those folks,” he says, adding that the company has “shipped a lot more major features in Chess.com than in previous years” using what they’ve learned from Classic Games’ faster development process.

In a recent development, chess.com might not be done growing its library of games, either. Cheng noted it will likely expand to “a lot more” games in the future.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On March 14, we submitted Hugging Face's response to the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy's request for information on the White House AI Action Blueprint.
  • Open approaches to AI development are not only (typically) more transparent, adaptable, and scientifically sound, they have also consistently reproduced or surpassed the performance of widely-used API-only commercial offerings on many tasks; and are increasingly doing so on shorter timelines, with increased resource efficiency.
  • Sources indicate that the most advanced AI systems to date all stand on a strong foundation of open research (attention mechanisms, transformer architectures, cheaper post-training algorithms) and open source software (PyTorch, Hugging Face libraries, supercomputer operating systems) — which indicates the critical value of continued support for openness in sustaining further progress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On March 14, we submitted Hugging Face's response to the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy's request for information on the White House AI Action Blueprint. We took this opportunity to (re-)assert the fundamental role that open AI systems and open science play in enabling the technology to be more performant and efficient, broadly and reliably adopted, and meeting the highest standards of security. This blog post provides a summary of our response, the full text is available here.

Open approaches to AI development are not only (typically) more transparent, adaptable, and scientifically sound, they have also consistently reproduced or surpassed the performance of widely-used API-only commercial offerings on many tasks; and are increasingly doing so on shorter timelines, with increased resource efficiency. Our team's recent OlympicCoder outperforming Claude 3.7 on complex coding tasks with 7B parameters and an open-source post-training recipe, or AI2's fully open OLMo 2 models (with open training data) matching o1-mini performances, are two of the most recent compelling examples. These successes show that a robust AI strategy must leverage open and collaborative development to best drive performance, adoption, and security of the technology. We make three major recommendations in this direction.

Sources indicate that the most advanced AI systems to date all stand on a strong foundation of open research (attention mechanisms, transformer architectures, cheaper post-training algorithms) and open source software (PyTorch, Hugging Face libraries, supercomputer operating systems) — which indicates the critical value of continued support for openness in sustaining further progress. Investment in systems that can freely be re-used and adapted has also been shown to have a strong economic impact multiplying effect, driving a significant percentage of countries' GDP. As AI systems with open weights and training techniques become increasingly attractive options for developers in terms of both performance and cost, prioritizing public research infrastructure and broad access to compute, customizable models, and trusted open datasets — especially for smaller developers and researchers — will be essential to the further technical and economic success of AI technology.

According to recent reports, addressing the resource constraints of organizations adopting and adapting AI technology will be essential to supporting its diffusion and fostering innovation from adopters across the entire development chain. Smaller models (that may even be used on edge devices), techniques to reduce computational requirements at inference, and efforts to facilitate mid-scale training for organizations with modest to moderate computational resources all support the development of models that meet the specific needs of their use context, especially in high-risk settings such as healthcare where fully generalist models have proven unreliable. More efficient and purpose-designed AI systems facilitate better in-context evaluation, better resource utilization, and enable organizations to build technical capacity at all stages of the AI development chain to ensure that all consumers can leverage the system that best fits their needs.

In a recent development, finally, if decades of information security and cybersecurity in open source software are any indication, open and transparent AI systems will have a fundamental role to play in securing AI development and deployment especially in the most critical settings — with different levels of openness needed for different security requirements. Fully transparent models providing access to their training data and procedures can support the most extensive safety certifications. Open infrastructure and open-source tooling implementing the latest training techniques can empower organizations to train the models they need in fully controlled environments. Open-weight models that can be run in air-gapped environments can be a critical component in managing information risks. Prioritizing adoption of the most transparent systems, supporting the development of the open resources outlined, and building capacity to leverage them especially in critical settings of AI adoption are essential to enabling more secure AI adoption.

Please refer to the full response for our more detailed recommendations!

Industry News: Resourceful PC owner repurposes CPU watercooler with dead pump as standalone LCD hardware monitor, vibecodes upcoming software for module

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (493 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AIO liquid coolers are notorious for shorter lifespans due to pump failure or leaks, which usually results in having to replace the entire unit.
  • According to the post, the pump on their NZXT Kraken AIO stopped working around a month ago.
  • It has been revealed that getting the display working properly required more than just pulling it out of the pump block.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AIO liquid coolers are notorious for shorter lifespans due to pump failure or leaks, which usually results in having to replace the entire unit. However, one enthusiast decided to salvage theirs uniquely, at least a part of it. Sharing their DIY project on Reddit, u/BodeeHav repurposed the LCD screen from a dead NZXT Kraken AIO into a standalone desktop monitor that displays live CPU and GPU temperatures and utilization after vibecoding entirely latest software.

According to the post, the pump on their NZXT Kraken AIO stopped working around a month ago. Rather than discarding a perfectly usable screen, they decided to dismantle the block and remove the LCD and its main board. They used the original black outer housing and 3D printed a stand to hold the LCD in place. To keep things tidy, they stripped the connector down to just its SATA power and USB pins. The display connects directly to the motherboard, presumably using the internal 9-pin USB header, although BodeeHav says they strategy to adapt it for external USB.

It has been revealed that getting the display working properly required more than just pulling it out of the pump block. BodeeHav initially used NZXT’s CAM software; however, he kept running into issues whenever the PC entered sleep or standby. To overcome this hurdle, they turned to AI and vibe coded an entirely newly introduced software as a replacement that offers full control of the LCD with various customization options.

BodeeHav has graciously made his entire project available on GitHub, where you can access the DesktopKraken software and an STL file for the stand. According to the official GitHub page, the software is a standalone Windows application that communicates with compatible NZXT Kraken Elite LCDs over USB without requiring NZXT CAM.

It has been revealed that the software presently only offers support for the 2023 Kraken Elite and 2024 Kraken Elite V2, which use circular LCDs with a 640x640 resolution. Apart from CPU and GPU temperatures and utilization, it can also display clock speeds, power consumption, memory usage, and VRAM information. Additionally, the software can be used for brightness control, screen orientation, sensor logging, and it even offers support for custom images, animated GIFs, thermal warning gauges, and automatic recovery after Windows sleep or a USB disconnect.

While it may cater to a very niche audience, the project is a great example of how a little ingenuity can give failed components a second life.
