Anthropic is rolling out a upcoming Claude app for Android that picks up a Material 3 Expressive redesign.

Confirmed on Twitter/X by Anthropic Product Manager Robert Bye, Claude is now rolling out a Material 3 Expressive redesign for its Android app that, while not a full embrace of Google’s design language, does make a clear attempt to better fit in on Android.

The updated design picks up a bottom-bar UI as opposed to relying fully on the old hamburger menu – it still exists, but it’s mainly for chat history now. You can see M3 elements throughout the app, including in the model switcher and the background of chats. It’s clearly themed to match Anthropic’s aesthetic, and there’s no obvious implementation of Material You colors, but it all fits within the general Material 3 guidelines – much more so than the original app.

The one flaw we spotted was the predictive back implementation, which gets a neat animation to move the search bar but is supposed to show a preview of the previous screen, but that’s just nit-picking, really.

The latest Claude app for Android is rolling out now.

Industry observers note that analytics and metrics are the cornerstone of understanding what's happening with your deployment. Are your Inference Endpoints overloaded? How many requests are they handling? Having well-visualized, relevant metrics displayed in real-time is crucial for monitoring and debugging.

We realized that our analytics dashboard needed a refresh. Since we debug a lot of endpoints ourselves, we’ve felt the same pain as our people. That’s why we sat down to proposal and make several improvements to provide a better experience for you.

According to recent reports, ⏰ Real-Time Metrics: Data now updates in real-time, ensuring you get an accurate and up-to-the-second view of your endpoint’s performance. Whether you’re monitoring request latency, response times, or error rates, you can now see the events as they happen. We’ve also reworked the backend of our analytics dashboard to ensure that data loads swiftly, especially for high-traffic endpoints. No more waiting around for metrics to populate. Just open the dashboard and get instant insights.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

USB-C chargers are pretty standardized at this point, but there’s a fun newly introduced trend of adding displays to your power brick that I’ve been very much enjoying, and the new PicoGo Pro from Baseus is a great example with three ports, optimized charging, and a cute little character to top it off – and for Black Friday, it’s pretty deeply discounted, too.

In a recent development, the Baseus PicoGo Pro (AH22) is a 100W, 3-port USB-C charger designed to top off your laptop, phone, and/or tablet, even all at the same time. For anyone who travels often or just has a lot of devices on hand, chargers like this are a must. Having something you don’t have to think twice about when it comes to charging rates is just so nice, and these have come a long way, too.

Recent findings suggest that using GaN tech, PicoGo Pro is very compact at about 2 inches tall and a little over an inch wide. I remember having single-port chargers that could barely fast-charge my phone that were twice this size just a few years ago. GaN just absolutely rules, and Baseus is using a special version that reduces heat and improves efficiency.

But the two reasons I really like this charger aren’t strictly to do with GaN.

Recent findings suggest that the first is the built-in display. Again, that’s a trend throughout the industry. Anker has several chargers out with built-in displays as the company helped to really make this popular – the Anker Prime 160W brick is really similar to PicoGo Pro (at a higher price), and it’s the only I’ve been using for months before trying out this Baseus model.

Baseus has a cute little animated character that accompanies your charging, with little eyes when the charger isn’t active and some fun animations to show your charging rate in real-time. Neat! You can “press” the button to move through the UI and even see the specific charging rate of each connected device. You’ll also see that the brick can recognize the device you have plugged in, though Android devices just show a generic “SAMSUNG” or whatever brand you plug in – Anker, again, had a similar set of features in a brick released earlier in 2026, but some of those features were iPhone-only, and that brick was only a 1-port, 45W charger anyway.

According to recent reports, but, like that Anker brick, Baseus supports “smart” charging that adjusts to your device. Plugging in a Galaxy Z Fold 8 that was around 65% full, I saw the brick adjust its charging speed to tailor to the phone, initially going up to full speed before settling down around 28W~. You can manually adjust this with “Turbo” or “Gentle” modes, the former maxing out the charging rate and the latter settling in around 15W for a slower charge. That flexibility is great because it means you can adjust the charging rate to what you need in that moment. Full-speed for a quick top-off on a busy day, slower charging overnight to preserve battery health.

Baseus isn’t doing much latest here, though the GaN tech mentioned earlier is enhanced by some architecture and algorithm adjustments the tech giant has made behind the scenes, but it’s a really good implementation.

Beyond that, it’s also priced pretty well.

Baseus PicoGo Pro’s full price is $59.99, but you’ll probably rarely see it there. Technically, today is its launch date, and it’s already down by over 30% at $39.70 for Black Friday. Value-wise, this one is hard to beat.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (316 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past month, Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Carbon brought frontier physical reasoning to robotics: understanding 3D scenes, reconstructing real environments in simulation, practicing tasks in sim before running them on hardware, and directly controlling robot arms from camera images.
  • To help developers put Hydrogen to work, today we're launching the Robotics plugin on Google Antigravity: a set of skills for hardware onboarding, simulation and robot control turning Antigravity into a one-stop robotics workbench.
  • Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon revealed that a general model can drive a robot arm directly, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen preserves that ability.

Over the past month, Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Carbon brought frontier physical reasoning to robotics: understanding 3D scenes, reconstructing real environments in simulation, practicing tasks in sim before running them on hardware, and directly controlling robot arms from camera images. Last week, we introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, which brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning to a much faster model built for speed and efficiency.

To help developers put Hydrogen to work, today we're launching the Robotics plugin on Google Antigravity: a set of skills for hardware onboarding, simulation and robot control turning Antigravity into a one-stop robotics workbench. Together, they enable a developer to go from a robot in a box to one that can perform a working application in an afternoon. To install the plugin, open Antigravity, go to Customizations and search for Robotics on the Build With Google shelf.

Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon revealed that a general model can drive a robot arm directly, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen preserves that ability. Give it a goal in plain language and a camera view, and it plans the task, writes and runs the control code, and keeps adjusting until the job is done. On the Artificial Analysis Robotics 0.1 benchmark, Gemini 4 Hydrogen controls a real 6-axis arm through eight everyday tabletop tasks, from pouring a drink to packing blocks into a box. Hydrogen scores 58, similar to Argon at a lower cost per token.

Recent findings suggest that hydrogen brings the specialized skills of our Gemini Robotics ER 2 (Embodied Reasoning) models into the core Gemini 4 model series, and it beats them on nearly every axis. On the public ERQA benchmark, Hydrogen outperforms Gemini Robotics ER 2 on spatial reasoning tasks such as multi-view correspondence and 3D trajectory reasoning. For developers using Gemini Robotics ER 2 today, we recommend trying out Gemini 4 Hydrogen for these workloads.

Sources indicate that the Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus has spent the last few days getting review-bombed on Steam after it was discovered that a particular segment of the game used AI music. Reddit user ShweetsStuff discovered the songs used during a Grand Theft Auto-themed section. They found several audio files with Suno metadata that pointed back to the tracks on Suno’s site.

It has been revealed that creator Edmund McMillen took to X to apologize and claimed he “had no idea” the in-game GTA parody used generative AI music. Adding to the drama, Valve requires developers to disclose how and when they use generative AI in the development process, and Nicalis, Inc., the studio behind Repentance Plus, doesn’t appear to have mentioned the AI music anywhere.

Within hours of the discovery, Nicalis shared on X that Repentance Plus had been updated and the generated music files had been removed. While reviews on Steam have yet to rebound, and the game is still rated as “overwhelmingly negative,” consumers on X seem to be giving McMillen the benefit of the doubt, likely because he’s been quite outspoken on AI in game development, calling it “uninspired and bland” in a TikTok from 2024.

Recent findings suggest that gradio’s gr.Dataframe component is one of our most popular components, we've seen it used in a variety of awesome apps, like leaderboards, dashboards, and interactive visualisations. Although we hadn't made any changes to the dataframe in quite some time, our backlog of issues had been growing, and some improvements had been in demand for a while.

Well — we’re now super excited to release a host of new updates to Gradio’s dataframe component. Over the last 6 weeks, we’ve closed over 70 dataframe complications - including bugs, improvements and enhancements.

In a recent development, you can select multiple cells at once! Copy or delete values across your selection with ease.

Add row number columns and keep critical columns in view while navigating wide datasets using the pinned_columns parameter. No more losing track of what you're looking at!

Sources indicate that easily copy cell values into a comma-separated format with our new copy button. Need a better view? The full screen button gives you interactivity without distractions and can be enabled with the show_full_screen parameter.

Look at all that data! Now we can just scroll to the top.

Improved keyboard navigation makes gr.Dataframe more accessible than ever. You can also take control of your dataframe’s look with a dedicated styler parameter and enhance the user experience of your app.

Access entire row data in select events for more intuitive interactivity and data manipulation.

Customise the interactivity of your dataframe by specifying non-editable columns using the static_columns parameter.

Quickly find the data you need with our powerful search feature by setting the show_search parameter to "search".

Narrow down your dataset to focus on exactly what you need with flexible filtering options with show_search set to "filter".

Experience smoother, more intuitive cell selection that behaves the way you expect.

With over 70 issues closed, we’ve made huge improvements, but there’s always more for us to work on. Looking ahead, we still have more ideas to implement and we’re excited to keep refining accessibility, performance, and integration. Look out for some cool demos on our socials using the dataframe on Gradio’s X.

Recent findings suggest that the updated dataframe is live in the latest Gradio release. Patch your installation with pip install --upgrade gradio.

In a recent development, check out the Gradio documentation for examples and tutorials to get started with these upcoming features. We’re eager to see what you create! Got thoughts or suggestions? Share them by raising an problem in our GitHub repo.

This is awesome, I hope it can get into Streamlit, which is a great library for making interactive dashboards in Python.

A mobile app sends POST /orders. The server creates the order, but the response is lost when the phone switches from Wi-Fi to 4G. The app sees a timeout and retries. Now the customer has two orders, and your support team has a refund to process.

It has been revealed that retrying is the right thing for a client to do. The problem is that POST is not idempotent: RFC 9110 defines GET, PUT and DELETE as idempotent methods, but not POST or PATCH. Repeating a POST can repeat its side effects.

In a recent development, an idempotency key fixes this. The client generates a unique key for each logical operation and sends it with every attempt. The server does the work once, stores the response against the key, and returns the stored response for any retry. The IETF HTTPAPI working group is standardizing this pattern as the Idempotency-Key HTTP header field, and this tutorial follows its recommendations.

We'll build it with Node.js, Express 5 and PostgreSQL. By the end you'll have a table that stores keys, a function that safely claims a key under concurrent requests, an Express route that replays stored responses, and a client that retries without creating duplicates.

The client's job is simple: generate a key, usually a UUID, and send the same key on every retry of the same operation. The draft defines the header value as a quoted string:.

The server's job is harder, because every request falls into one of five cases:.

In a recent development, to tell case 3 from case 4, the server stores a fingerprint of the request alongside the key. A matching fingerprint means a genuine retry; a different one means key reuse. Case 5 is the one most implementations get wrong, because it only indicates up under concurrency. A database constraint handles it for us.

Create a project and install the two dependencies:.

The key table records who sent the key, the request fingerprint, whether the work has finished, and the response to replay:.

According to recent reports, two details matter here. The primary key includes client_id, so keys are scoped per client: two customers who happen to generate the same value can't see each other's responses. And locked_until lets the server recover a key whose request crashed halfway, which we'll use in Step 3.

It has been revealed that the draft defines the header value as a structured field string, which means it arrives wrapped in double quotes. Many clients send it without quotes, so the parser below accepts both and limits the characters and length it will store:.

In a recent development, the fingerprint has to be identical for identical requests, even if a client serializes the JSON body with its properties in a different order. Sorting object keys before hashing takes care of that. The hash uses SHA-256 from Node's built-in crypto module:.

Including the method and path means a key reused on a different endpoint counts as a mismatch, not as a retry.

In a recent development, the tempting approach is to SELECT the key, and insert it if nothing comes back. Under concurrency that fails: two retries arriving a few milliseconds apart both see no row, and both do the work.

In a recent development, instead, let the primary key decide. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING either inserts the row or does nothing, atomically, even across many application processes. The PostgreSQL INSERT documentation describes this behavior in detail. If the insert returns a row, this request owns the key. If not, we read the existing row and decide which case we're in:.

Industry observers note that the PATCH in the last step is also atomic. If two retries find the same expired lock, only one of them matches the locked_until < now() condition and gets the key. If the row disappears between the two queries, for example because it was released after a failure, the function reports in_progress and the client simply retries.

Set LOCK_SECONDS comfortably above the slowest time your operation takes. If the lock expires while the original request is still running, a retry can take over and run the work a second time.

Industry observers note that once a request owns the key, it creates the order and marks the key as completed. Both writes happen in one transaction, so there is no moment where the order exists but the key still indicates in_progress, or the other way round. Note that a transaction in node-postgres has to use a single client checked out from the pool, as the node-postgres transaction documentation explains:.

According to recent reports, releaseKey runs when the work fails. Deleting the claim lets the client retry with the same key instead of waiting for the lock to expire. It only deletes rows that are still in progress, so a completed response is never thrown away.

Industry observers note that the route validates the body first. A request with invalid input never touches the key table, so the client can fix the input and resend with the same key. Error responses use the application/problem+json format from RFC 9457, which the idempotency draft also uses in its examples:.

It has been revealed that the server side only works if the client keeps the key stable. The most common client bug is generating a upcoming key inside the retry loop, which turns every retry into a new operation. Generate the key once per logical action, before the first attempt:.

It has been revealed that the catch branch is the reason idempotency keys exist. After a timeout, the client can't know whether the order was created. With a stable key, retrying is safe either way: if the first attempt succeeded, the retry returns the stored order; if it didn't, the retry creates it. The random jitter spreads retries out, so many clients recovering from the same outage don't all hit the server at once.

Sources indicate that in a browser or mobile app, store the key with the pending action, for example in the form state or a local queue. If the user taps "Place order" again after an error, reuse it. Only generate a new key when the user starts a genuinely new action.

In a recent development, keys can't live forever, or the table grows without limit. The draft leaves the retention period to the server but indicates it should be published in the API documentation, so clients know how long a retry stays safe. Twenty-four hours covers most retry scenarios. A scheduled job can delete older rows in batches:.

In a recent development, run it every few minutes from cron or your job scheduler until it deletes zero rows. Deleting in batches keeps each transaction short, and the created_at index from Step 1 keeps the inner query fast. A retry that arrives after its key has expired is treated as a newly introduced request, which is why the retention period belongs in your documentation.

Start the server with node server.js, then send the same request twice:.

In a recent development, the second request lists the properties in a different order, and it's still recognized as a retry because of the canonical fingerprint. Both responses carry the same order ID, and the orders table contains one row.

Sources indicate that now change the quantity while keeping the key. The server answers 422, because the key now belongs to a different request:.

To see the concurrent case, add await fresh Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 3000)); before completeKey in the route, restart the server, and fire two requests with a new key at the same time:.

Recent findings suggest that one request prints 201 and the other 409. Without the ON CONFLICT claim, both would have printed 201 and created two orders. Remove the delay when you're done.

Industry observers note that this design guarantees that the database work in Step 4 happens once per key. Two situations need extra care:.

Idempotency keys don't replace other safeguards either. A unique constraint on a natural business key, such as one payment per invoice, still catches duplicates that arrive with different keys, for example when a user submits the same form from two tabs.

In a recent development, with one table, an atomic claim and a transaction that stores the response next to the work, POST endpoints become safe to retry. Clients get a simple rule: generate one key per action, reuse it on every retry. The server takes care of the rest, including the concurrent retries that a SELECT-then-INSERT approach misses.

The same pattern works for PATCH endpoints and for webhooks you send to other systems. Start with the endpoints where a duplicate costs real money or confuses a customer, and publish your key format and retention period in the API documentation so client developers know what to send.

Training and Finetuning Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 26 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for a wide range of applications, such as retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, semantic textual similarity, paraphrase mining, and more. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use it to finetune a reranker model (also known as a cross-encoder) that beats all existing options on exactly your data. This method can also train extremely strong fresh reranker models from scratch.

Finetuning reranker models involves several components: datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class itself. I'll have a look at each of these components, accompanied by practical examples of how they can be used for finetuning strong reranker models.

In a recent development, lastly, in the Evaluation section, I'll show you that my small finetuned tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-base-gooaq-bce reranker model that I trained alongside this blogpost easily outperforms the 13 most commonly used public reranker models on my evaluation dataset. It even beats models that are 4x bigger.

Repeating the recipe with a bigger base model results in tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-large-gooaq-bce, a reranker model that blows all existing general-purpose reranker models out of the water on my data.

If you're interested in finetuning embedding models instead, then consider reading through my prior Training and Finetuning Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers blogpost as well.

In a recent development, reranker models, often implemented using Cross Encoder architectures, are designed to evaluate the relevance between pairs of texts (e.g., a query and a document, or two sentences). Unlike Sentence Transformers (a.k.a. bi-encoders, embedding models), which independently embed each text into vectors and compute similarity via a distance metric, Cross Encoder process the paired texts together through a shared neural network, resulting in one output score. By letting the two texts attend to each other, Cross Encoder models can outperform embedding models.

However, this strength comes with a trade-off: Cross Encoder models are slower as they process every possible pair of texts (e.g., 10 queries with 500 candidate documents requires 5,000 computations instead of 510 for embedding models). This makes them less efficient for large-scale initial retrieval but ideal for reranking: refining the top-k results first identified by faster Sentence Transformer models. The strongest search systems commonly use this 2-stage "retrieve and rerank" approach.

Throughout this blogpost, I'll use "reranker model" and "Cross Encoder model" interchangeably.

Reranker models are often tasked with a challenging problem:.

Which of these kkk highly-related documents answers the query the best?

General-purpose reranker models are trained to perform adequately on this exact question in a wide range of domains and topics, preventing them from reaching their maximum potential in your specific domain. Through finetuning, the model can learn to focus exclusively on the domain and/or language that matters to you.

Sources indicate that in the Evaluation section end of this blogpost, I'll show that training a model on your domain can outperform any general-purpose reranker model, even if those baselines are much bigger. Don't underestimate the power of finetuning on your domain!

Training reranker models involves the following components:.

Let's take a closer look at each component.

Sources indicate that the CrossEncoderTrainer uses datasets.Dataset or datasets.DatasetDict instances for training and evaluation. You can load data from the Hugging Face Datasets Hub or use your local data in whatever format you prefer (e.g. CSV, JSON, Parquet, Arrow, or SQL).

Note: Lots of public datasets that work out of the box with Sentence Transformers have been tagged with sentence-transformers on the Hugging Face Hub, so you can easily find them on https://huggingface.co/datasets?other=sentence-transformers. Consider browsing through these to find ready-to-go datasets that might be useful for your tasks, domains, or languages.

You can use the load_dataset function to load data from datasets in the Hugging Face Hub.

Some datasets, like nthakur/swim-ir-monolingual, have multiple subsets with different data formats. You need to specify the subset name along with the dataset name, e.g. dataset = load_dataset("nthakur/swim-ir-monolingual", "de", split="train").

You can also use load_dataset for loading local data in certain file formats:.

You can use datasets.Dataset.from_dict if your local data requires pre-processing. This allows you to initialize your dataset with a dictionary of lists:.

Each key in the dictionary becomes a column in the resulting dataset.

In a recent development, it is crucial that your dataset format matches your loss function (or that you choose a loss function that matches your dataset format and model). Verifying whether a dataset format and model work with a loss function involves three steps:.

For example, given a dataset with columns ["text1", "text2", "label"] where the "label" column has float similarity score ranging from 0 to 1 and a model outputting 1 label, we can use it with BinaryCrossEntropyLoss because:.

Be sure to re-order your dataset columns with Dataset.select_columns if your columns are not ordered correctly. For example, if your dataset has ["good_answer", "bad_answer", "question"] as columns, then this dataset can technically be used with a loss that requires (anchor, positive, negative) triplets, but the good_answer column will be taken as the anchor, bad_answer as the positive, and question as the negative.

Additionally, if your dataset has extraneous columns (e.g. sample_id, metadata, source, type), you should remove these with Dataset.remove_columns as they will be used as inputs otherwise. You can also use Dataset.select_columns to keep only the desired columns.

The success of training reranker models often depends on the quality of the negatives, i.e. the passages for which the query-negative score should be low. Negatives can be divided into two types:.

Recent findings suggest that the strongest CrossEncoder models are generally trained to recognize hard negatives, and so it's valuable to be able to "mine" hard negatives to train with. Sentence Transformers supports a strong mine_hard_negatives function that can assist, given a dataset of query-answer pairs:.

Sources indicate that loss functions help evaluate a model's performance on a set of data and direct the training process. The right loss function for your task depends on the data you have and what you're trying to achieve. You can find a full list of available loss functions in the Loss Overview.

Most loss functions are easy to set up - you just need to provide the CrossEncoder model you're training:.

Recent findings suggest that you can customize the training process using the CrossEncoderTrainingArguments class. This class lets you adjust parameters that can impact training speed and help you understand what's happening during training.

Sources indicate that for more information on the most useful training arguments, check out the Cross Encoder > Training Overview > Training Arguments. It's worth reading to get the most out of your training.

Here's an example of how to set up CrossEncoderTrainingArguments:.

Recent findings suggest that to track your model's performance during training, you can pass an eval_dataset to the CrossEncoderTrainer. However, you might want more detailed metrics beyond just the evaluation loss. That's where evaluators can help you assess your model's performance using specific metrics at various stages of training. You can use an evaluation dataset, an evaluator, both, or neither, depending on your needs. The evaluation strategy and frequency are controlled by the eval_strategy and eval_steps Training Arguments.

Sentence Transformers includes the following built-in evaluators:.

Recent findings suggest that you can also use SequentialEvaluator to join multiple evaluators into one, which can then be passed to the CrossEncoderTrainer. You can also just pass a list of evaluators to the trainer.

Sometimes you don't have the required evaluation data to prepare one of these evaluators on your own, but you still want to track how well the model performs on some common benchmarks. In that case, you can use these evaluators with data from Hugging Face.

Industry observers note that the STS Benchmark (a.k.a. STSb) is a commonly used benchmarking dataset to measure the model's understanding of semantic textual similarity of short texts like "A man is feeding a mouse to a snake.".

Feel free to browse the sentence-transformers/stsb dataset on Hugging Face.

Preparing data for CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator can be difficult as you need negatives in addition to your query-positive data.

In a recent development, the mine_hard_negatives function has a convenient include_positives parameter, which can be set to True to also mine for the positive texts. When supplied as documents (which have to be 1. ranked and 2. contain positives) to CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator, the evaluator will not just evaluate the reranking performance of the CrossEncoder, but also the original rankings by the embedding model used for mining.

It has been revealed that note that by default, if you are using CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator with documents, the evaluator will rerank with all positives, even if they are not in the documents. This is useful for getting a stronger signal out of your evaluator, but does give a slightly unrealistic performance. After all, the maximum performance is now 100, whereas normally its bounded by whether the first-stage retriever actually retrieved the positives.

Recent findings suggest that you can enable the realistic behaviour by setting always_rerank_positives=False when initializing CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator. Repeating the same script with this realistic two-stage performance results in::.

The CrossEncoderTrainer is where all previous components come together. We only have to specify the trainer with the model, training arguments (optional), training dataset, evaluation dataset (optional), loss function, evaluator (optional) and we can start training. Let’s have a look at a script where all of these components come together:.

In a recent development, in this example I'm finetuning from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, a base model that is not yet a Cross Encoder model. This generally requires more training data than finetuning an existing reranker model like Alibaba-NLP/gte-multilingual-reranker-base. I'm using 99k query-answer pairs from the GooAQ dataset, after which I mine hard negatives using the sentence-transformers/static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 embedding model. This results in 578k labeled pairs: 99k positive pairs (i.e. label=1) and 479k negative pairs (i.e. label=0).

Industry observers note that I use the BinaryCrossEntropyLoss, which is well suited for these labeled pairs. I also set up 2 forms of evaluation: CrossEncoderNanoBEIREvaluator which evaluates against the NanoBEIR benchmark and CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator which evaluates the performance of reranking the top 30 results from the aforementioned static embedding model. Afterwards, I define a fairly standard set of hyperparameters, including learning rates, warmup ratios, bf16, loading the best model at the end, and some debugging parameters. Lastly, I run the trainer, perform post-training evaluation, and save the model both locally and on the Hugging Face Hub.

After running this script, the tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-base-gooaq-bce model was uploaded for me. See the upcoming Evaluation section with evidence that this model outperformed 13 commonly used open-source alternatives, including much bigger models. I also ran the model with answerdotai/ModernBERT-large as the base model, resulting in tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-large-gooaq-bce.

Evaluation results are automatically stored in the generated model card upon saving a model, alongside the base model, language, license, evaluation results, training & evaluation dataset info, hyperparameters, training logs, and more. Without any effort, your uploaded models should contain all the information that your potential people would need to determine whether your model is suitable for them.

The CrossEncoder trainer supports various transformers.TrainerCallback subclasses, including:.

These are automatically used without you having to specify anything, as long as the required dependency is installed.

Refer to the Transformers Callbacks documentation for more information on these callbacks and how to create your own.

According to recent reports, typically, top-performing general-purpose models are trained on multiple datasets simultaneously. However, this approach can be challenging due to the varying formats of each dataset. Fortunately, the CrossEncoderTrainer allows you to train on multiple datasets without requiring a uniform format. Additionally, it provides the flexibility to apply different loss functions to each dataset. Here are the steps to train with multiple datasets at once:.

Industry observers note that each training/evaluation batch will only contain samples from one of the datasets. The order in which batches are sampled from the multiple datasets is defined by the MultiDatasetBatchSamplers enum, which can be passed to the CrossEncoderTrainingArguments via multi_dataset_batch_sampler. Valid options are:.

Cross Encoder models have their own unique quirks, so here’s some tips to help you out:.

CrossEncoder models overfit rather rapidly, so it’s recommended to use an evaluator like CrossEncoderNanoBEIREvaluator or CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator together with the load_best_model_at_end and metric_for_best_model training arguments to load the model with the best evaluation performance after training.

CrossEncoders are particularly receptive to strong hard negatives (mine_hard_negatives). They teach the model to be very strict, useful e.g. when distinguishing between passages that answer a question or passages that relate to a question.

Don’t underestimate BinaryCrossEntropyLoss, it remains a very strong option despite being simpler than learning-to-rank (LambdaLoss, ListNetLoss) or in-batch negatives (CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, MultipleNegativesRankingLoss) losses, and its data is easy to prepare, especially using mine_hard_negatives.

According to recent reports, I ran a reranking evaluation of my model from the Trainer section against several baselines on the GooAQ development set with both always_rerank_positives=False and with always_rerank_positives=True in the reranking evaluator. These represent the realistic (only rerank what the retriever found) and evaluation (rerank all positives, even if the retriever didn't find it) formats, respectively.

As a reminder, I used the extremely efficient sentence-transformers/static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 static embedding model to retrieve the top 30 for reranking.

Which uses the rerank subset from my tomaarsen/gooaq-reranker-blogpost-datasets dataset. This dataset contains:.

Sources indicate that with just 99k out of 3 million training pairs from the gooaq dataset and just 30 minutes of training on my RTX 3090, my small 150M tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-base-gooaq-bce was able to handily outperform every single <1B parameter general-purpose reranker. The larger tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-large-gooaq-bce took less than an hour to train, and is in a league of its own with a massive 79.42 NDCG@10 in the realistic setting. The GooAQ training and evaluation dataset aligns very well with what these baselines were trained for, so the difference should be even larger when training for a more niche domain.

It has been revealed that note that this does not mean that tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-large-gooaq-bce is the strongest model here on all domains: It's simply the strongest in our domain. This is totally fine, as we just need this reranker to work well on our data.

It has been revealed that don't underestimate the power of finetuning reranker models on your domain. You can improve both the search performance and the latency of your search stack by finetuning a (small) reranker!

This week, a fresh model from DeepSeek silently landed on the Hub. It’s an updated version of DeepSeek-V3, the base model underlying the R1 reasoning model. There isn’t much information shared yet on this new model, but we do know a few things!

The model has the same architecture as the original DeepSeek-V3 and now also comes with an MIT license, while the previous V3 model had a custom model license. The focus of this model release was on improving the instruction following as well as code and math capabilities. Let’s have a look!

The DeepSeek team has evaluated the model on a range of math and coding tasks and we can see the model’s strong capabilities compared to other frontier models:.

Clearly, the model plays in the top league: often on par with GPT-4.5 and generally stronger than Claude-Sonnet-3.7.

To summarise the model has seen significant improvements across benchmarks.

Specifically, in the model card the DeepSeek mentions targeted improvements in the following areas:.

So the question might pop-up: how did they actually do this? Let’s speculate a bit!

Given the naming and architecture it is fairly safe to assume that the newly introduced model is based on the previous V3 model and trained on top of it. There are two possible areas how they improved the models:.

Until the team releases a technical report we don’t know for sure what they tweaked but the post-training pipeline is quite likely and potentially also adding a bit of pretraining. So have a look at how to use the models next!

You can use Hugging Face’s Inference Providers to promptly experiment with this model. It’s available through Fireworks, Hyperbolic, and Novita.

Industry observers note that here’s an example using the huggingface_hub library. You can also use the OpenAI client library like in this example.

According to recent reports, TGI supports running DeepSeek V3-0324 with its latest release as well. You can use it directly with the tagged docker image on a node of H100s.

SGLang supports running DeepSeek V3-0324 out of the box along with the Multi Latent Attention and Data Parallelism optimisations as well. To use you can simply just run the following on a node of H100s. For more information follow along here.

Dynamic Quants from Unsloth and Llama.cpp.

Running large LLMs like DeepSeek V3-0324 can be quite compute intensive and would require a large amount GPU VRAM to run. This is where Quantization comes in, it allows the end user to use the same model but with much lower VRAM consumption with a small trade-off in downstream performance.

Industry observers note that unsloth AI created Dynamic quantisations which allow one to run DeepSeek V3 with half the amount of compute as one node of H100 and can run with llama.cpp without as much degradation in benchmarks. Read more about it here: https://huggingface.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-V3-0324-GGUF.

Running language model safely has always been at the center of attention, ever since the first GPT models have been released. With the immense popularity of the DeepSeek models and their origin the question has found new interest. Let us run down the things that are safe to do and areas where some caution is a good idea. This is not DeepSeek specific but true for any open model!

First of all - is it safe to even download the model?

Sources indicate that yes, downloading the model is safe. There are a few precautions on the Hub side that make sure it’s safe to download and run models:.

Sources indicate that so downloading the weights is safe, and upon code review so is executing the modeling code. This means you can run the DeepSeek model locally without the risk of backdoors or malicious code execution.

According to recent reports, so what would be the main risks outside of downloading and running the model? It depends on what you do with the model outputs!

The advice that follows is not specific to any model, and applies to both open and closed models: whether considering risks stemming from built-in secret behaviours in the model or from a model accidentally producing bad outputs.

We’ll cover risks in three areas: alignment, code generation and agents.

Sources indicate that alignment mismatch: Every model provider chooses how and to which values their models are aligned. What these values are and how they are chosen typically remains opaque and they might also change over time (see this study). The advantage of open models is that the alignment can be changed with custom fine-tuning at a later stage still as the example of Perplexity’s DeepSeek 1776 highlights.

As a rule, customers should be aware that any LLM is biased in one way or another and treat the model outputs accordingly.

Code generation: One of the most popular use-cases of LLMs is as coding assistants. However, this is also where indiscriminate usage of the model outputs can have the most negative effects. Models are trained on vast amounts of published code, latest and old. This typically includes potentially malicious code or code that contains known vulnerabilities. So models might produce similar vulnerabilities when proposing code solutions.

So, how can you prevent security problems when using LLMs for code development? Run thorough code reviews of the proposed changes and scan the code with appropriate tools for vulnerabilities, as you would with any other code contribution.

It has been revealed that agents: In the past few months agent applications have gained significant interest, giving LLMs more autonomy and agency also bears risks. It’s important to be careful about what kind of system access agents have and which information you provide them. Some good practices:.

It has been revealed that TL;DR: Is it safe to run the models? Yes, downloading and running the models is safe, but, as with any model, you should take precautions to use the models generations with the appropriate safety measures.

In a recent development, that’s why it matters even more to use truly free software models, which are free software licenses are promoted by projects like GNU and Free Software Foundation: They allow for inspection by anyone involved in their development or maintenance.With such a model of transparency—where code is Free Software so others may see and change the program it becomes easier to make sure that there aren’t any hidden backdoors lurking inside. 👩‍💻✨.

Industry observers note that one of the most intriguing games of the year is called Tenebrae Lux. It’s a moody, black-and-white title with obtuse puzzles and a main character that constantly narrates to himself with dramatic language. Its credits attribute pretty much everything to a developer named Johannes Zuch. It’s generated a lot of discussion for seemingly mocking games like Jonathan Blow’s The Witness or The Chinese Room’s Dear Esther. It’s also a game that only exists inside of Grand Theft Auto VI.

According to recent reports, developer Rockstar Games has stuffed a lot of satirical media inside of GTA VI, including TV indicates you can watch, books you can read, and radio shows you can listen to. It’s all in service of making the world feel like a funhouse-mirror version of our current reality — Ted Lasso star Jason Sudeikis plays a right-wing radio host, for example. There are more games you can play inside GTA VI in addition to Tenebrae Lux, including a zombie-themed roguelike. But Tenebrae Lux, which you have to see as part of GTA VI’s main story, is the one that has struck a chord, including with indie developers like Sam Barlow and Robert Yang.

“I have to admit it’s kind of funny for the biggest blockbuster game of all time to go after arthouse indie,” Yang tells The Verge, noting that it’s “like a fighter jet getting obsessed with an ant, petty in a funny way.” (Given that GTA VI earned $3.79 billion in its first day, the gulf between Rockstar and indie game studios that are struggling to get by is vast.).

But Yang suggested that Rockstar developers are probably well versed in the types of games they’re lampooning in GTA VI. “I don’t think gamers understand how much indie experimental stuff any decent AAA dev plays,” Yang remarked, pointing out that Rockstar’s environmental artists and level designers “all probably love Dear Esther,” the influential first-person game that helped popularize the “walking sim” concept when it debuted in 2012.

“I was mostly taken with what it meant that the millions of people playing the game were having to sit down and play through an extended gag about indie games,” Barlow tells The Verge. “That made me feel like we were part of larger culture.” He added that he hopes some of these players might “seek out what these arty indie games might be.”.

It has been revealed that rockstar is self-aware enough to use its video games to poke fun at the medium itself. As part of a long conversation between protagonist Jason Duval and his friend Cal Hampton before they start playing Tenebrae Lux, Cal hypes the game by saying that none of it is “just sitting around waiting for people to finish talking.” Initially, you only play Tenebrae Lux for a few minutes, which is enough time to get stumped on the initial puzzles, before the game cuts back to Jason being bored. “Got anything else, a little less, uh… y’know?” he asks. They play the zombie game, titled Street Trash 3 Dezombifier, right after. (You can go back and play the entirety of Tenebrae Lux later if you want.).

It has been revealed that barlow said that the cut “felt very true to the character and story. I gather there is more to the game, but it felt natural to me to hit a wall with the pretentious puzzle design and then move on!”.

Yang also pointed out that from a design perspective, GTA VI has more in common with Tenebrae Lux than Street Trash 3 Dezombifier. GTA VI is “basically a walking sim where you walk around Florida and listen to people talk,” Yang stated. “What’s the difference? Well, just like a billion dollars I guess.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Android’s source code is major – the Android 17 open source release has 1,084 Git repositories, 1.62 million files, and takes 300 GB for a built workspace.
  • Sources indicate that we built Another Build File Service (ABFS) to address these bottlenecks.
  • Today, we are excited to announce that ABFS is open source on GitHub.The impact of ABFS to Android is:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Android’s source code is major – the Android 17 open source release has 1,084 Git repositories, 1.62 million files, and takes 300 GB for a built workspace. Additionally, in a typical Android source tree with hardware vendor code and first-party applications, the size increases by 2-3x. Traditionally, it took over 30 minutes to fetch Android Open Source Project (AOSP) source code and well over an hour to build on even highly capable developer workstations. As software development evolved over the last 2 years, modern coding harnesses and LLMs have accelerated the development of many projects. These tools are used today for Android operating system development, but the long sync and build times make them less efficient. Both human developers and agents need quick setup, parallel workspaces, and fast build-and-test iteration times.

Sources indicate that we built Another Build File Service (ABFS) to address these bottlenecks. ABFS is a full suite of software across a Linux kernel filesystem module, user-space daemons, and server-side infrastructure. ABFS uses content-addressability across the entire stack to lazy-load and cache source code, developer workspaces, intermediate build files, and build results.

Today, we are excited to announce that ABFS is open source on GitHub.The impact of ABFS to Android is:.

ABFS already powers parallel workflows for developers and agents in Android, but it is designed to scale to other massive Git-based projects.

In the Android build system, developers define build rules in Blueprint files (Android.bp), Soong compiles them into Ninja files, and Ninja executes the final build graph (see the Android build overview). Similar to the Make build tool, Ninja is timestamp-based. If a build step’s input file is newer than the existing output file, Ninja rebuilds the output file.

Analyzing the AOSP code for Android 17 shows the sheer disk footprint and file count involved in a single checkout and build.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A newly leaked document purportedly details no less than seven latest Nova Lake-S desktop processors based on C1 stepping qualification samples, including 28-core models, three months before Intel is expected to officially take the wraps off them. The new leak, from VideoCardz, includes an Intel warning that clock speeds and performance may change before the final products are ready to be shipped. But given the fact that this rarely happens when dealing with qualification samples, it's believed that the chips will likely be released just as they are outlined in the document, if the leak is accurate.

Recent findings suggest that of the seven chips that have been detailed, the top-of-the-line Core Ultra 9 4970K BFC will be the one of most interest. It will reportedly feature 28 cores comprising eight performance cores, 16 efficiency cores, and four low-power efficient cores. Its base efficiency core clock speed of 2.7 GHz is eclipsed by the 5.5 GHz boost speed its performance cores will reach, while 144 MB of L3 cache and a 125-watt power rating round out the main figures. According to the leak, it will be joined by a Core Ultra 9 4950K with the same core count and almost identical clock speeds, albeit with a much smaller 36 MB L3 cache. Beyond that, the report says the Core 9 4900 BFC will be locked at 65 watts, have 22 cores, and a 120 MB L3 cache.

If the leak holds up, the mid-range will be catered for by the Core Ultra 7 4870K and 4850K chips. Both will reportedly have a 125-watt power rating and 24 cores, but will again differ in terms of L3 cache — the former will have 144 MB, the latter just 36 MB. Both will boost to 5.2 GHz.

The report notes the entry-level models will include the Core Ultra 5 4650K and 4650KF, both packing 22 cores and 30 MB L3 caches, and that they'll also have the same 125-watt power rating and top out at a boosted 5.1 GHz, according to the documentation.

It has been revealed that the document reportedly states that all seven processors will support DDR5-8000 RAM, an increase over the DDR5-6400 that the Arrow Lake-S chips top out at. The specs also indicate a maximum of 256 GB of RAM is supported, with 24 CPU PCIe lanes and a 77 PTOPS integrated NPU. Integrated graphics are set to range from 2.9 to 3.1 GHz depending on the chosen chip, with support for the DNx, XAVC, JPEG-XS, and VVC decoding all included alongside AV1 High and Professional profile support.

Recent findings suggest that it has previously been reported that Intel is likely to announce its next-gen chips at an event in Berlin, Germany, between February 22 and 25, 2026. But we can also expect that motherboard manufacturers will show off products compatible with the new chips before that — no doubt at the CES 2027 event in Las Vegas in January. It's already been confirmed that new motherboards will be needed if you blueprint on picking up any of the next-gen chips.

Sources indicate that this latest leak comes weeks after it was reported that the new Nova Lake chips would "universally limit the maximum core frequency to 5.1 GHz when above 90°C." However, it's important to remember that the limitation only applies when the chips reach that temperature. Machines with adequate cooling will not experience that limitation, although it remains to be seen how easy these chips are to cool.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hugging Face has become synonymous with advancing AI at scale. With over 4 million builders deploying models on the Hub, the rapid growth of the platform necessitated a rethinking of how sensitive configuration data —secrets— are managed.

According to recent reports, last year, the engineering teams set out to improve the handling of their secrets and credentials. After evaluating tools like HashiCorp Vault, they ultimately chose Infisical.

This case study details their migration to Infisical, explains how they integrated its powerful features, and highlights how it enabled engineers to work more efficiently and securely.

As Hugging Face's infrastructure evolved from an AWS-only setup to a multi-cloud environment that includes Azure and GCP, the engineering team needed a more agile, secure, and centralized way to manage secrets. Instead of reworking legacy systems or adopting heavyweight solutions like HashiCorp Vault, they turned to Infisical due to its developer-friendly workflows, multi-cloud abstraction, and robust security capabilities.

The key challenges they faced were:.

In addition, the team needed a solution that adhered to infrastructure-as-code practices, supported project-by-project secret management, and provided a smooth balance between automation and manual control during deployments.

Infisical’s flexible architecture was an ideal solution. The engineering team seized the opportunity to re-examine their internal project structure, splitting projects into distinct infrastructure and application domains. This allowed them to implement a clearer separation of concerns and standardize secret rotation practices—a priority in the wake of a recent security incident.

In a recent development, by leveraging Terraform, which was previously used to create Kubernetes secrets from AWS configurations, they found the transition to the Infisical Kubernetes Operator exceptionally smooth. This integration enabled security improvements while standardizing secrets management across all environments.

According to recent reports, kubernetes is at the heart of Hugging Face’s production environment, and Infisical's Kubernetes Operator has been instrumental in automating secret updates. The Operator continuously monitors for changes to any secret in Infisical and ensures that these updates are propagated to the corresponding Kubernetes objects. Whenever a change is detected, it can automatically reload dependent Deployments, ensuring that containers always run with the most recent secrets.

According to recent reports, A new secret is required by an application running in Kubernetes. The secret can be created via the Infisical's CLI or the web UI, then the developer creates an InfisicalSecret resource in Kubernetes that specifies which secret from Infisical should be synced:.

Industry observers note that once the CRD is applied, the Infisical Operator continuously watches for updates. When changes are detected in Infisical, the Operator automatically updates the Kubernetes secret (my-app-k8s-secret).

Better yet, since the application's Deployment references my-app-k8s-secret as an environment variable source or mounted volume, the Operator can automatically trigger a container reload when the secret changes.

Sources indicate that in practice, Hugging Face engineers favor waiting for manual redeployments despite the Operator’s ability to automatically trigger container restarts. This decision was driven by the need for precise control over deployments, particularly when high traffic (over 10 million requests per minute) and numerous replicas are involved.

For local development, Infisical’s CLI streamlines workflows by injecting secrets directly into development environments. This removes the need for insecure local .env files, aligning local configurations with production standards and reducing onboarding friction.

Security improvements form the backbone of this migration. By integrating Infisical with existing identity providers such as Okta, Hugging Face established a fine-grained RBAC system. Permissions are automatically mapped from Okta groups, ensuring that developers retain administrative rights over their projects, while frontend and backend teams receive appropriately restricted read or write access.

Additionally, the secret sharing functionality allows secure credentials sharing among ML/AI researchers at Hugging Face. The centralized Infisical platform also simplifies auditing and managing secret rotations—a necessity highlighted by previous security incidents.

Seamless integration with CI/CD pipelines further enhanced the overall security posture. Infisical was embedded into the deployment pipeline via GitHub Actions using OIDC authentication and Terraform integration. By operating self-hosted runners within a secure environment, every deployment adhered to production-grade security standards. This integrated approach minimized risks and ensured a uniform experience from local development to cloud deployment.

Centralizing secrets management with Infisical brought tangible improvements:.

As noted by Adrien Carreira, Head of Infrastructure at Hugging Face,.

"Infisical provided all the functionality and security settings we needed to boost our security posture and save engineering time. Whether you're working locally, running kubernetes clusters in production, or operating secrets within CI/CD pipelines, Infisical has a seamless prebuilt workflow.".

Sources indicate that hugging Face's migration to Infisical demonstrates how a technically driven, engineering-centric approach to managing secrets across multiple cloud platforms delivers significant benefits. For tackling similar challenges, using Infisical is a practical way to work more efficiently while keeping security strong.

#127513. Efficient Request Queueing – Optimizing LLM Performance

Efficient Request Queueing – Optimizing LLM Performance

📅 02 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1666 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Serving LLMs to many applications and people in parallel is challenging because they compete for limited GPU resources.
  • An inference engine like vLLM or HuggingFace TGI consists of.
  • Sources indicate that why do we need a queue here?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Serving LLMs to many applications and people in parallel is challenging because they compete for limited GPU resources. This article is the first in a series on LLM performance, based on our experience with serving self-hosted LLMs at TNG Technology Consulting GmbH. In the first part, we focus on the impact of queuing and discuss different scheduling strategies.

An inference engine like vLLM or HuggingFace TGI consists of.

Sources indicate that why do we need a queue here? Because calculations on the GPU are more performant and resource-efficient when they are done batch-wise instead of isolated for individual requests. This backend queue allows the scheduler to pick multiple requests and put them on the same batch to be processed.

Note that typically each inference engine serves only a single model, and we have multiple deployments running for different models in parallel.

According to recent reports, when a single user "A" sends a large number of requests, they will quickly fill up the queue. Other consumers ("B" and "C") that send their requests only shortly after are blocked from using the same model (until all requests from "A" have been processed). Note that the picture focuses on vLLM as inference engine, but the problem is more general and applies to other backends as well.

It has been revealed that at TNG, users don't send requests directly to the vLLM backend but to an API Server (what we call "LLM-Server"). Here we can have separate queues for each user (and model), and a scheduler that is not FIFO (first in - first out) but goes round-robin through all user queues. This achieves some "fair scheduling": for example, in the diagram users B and C send their request a bit later, when user A's first request has already been scheduled. At that time, three requests from user A had been waiting already for some time, but user C has to wait for only one request from user A to be completed.

The key idea is: prioritize requests from different customers in our own component and not in the inference backend! Typically, you can't change the order of requests once they have been sent to the inference engine, so you have to bring them in the right order while they are still in the LLM-Server, where we have full control.

According to recent reports, you can consider different aspects in order to decide what "fair" scheduling is. In the above example, any fresh user with a single request should be served before any user is served two or more times in a row. This is "fair" on a number-of-requests level. But you could also look at processing time: how long does a request keep the backend busy? Long prompts and long generations will "block" the LLM for other users for a longer time, so maybe shorter requests should have precedence? Unfortunately, it is very difficult to estimate the generation length. While there are some requests with a "max_tokens" limit, a typical chat message from an interactive AI assistant has no token limit, and can vary between a very short generation ("summarize this text") and a very long one ("tell me a story" / "write all code for xyz").

Sources indicate that depending on the prompts, there can be some benefit in arranging requests based on similarity, so that vLLM can maximize cache hits, which speeds up the performance. This kind of KV-cache-aware routing has recently gained attention by frameworks like NVIDIA Dynamo and AIBrix.

In a business context, and for hosted LLMs, the cost of individual requests can be another metric to consider, but comes with similar challenges.

The solution can also be extended by having not only one queue per user (and model) but several queues with different priorities. For example, interactive applications like TNG's AI Assistant with chat interface should have higher priority because users who don't see any progress within five seconds will think the application is broken. Users who generate code reviews for tens of files and several thousand lines of code, however, will expect the LLM requests to take some time. And some use cases (like benchmark runs, scheduled via a batch API) should have such low priority that they don't disturb other use cases and are just scheduled when nothing else is running.

Recent findings suggest that consider again the scenario that one user A sends a lot of requests at once, and some time later a new user C joins and wants to schedule a single request. If the scheduler on LLM-Server side sent every request (according to the fair prioritization) immediately to the backend, all requests from A would accumulate again in the FIFO queue. The new user C would have to wait again until all previously received requests have been processed. There would be almost no improvement to the initial scenario without LLM-Server.

In a recent development, ideally, you could limit the number of maximum elements in the backend queue, but vLLM doesn't give you that option. Therefore, we have to dynamically adjust the rate at which the scheduler on LLM-Server side sends latest requests to the backend. Here, our goal is: keep the backend queue length short in order to minimize latencies experienced by new users.

(The simplest approach would be a static rate limit, but this would likely result in underutilization when most requests are short and hard to calibrate for different models and load patterns).

In order to make the backend queue length available in the LLM-Server, we need to fetch the respective Prometheus metrics from the vLLM /metrics endpoint. Our fair scheduler is only allowed to send requests to the backend as long as the backend queue length metric is smaller than three, for example. This target length for the backend queue can be lowered for an even shorter latency for latest people, until it results in under-utilized batches and a reduced efficiency - there is a trade-off. Keep in mind, though, that the target queue length does NOT reflect maximum concurrency; there can still be more than three requests being processed in parallel; vLLM will add queuing requests to the current batch as soon as there is sufficient space ("continuous batching").

Industry observers note that once you have the feedback loop between backend queue and scheduler in the LLM-Server, you can easily extend the set of vLLM metrics used for making scheduling decisions. For example, for a good user experience in TNG's interactive AI Assistant we aim for a high token generation speed (e.g., >7 tokens/s, that is ~150ms per token), and if the reported time-per-output-token metric rises above 150ms, no new requests will be scheduled.

Sources indicate that you can also program different metric thresholds for different request priorities. For example, for low-priority requests from the batch API we only schedule a request when the backend queue is completely empty: we rather risk short periods of underutilized GPUs than causing increased latencies for any later request with higher priority.

It has been revealed that there is quite some potential for optimizations: for example, if you allow scheduling for a backend length shorter than three and the current metric is zero, you can immediately send three requests to the backend before having to fetch the metrics again. In the worst case, none of them fit into the current batch and all of them are in the backend queue (in which case the latest length is three, just fine).

Recently, vLLM added a priority-based scheduling option instead of sticking with FIFO. For this newly introduced feature, requests are tagged with a priority before they are sent to the backend. And vLLM would regularly check if any higher-priority request is queuing and then sort all requests by priority (both the running batch and the waiting queue). This would not only let the high-priority request literally jump the queue but even move it directly to the processed batch. The price is (aside from some overhead due to sorting) that lower priority requests would be evicted from the running batch and put back in the waiting queue again.

According to recent reports, vLLM understands the request priority as a continuous number. This does not only allow you to distinguish between default, high priority (interactive AI assistant) and low priority (batch API) but you could even make smaller decrements for every request that the user has already sent to the backend and where the response is pending. For example, consumers B and C send only single requests, which will have priority zero. User A sends four requests at once; the first one has priority zero, too, but the next ones will have priorities one, two, and three, and will be processed later (higher number = lower priority).

Overall, backend-side priority scheduling can be a good strategy for vLLM-based systems, because it simplifies queueing logic on the upstream LLM-Server. Unfortunately, in a realistic setting you cannot get rid of the LLM-Server as an additional scheduling layer, since you need some objective instance to assign priorities to individual requests.

Industry observers note that queueing and scheduling are crucial for applications with multiple customers and clients of varying priorities, as they significantly impact the user experience. This is especially true in scenarios where multiple clients submit requests in parallel, benefiting from a dedicated "fair scheduling" strategy. Although backend features like priority scheduling can simplify optimization, an upstream gateway server is still necessary to fully manage these complexities.

In the next part of this blogpost series, we will shift gears and focus on the token generation in the inference engine during prefill and decode phases. In particular, we will discuss resource utilization and strategies for concurrent processing of multiple requests.

Industry observers note that has Disaggregated Prefill been improved in 0.9.1? Many people use 1P and ND mode now.

yes, disaggregated prefill has improved by now, although it still takes some custom work to set it up correctly.The original challenge of multi-user serving with heterogeneous load patterns and priorities remains, though.

For photographers, videographers and content creators, an SD card is more than a storage device. It holds the raw material behind a finished project: wedding photographs, travel footage, product demos and drone recordings that may be impossible to recreate. Data loss can happen at almost any stage of that workflow, from a folder deleted to make space to a card formatted before the footage was backed up.

According to recent reports, this article explains why files on a card become unavailable, what to do in the first minutes, how recovery tools find data, and how to compare options. It includes a small Python example that recovers JPEG files from a disk image, so you can see the mechanism for yourself. It also compares free open-source tools with paid graphical ones, using criteria you can apply yourself. Recovery is never guaranteed, and tool features change, so confirm details against each vendor’s current documentation.

Recovery is not just a matter of finding a deleted filename. Several different problems can make files unavailable, and they call for different approaches.

These steps cannot guarantee recovery, but they reduce avoidable risk.

Most tools combine two methods, and understanding them helps you read scan results.

Carving has a cost. Because file system information is ignored, names and folder structure are usually lost, which is why scan results often show generic names. Fragmented files can also be recovered incomplete, since the tool assumes the pieces are stored one after another. Free tools build on these same ideas. Wondershare Recoverit V15, which also offers a free version for Windows and Mac, adds a graphical interface, while PhotoRec and ddrescue stay closer to the command line.

Industry observers note that the script below is a teaching sketch, not a recovery product. It reads a raw disk image, finds JPEG start markers, and writes out the bytes up to the last end marker before the next start. That detail matters because a JPEG can contain an embedded thumbnail with its own markers, so stopping at the first end marker would cut a file short.

A short test builds two real JPEGs, hides them in random bytes, and checks that both are carved and open as valid images:.

Use it on an image rather than the card itself. On Linux you can make one with a read-only copy, for example with the GNU ddrescue tool, which is designed to copy data from failing media. Then run the carver against the image and save the output to a different drive. Real tools handle many more formats, trim files using header information, and deal with video containers, so treat this as a way to understand the idea.

The right choice depends on the problem, your platform and how comfortable you are with the command line. The table summarizes what each project’s own documentation states.

Graphical tools follow the same logic and mainly change step 3, with thumbnails, filters and search that make large result sets easier to browse. Whether that is worth paying for depends on how many files you need to sift through and how comfortable you are on the command line. When comparing any tool, ask:.

Features such as search by capture time, folder or AI-based tagging depend on metadata surviving the loss, and they narrow results without proving a file is intact. Treat them as convenience, not verification.

Recent findings suggest that recovering a video file does not necessarily mean recovering a playable video. A recording interrupted during writing can lack the structural information a player needs, and other files may be damaged in ways that block playback.

The distinction matters. Recovery retrieves missing or inaccessible data, while repair tries to fix damage that affects a file’s usability. Some cases need one, the other or both. Repair has limits too: if essential video data was overwritten or never recorded, software cannot recreate the original footage in full. After any recovery or repair, play the file all the way through and compare it with what you expect.

#127506. Journey to 1 Million Gradio Users!

📅 04 Apr 2025 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1196 w)
